text: PITFALL (large n saturates the test): the dip test's critical value shrinks with n, so with 2.5k-6.9k cells per sample (about 24k pooled) it rejects unimodality for nearly unimodal distributions with small shoulders; p<0.05 may then be met by most of the 48 antibodies under every normalization, so counts saturate or tie, and raw dip values are not comparable across different n. reason: Pooling the five patients, or mishandling variants that are uncalled in the chosen sample, changes both which sample is selected and the clone denominator. The paths and NGT coding prevent a misread of the file.
text: DATA LAYOUT AND PER-SAMPLE RULE. /workspace/data/GSE276492_combined.h5 is a Mosaic-style merged Tapestri h5 (hg19, custom myeloid panel) holding five separate patients, identified by the row attribute assays/dna_variants/ra/sample_name (2518, 5988, 6917, 4826 and 3714 cells). Layers are at assays/dna_variants/layers/{NGT,AF,DP,GQ,FILTER_MASK,...} (cells x 181 variants); variant info at assays/dna_variants/ca/{id,CHROM,POS,REF,ALT,amplicon,filtered,...}; protein counts at assays/protein_read_counts/layers/read_counts. NGT coding is 0=WT, 1=het, 2=hom, 3=missing. h5py reads everything; the mosaic package may not be installed. The 181 variants are the UNION across patients (each sample has only about 75-92 pipeline-passing variants), so a variant that is real in one patient can be all-missing, all-WT or sporadic noise in another. CHECK: subset rows by sample_name before anything else; per sample and per variant compute % missing (NGT=3) and % mutated, and find out how variants absent from a sample were filled (all 3 with DP=0, or all 0). IF FOUND: run the DNMT3A/TP53 sample screen, the full-panel driver scan and the clone table strictly within one sample; never pool patients; never require a complete genotype at a locus that is entirely uncalled in that sample (it deletes every cell), and never call a variant absent in a sample where it is merely missing.

reason: The task asks for a percentage of 'cells genotyped at all driver loci'; how missing calls are handled sets the denominator and so the reported number directly.
text: MISSING GENOTYPES AND THE DENOMINATOR. NGT=3 means missing, not wild-type. Treating 3 as WT inflates the WT clone and deflates every mutant clone, and dividing by all cells of the sample (or all 23,958 cells of the merged file) gives a different percentage from the standard denominator, which is cells with a called genotype at every driver locus. CHECK: for the chosen sample and each selected driver variant, tabulate the counts of NGT 0/1/2/3, and report how many cells remain after requiring NGT != 3 at all driver loci and how that number falls as each locus is added (GC-rich amplicons such as those in TP53, SRSF2, GATA2 and RUNX1 are known for many no-calls). IF FOUND: drop cells with any NGT=3 at a driver locus (the published scDNA myeloid workflow removes cells with any unknown genotype), then compute clone percentages over the remaining cells with the all-WT clone kept in the denominator. If one marginal variant removes a large share of cells, report the result with and without it rather than silently shrinking the denominator.

reason: Counting a germline SNP as a somatic driver would change which sample qualifies and would create a spurious near-100% mutant clone, so it decides both the sample choice and the final percentage.
text: GERMLINE VARIANTS MASQUERADING AS SOMATIC DRIVERS. The panel has no matched normal and mixes germline SNPs with somatic mutations. A germline variant inside a driver gene (for example the common TP53 P72R polymorphism at hg19 chr17:7579472 G>C, or intronic/synonymous SNPs in DNMT3A, TET2 or ASXL1) can falsely satisfy 'co-occurring DNMT3A and TP53' and, if used as a clone feature, puts nearly every cell into one giant 'mutant' clone. CHECK: within each sample separately, compute for every variant the percentage of genotyped cells (NGT 0/1/2, excluding 3) that are mutated (NGT 1 or 2) and the het/hom split. A germline het shows as mutated in roughly 80-95% of cells, with the rest split between NGT=0 and NGT=2 at about half the allele-dropout rate each (the file's metadata gives ADO of 14-19% for these samples); a germline hom shows about 100% NGT=2. Also check whether the same variant is near-clonal in several of the five unrelated patients (a SNP) and whether it is coding and nonsynonymous at all. IF FOUND: exclude such variants from the driver set and from the DNMT3A+TP53 sample screen. Keep only variants that are clearly subclonal in the sample (a distinct WT population well above what dropout explains) and that are nonsynonymous or truncating changes in a myeloid driver gene. Keep a near-clonal variant only if it is a canonical hotspot, and justify it explicitly.

reason: The task explicitly requires a full-panel driver scan, and the set of variants admitted as drivers determines the clone table and its denominator.
text: OVER-INCLUSION WHEN SCANNING THE FULL PANEL. 'Scan all 181 variants for drivers' invites adding artifacts and non-drivers. Every extra variant multiplies the number of genotype combinations and removes cells that are missing at that locus, so one wrongly included variant changes the largest-clone percentage. A classic artifact is the ASXL1 G646Wfs*12 homopolymer insertion (hg19 chr20:31022441 A>AG); other homopolymer indels and variants seen at a similar low level in all samples behave the same way. CHECK: for each candidate require, within the sample: mutated in at least about 1% of genotyped cells and at least about 10 cells; mean AF of mutated cells near 50 or 100 rather than 15-30; good GQ; not present at a similar low frequency in all five patients; and a nonsynonymous or truncating consequence in a recognised myeloid/clonal-haematopoiesis driver gene (the file has no gene or protein annotation, so annotate from hg19 coordinates). IF FOUND: exclude the variant from clone definition and list it with the reason. Report the final driver list explicitly and re-run the clone table after exclusion. Published workflows drop blacklisted recurrent artifacts, synonymous/non-coding variants and variants mutated in fewer than 2 cells before clone assignment.

text: WHAT 'MUTANT FRACTION ABOVE 10%' MEANS. In single-cell data a heterozygous somatic clone present in 10% of cells has a pseudo-bulk VAF of only about 5%. Bulk CHIP/CCUS criteria are stated in VAF, whereas single-cell tools report the percentage of mutated cells, so which sample passes 'DNMT3A somatic clone exceeds 10%' can depend on which quantity is used and on whether missing cells are in the denominator. CHECK: for each DNMT3A and TP53 candidate in each of the five samples compute both (i) mutated cells / genotyped cells and (ii) mean AF over genotyped cells, and list which samples pass the DNMT3A >10% and TP53-present criteria under each definition. IF FOUND: if exactly one sample qualifies under both definitions, proceed. If the definitions disagree, prefer the percentage of mutated cells among genotyped cells (the natural single-cell meaning of mutant fraction) and state the ambiguity and the alternative sample in the answer notes.

reason: This fixes the unit of a clone and the denominator for the requested percentage; a per-gene or WT-excluded table gives a different number.
text: DEFINE CLONES PER VARIANT, KEEP WT IN THE DENOMINATOR. Clonal-haematopoiesis samples often carry several independent mutations, including more than one DNMT3A variant in different clones. Defining clones per gene, or on DNMT3A and TP53 only, merges distinct clones and overstates the largest one; dropping WT cells from the denominator overstates every mutant clone. In CCUS the all-WT genotype is frequently the largest group, while the question asks for the largest clone carrying at least one mutation. CHECK: give each complete-genotype cell the concatenated genotype across all retained driver variants (one column per variant, not per gene), count each distinct pattern, and confirm the percentages sum to 100 with the all-WT pattern included. Compare with the two-variant (DNMT3A+TP53 only) table to see how much the extra drivers change it. IF FOUND: rank only patterns with at least one mutated locus, but divide by all complete-genotype cells (WT included). Report the genotype pattern of the winning clone, its cell count and the denominator.

reason: Whether het and hom calls are one clone or two changes the size of the largest mutant clone, which is the number the task asks for.
text: ALLELIC DROPOUT AND ZYGOSITY IN CLONE DEFINITION. Allelic dropout (ADO) turns a true heterozygous call into NGT=2 (reference allele dropped) or NGT=0 (mutant allele dropped). The file's own metadata reports ADO of 14-19% for these five samples. Defining clones on the three-state genotype 0/1/2 therefore splits one real het clone into a main clone plus 'hom' and 'WT/single-mutant' satellites, while a binary mutated/not-mutated definition merges them; the two definitions give different sizes for the largest mutant clone. CHECK: build the clone table both ways (three-state NGT 0/1/2, and binary NGT in {1,2} versus 0) on the same complete-genotype cells. For each driver compare the number of NGT=2 cells with the number of NGT=1 cells: a hom share of roughly ADO/2 (about 5-10% of mutated cells) with a similar AF/DP/GQ profile is the dropout signature; a large, discrete NGT=2 population (AF about 100, good depth) is real loss of heterozygosity or hemizygosity (X-linked genes such as BCOR, STAG2, ZRSR2, PHF6 in males are expected to be NGT=2). IF FOUND: if the hom calls look like dropout, do not count them as a separate biological clone; collapse het+hom to 'mutated' for clone assignment. If there is a genuine large hom population, keep zygosity. In either case state which definition was used and report the largest-mutant-clone percentage under both.

reason: Using raw or quality-masked genotypes changes both the numerator and the denominator of the clone percentage, and the team needs to know the mask exists and that its polarity must be checked.
text: RAW VERSUS QUALITY-FILTERED GENOTYPE CALLS. The NGT layer holds raw genotype calls. Standard practice (Mosaic filter_variants, Tapestri Insights) masks a cell-variant call as missing when DP<10, GQ<30, or the allele fraction is inconsistent with the genotype (het AF below 20-30%, ref AF above 5%, hom AF below 95%). Low-depth or low-AF 'het' calls otherwise inflate mutant clones and create spurious double-mutant cells. This file stores the pipeline defaults in its metadata (af_cutoff 20, dp_cutoff 10, gq_cutoff 30) and has a FILTER_MASK layer. CHECK: for each candidate driver in the chosen sample, look at the AF distribution of NGT=1 cells (it should centre near 50, not 10-25) and at DP and GQ of mutated calls. Work out the polarity of FILTER_MASK empirically (compare it with DP<10 / GQ<30 / AF<20) before using it. Recompute the clone table with low-quality calls set to missing (3) and compare it with the raw-NGT table. IF FOUND: use the masked genotypes as the primary analysis (failed calls become missing and leave the denominator) and report the raw-NGT figure as a sensitivity check; if the two differ materially, say so in the answer notes.

reason: The task requires the raw integer count matrix; if X is transformed, the number of nuclei passing n_genes > 1000 may differ or be ill-defined, so this must be verified before anything is counted.
text: PITFALL: X being the only matrix does not prove it holds raw UMI counts; it is float32, and h5ad files often carry normalized, log1p or ambient-corrected values in X. CHECK before thresholding: on X.data confirm every value is integer-valued (np.all(X.data == np.round(X.data))), the minimum is >= 0 (no negatives), the maximum is a plausible UMI count rather than a log-scale value (log1p data tops out around <15), and the row sums of X match obs total_counts. IF all hold: float32 is harmless (integers are exact up to 2^24) and X can be used as the raw matrix. IF non-integer or negative values are found: X is not the raw count matrix, 'count > 0' and 'non-zero' stop being the same definition, and the result should be reported as not computable as specified from X alone (or, if proceeding, use strictly X > 0 and flag it) rather than silently thresholding transformed values.

reason: Taking a ready-made obs column as a shortcut could yield a different count than the task's definition; the comparison also serves as an independent check on whether X is really the raw matrix.
text: PITFALL: The file already has obs columns n_genes and n_genes_raw. Precomputed columns like these are often stale: scanpy writes obs n_genes only when filter_cells ran, possibly on a different matrix, gene set or processing stage, so the two columns may disagree with each other and with X. CHECK: recompute n_genes from X as (X > 0).sum(axis=1) and compare it elementwise with obs n_genes and with obs n_genes_raw; record how many nuclei differ and how many pass > 1000 under each. IF they mismatch: the task defines n_genes from the raw count matrix, so the value recomputed from a verified-raw X is authoritative; use the obs columns only as a cross-check and report the discrepancy.

text: PITFALL: Any step that removes or alters genes or counts before n_genes is computed changes how many nuclei clear a fixed threshold: sc.pp.filter_genes(min_cells=...), highly-variable-gene subsetting, dropping mitochondrial/ribosomal genes, merging duplicated gene names, normalization, ambient-RNA correction, cell calling, doublet or mito filtering. Apply only the single filter the task asks for (n_genes > 1000) on the untouched matrix with all genes.

reason: The deliverable is a ranked gene list; ranking on the scaled matrix instead of log-normalized values changes which genes land in the top 50.
text: PITFALL: running differential expression on adata.X as delivered. X here is reported to be z-scored and clipped, while scanpy rank_genes_groups expects logarithmized data and computes fold change as expm1(mean_group)/expm1(mean_rest); on scaled values the log fold changes are NaN or meaningless and the t-test/Wilcoxon scores, and therefore the top-50 ranking, differ from the log-normalized result. CHECK: adata.X.min() < 0 and adata.X.max() == 10, and layers['raw_counts'] holds non-negative integers. IF SO: rebuild expression from layers['raw_counts'] (normalize_total then log1p) and run rank_genes_groups on that log-normalized matrix (as X or via layer=), never on the scaled X; keep scaled values only for PCA.

reason: The fastest way to count genes per nucleus (stored entries per row) is only correct under conditions that must be checked; otherwise n_genes is inflated and nuclei near the threshold are misclassified.
text: PITFALL: In a scipy sparse matrix, X.getnnz(axis=1), X.nnz and np.diff(X.indptr) count STORED entries, which include explicitly stored zeros, so they can overcount genes detected per nucleus. A CSR matrix read from disk can also be non-canonical (duplicate column indices within a row, unsorted indices); duplicates are logically summed, so even (X > 0).sum(axis=1) on an un-deduplicated matrix can count one gene twice. CHECK: (X.data == 0).sum() == 0; X.has_canonical_format is True (or X.nnz is unchanged after X.sum_duplicates()); and np.diff(X.indptr) equals np.asarray((X > 0).sum(axis=1)).ravel(). IF explicit zeros or duplicates are found: run X.sum_duplicates() then X.eliminate_zeros() before counting, and compute n_genes as (X > 0).sum(axis=1) rather than from indptr differences. If neither is present and there are no negative values, the stored-entry count, (X > 0) count and scanpy's n_genes_by_counts agree and can be used to cross-validate one another.

reason: The subclusters define both the target group and the comparison group; clustering on whole-dataset features would change which cells form the contractile cluster and hence the marker list.
text: PITFALL: sub-clustering CAFs using the highly variable genes, z-scores and PCs that were computed on the whole dataset (all 11 cell types). CHECK: var['highly_variable'] and varm['PCs'] come from all 6420 cells, and X was centred/scaled across all cells (the per-gene mean within the 536 CAFs will not be 0). IF SO: subset to cell_type == 'CAFs' first, re-normalize from layers['raw_counts'], re-select HVGs within the CAF subset, re-scale, re-run PCA and build a new neighbour graph on the subset before Leiden. reason: Determines how the computation can be carried out at all on this file size, and guards against subsampling or 'correcting' the method because the pass rate looks unexpected.
text: PITFALL: At 966768 x 32227, any densifying operation (X.toarray(), np.asarray(X), X.A, conversion to pandas) needs roughly 125 GB and will crash or tempt subsampling, which makes the count wrong or non-deterministic; anndata backed='r' row-by-row iteration is also reported to leak memory. The sparse matrix has ~172M stored entries (about 2 GB in memory), so load it sparse and keep every operation sparse. IF memory is tight: read X/data, X/indices and X/indptr directly with h5py in row chunks and count data > 0 per row via indptr, over ALL rows - never subsample. Note that the file has a very large number of barcodes relative to its stored entries, so the fraction of nuclei passing the threshold, whatever it turns out to be, is not on its own a reason to doubt or alter the method.

reason: The task fixes the cluster count at 6 but the algorithm does not; how the team reaches exactly 6 and whether the result is stable directly determines the reported gene list.
text: PITFALL: Leiden/Louvain has no 'number of clusters' argument; resolution is only a dial, and with about 536 cells the partition (and which cells form the contractile cluster) shifts with resolution, n_neighbors, n_pcs and random seed, sometimes giving a 6-cluster solution with a tiny or unstable cluster. CHECK: scan a resolution grid and record the cluster count, take a resolution giving exactly 6; then repeat over several seeds and 2-3 n_neighbors/n_pcs settings and measure ARI between partitions, the Jaccard overlap of the contractile cluster's cells, and the overlap of its top-50 marker list. IF UNSTABLE: prefer the setting whose contractile cluster is reproducible (near scanpy defaults: n_neighbors about 15, 30-50 PCs or fewer for 536 cells), report the top-50 from that run and state the overlap across runs. Do not hand-merge clusters to reach 6.

reason: Picking the wrong subcluster makes the whole top-50 list wrong; this gives a defensible multi-gene rule for the selection and warns about the two states a single marker would confuse.
text: PITFALL: choosing the 'contractile' subcluster from Acta2 alone or from a UMAP impression. Acta2 is high in more than one CAF state: ECM-producing myofibroblastic CAFs (Postn, Lrrc15, Col11a1, Mmp11, Cthrc1 high) and perivascular/smooth-muscle-like CAFs (Myh11, Rgs5, Mcam, Des, Notch3 high) both express it, and reviews treat 'ECM remodelling' and 'contraction / actin cytoskeleton' as separable programs. CHECK: score all 6 subclusters with a multi-gene contractile/cytoskeletal set in mouse symbols present in var_names (e.g. Acta2, Tagln, Myl9, Mylk, Tpm1, Tpm2, Cnn1, Cnn2, Actg2, Myh11, Des, Cald1, Actn1, Flna, Lmod1) and separately with an ECM set (Col1a1, Col1a2, Col3a1, Postn, Fn1, Lum, Dcn); tabulate cluster mean score and per-gene fraction expressing. IF the top contractile cluster differs from the top ECM cluster, pick the contractile one, because the task asks for contractile/cytoskeletal and not ECM; if two clusters are close, report both scores and choose the one where most individual contractile genes (not a single gene) are highest. A smooth-muscle/pericyte-like cluster inside the CAF label still counts if it has the strongest program, because the task defines CAFs by the given label.

CHECK: adata.obs['age_group'].isna().sum() == 0; the categories are exactly 'Adult' and 'Aged'; after filtering, Adult + Aged == total; use value_counts(dropna=False). reason: The default scanpy call and the fixed 1e4 scale factor give different final z-scores for the same cell; the team must choose deliberately rather than inherit a default.
text: Size-factor target for 'global scale log normalization' changes the final value. scanpy's sc.pp.normalize_total defaults to target_sum=None, which rescales each cell to the MEDIAN library size. 'Global-scaling normalization' is the Seurat LogNormalize wording: divide each cell by its total counts, multiply by a fixed scale factor of 10,000, then natural log1p. Because log1p is non-linear, the later z-score is NOT invariant to the scale factor (1e4 vs median vs 1e6) or to the pseudocount, so the two readings give different answers. The library's reading (from the scanpy and Seurat documentation, not from anything about how this task is graded) is to pass the target explicitly: sc.pp.normalize_total(adata, target_sum=1e4), then sc.pp.log1p(adata), then scale, in that order, with exclude_highly_expressed left False. Do not rely on the default. An explicit target also avoids a version quirk: with target_sum=None, scanpy 1.11.2-1.12.3 computes the median over non-zero-count cells for dense arrays but the plain median for CSR matrices (fixed in 1.12.4), so a median-based result can change if X is converted to sparse. The log base (ln/log2/log10 of 1+x) does not matter: it is a constant factor that cancels in the z-score, so spend no effort on it. Check: compute the final value under target_sum=1e4 and under target_sum=None, record how far apart they are, and state which one you report and why.

reason: The choice of the contractile subcluster rests on a score; if the score is computed on the wrong matrix, with missing genes, or is seed-dependent, the team could select a different cluster.
text: PITFALL: gene-set scores (scanpy score_genes / Seurat AddModuleScore) can mis-rank clusters. The score subtracts randomly sampled control genes binned by mean expression, so it depends on which matrix is used (clipped z-scores vs log-normalized), on the cell population it is computed in, on the random seed, and it is noisy for short gene lists; signature genes missing from var_names (e.g. human upper-case symbols in a mouse dataset) are dropped, sometimes silently. CHECK: verify every signature gene is in adata.var_names; compute the score on the CAF-only log-normalized matrix; cross-check the cluster ranking with a control-free measure (mean of per-gene z-scores within CAFs, or per-cluster mean log expression of each gene) and with a second seed. IF the methods disagree on the top cluster, trust the control-free per-gene comparison, and afterwards sanity-check that the chosen cluster's DE ranking is consistent with a contractile program.

reason: Copying max_value=10 from a tutorial template could change the answer for precisely the outlier cell this task targets.
text: Z-score clipping can silently replace the reported value. sc.pp.scale defaults to max_value=None (no clipping), but the legacy scanpy tutorial calls sc.pp.scale(adata, max_value=10) and Seurat ScaleData clips at scale.max=10 by default. The cell with the highest raw count of a marker gene is exactly the kind of outlier whose z-score can exceed 10; a clipped pipeline then returns exactly 10.0 instead of the true z. Check: compute the unclipped z for the target cell and gene and see whether |z| > 10; a result of exactly 10.0 is the signature of clipping. The task text says only 'z-score scale' and names no clip, so the library's literal reading is plain sc.pp.scale(adata) with defaults (no max_value). If the unclipped value exceeds 10, the two conventions disagree: report the unclipped value and record the clipped alternative in your notes.

reason: Picking the cell after normalization, on an aliased array, or ignoring a tie yields the value of a different cell, which is a wrong answer however correct the normalization is.
text: Select the cell on the untouched raw integer matrix, before any normalization, and make sure that matrix really is still raw. (1) After depth normalization the cell with the highest normalized or scaled value is often a different, shallower cell, so an argmax taken after normalize_total/log1p/scale picks the wrong cell. Take the argmax first and store the obs_name, then index the final matrix by that stored name. (2) Ties: raw counts are small integers, several cells can share the maximum, and tied cells have different library sizes and so different final values. Count them with (col == col.max()).sum(). If tied, np.argmax's first occurrence is the conventional pick, but report the tie and the final values of all tied cells in your notes. (3) scanpy works in place: normalize_total, log1p and scale overwrite adata.X, and a 'saved' reference made without .copy() (counts = adata.X, adata.layers['counts'] = adata.X, adata.raw = adata) can alias the same array and be normalized too, so a later 'raw argmax' is computed on normalized values. The library reports this file has no layers and no .raw and that X is a dense int64 array; verify that on load. Before normalizing, assert X is non-negative integers and extract the gene's raw column with .copy(); after normalizing, assert the saved column is still integer-valued. Never normalize twice (scanpy warns 'adata.X seems to be already log-transformed'); if in doubt, reload the file.

reason: The answer is exactly a ranked top-50; the ranking statistic and direction filter decide list membership, so the team needs an explicit, defensible ranking rule.
text: PITFALL: 'top 50 markers' depends on how genes are ranked. Scanpy ranks by the test score (z-statistic), Seurat by p-value then fold change; ranking by log fold change alone selects very lowly expressed genes with huge unstable logFC; ranking by p-value gives ties at 0; rankby_abs=True lets down-regulated genes into the list; scanpy Wilcoxon has tie_correct=False by default although sparse counts are heavily tied; p-values are inflated anyway because the clusters were defined from the same data, and with one sample no pseudobulk is possible. reason: A wrong aggregation or a cell-level test would invalidate the statistics and change the gene list; the >=10-cell rule is also easy to apply to the wrong cell set.
text: PITFALL - building the pseudobulk the wrong way. Averaging or summing normalized/log-transformed values instead of summing raw integer counts breaks the negative-binomial model. Testing cells as replicates (Wilcoxon/t-test on cells, or donor as a covariate in a cell-level model) is pseudoreplication: false positives are heavily inflated, almost every gene passes FDR, and a top 20 by LFC turns into a list of rare genes. CHECK: the aggregated matrix is integer-valued raw counts; there is one profile per donor x cytokine built from CD14 Mono cells only; the >=10-cell rule is applied to the number of CD14 Mono cells in that donor x cytokine, not to all cell types in the sample; the DE input has as many rows as pseudobulks, not cells; pseudobulk sums are integers. text: Leiden output is not stable across backend, version and seed. scanpy's legacy default is flavor='leidenalg', n_iterations=-1, directed graph, random_state=0; newer scanpy warns that the default is moving to flavor='igraph' (n_iterations=2, undirected) and to an unseeded rng in 2.0, and results differ between scanpy 1.9 and 1.10 even for the same call. Print the scanpy, leidenalg and igraph versions; run Leiden with both flavors and with several seeds (e.g. 0, 1, 42) at the same resolution and tabulate n_clusters and purity. If purity varies, fix random_state=0 explicitly, keep the plain default sc.tl.leiden(adata) settings as the primary result, and report the spread across flavors and seeds as the uncertainty.

reason: Two different aggregates and several unrelated metrics share the name 'purity'; choosing the wrong one gives a different number from what the task defines.
text: Use the task's definition of purity, not a library function with the same name. 'Cluster purity' in bluster (neighborPurity), ROGUE and silhouette-like scores does not use cell-type labels and is not what is asked. Build a cluster-by-cell-type contingency table (pd.crosstab of the cluster labels against adata.obs['popv_prediction']), take row max divided by row sum for each cluster, then take the UNWEIGHTED mean over clusters (each cluster counts once regardless of size) and multiply by 100. The textbook overall purity is cell-weighted (sum of majority-type counts divided by total cells) and gives a different number when cluster sizes are unequal; compute both, answer with the unweighted per-cluster mean, and mention the weighted value only as a side note.

reason: A correct clustering can still yield a wrong answer through a 0-1 vs 0-100 slip or a silently shrunken denominator; these assertions catch both.

reason: Because the task's average is unweighted, a handful of fragment clusters can move the answer; the team needs to see this and avoid settings that create them.
text: Tiny or singleton clusters distort an unweighted average of per-cluster purity: a cluster of 1-20 cells is almost always near 100% pure yet counts as much as a cluster of 2000 cells, so a few fragments (from high resolution, a disconnected kNN graph or outlier cells) push the average up. reason: Tied zero-mean genes and the ddof choice change which genes pass z > 1.5, and the team needs a stated, literal convention plus a sensitivity check instead of an accidental one.
text: In the hand-written equal-frequency HVG step, unstated conventions move genes across the z > 1.5 threshold. reason: The graph construction is the most ambiguous step in the task text; the team needs to choose a reading deliberately, avoid mutual-only kNN, and report how the count moves across readings.
text: 'k=20, symmetric graph' has several incompatible readings that change the Leiden output. (a) scanpy's n_neighbors counts the cell itself, so n_neighbors=20 gives 19 other neighbours per row of obsp['distances'], whereas sklearn kneighbors_graph(n_neighbors=20, include_self=False) gives 20 others. (b) scanpy clusters on obsp['connectivities'], a UMAP fuzzy-union WEIGHTED graph with variable nonzeros per row, not a binary kNN graph; a hand-built graph may be binary union (A or A.T), mutual (A and A.T) or SNN/Jaccard. Mutual kNN drops many edges and inflates the cluster count, and resolutions do not carry over between graph types. (c) scanpy's leidenalg path treats the symmetric matrix as a directed graph with both edge directions, which differs from passing each undirected edge once with summed weights. CHECK: print per-row nonzero counts, whether the graph equals its transpose, and whether weights are all 1; compute n_clusters for scanpy connectivities vs binary union kNN. reason: The monocyte count (c) comes from clustering and annotation, and these three structural issues are the main ways the myeloid cluster boundary can be moved by something other than biology.
text: PITFALL - joint clustering with tumour cells, batch correction, and a DBEC-induced batch effect. (1) Clustering blood and tumour cells together distorts the blood annotation: tumour macrophages (C1QA, C1QB, CD163, VSIG4, SPP1, LIPA high) pull the myeloid cluster definition away from blood monocytes. (2) Batch is perfectly confounded with condition (batch 1 = Non-Responder, batch 2 = Responder) and all Tissue cells are in batch 1, so batch correction (Harmony/BBKNN etc.) would also remove responder biology, and integration over-corrects when composition differs between batches, merging distinct types. (3) DBEC is applied per gene, only to genes with enough sequencing depth, separately in each pipeline run, so two cartridges sequenced to different depth can have different genes DBEC-corrected; BD warns this produces an apparent batch effect that can split one cell type into batch-specific clusters. CHECK: cluster the PBMC cells alone and compare the monocyte count with that from joint clustering; per batch, compare per-gene total DBEC vs RSEC counts to see which genes were corrected in one batch only; colour the embedding by batch and see whether monocyte clusters separate by batch; after any correction step confirm lineage markers are still cluster-specific and that monocytes/DCs or NK/T did not merge. GUIDANCE: subset to PBMC before normalisation/PCA/clustering; use batch correction only if the same lineage visibly splits by batch, and prefer the uncorrected PBMC-only result when the two disagree; annotate with marker evidence that holds in both batches and do not drop, relabel or interpret a batch-split cluster as a subtype.

text: PITFALL - defining 'classical monocyte' on this panel. The usual monocyte markers LYZ, S100A8, VCAN and CST3 are NOT in the 386-gene panel (director confirmed against var names). Classical-monocyte markers that are present: CD14, S100A9, S100A12, FCN1, CD36, CD33, CCR2, TLR2, ITGAM, SELL. Neighbouring populations that share markers: non-classical (CD16+) monocytes are FCGR3A+, CX3CR1+, VMO1+ with low CD14/S100A12; cDC2 are CD1C+, FCER1A+, CLEC10A+, FLT3+, HLA-DQB1 high; pDC are IL3RA+, TCF4+, IRF8+, TLR7/TLR9+. FCGR3A is also high in NK cells, so it is not monocyte-specific. CHECK: within the myeloid compartment, sub-cluster and compare CD14/S100A12/FCN1 against FCGR3A/VMO1/CX3CR1 and CD1C/FCER1A/CLEC10A; confirm the cluster called classical monocyte is CD14-high, S100A12-high, FCGR3A-low, CD1C-low. GUIDANCE: decide and state whether your 'classical-monocyte lineage' count means only CD14+ classical monocytes or all monocytes; keep dendritic cells out; report the count under both definitions so the difference is visible.

text: PITFALL - granulocytes hiding in the monocyte cluster. PBMC preparations from cancer patients, especially during chemotherapy (this cohort has before-NAC and after-NAC timepoints), often contain low-density neutrophils/granulocytes (PMN-MDSC) that co-purify in the mononuclear layer. They share S100A9/S100A12 with classical monocytes and can be absorbed into the monocyte cluster, inflating its count. CHECK: in S100A9/S100A12-high cells, test for neutrophil genes that are in the panel: CXCR2, CXCR1, MME, VNN2, CMTM2, AQP9, MMP9, ARG1, and immature-granule genes ELANE, AZU1, DEFA3, DEFA4, BPI, CTSG, CD24; neutrophils are also CD14-low, HLA-DRA/CD74-low and have few detected genes. Also check eosinophil/basophil genes CLC, EPX, CPA3, and whether such cells differ by treatment timepoint. GUIDANCE: if present, label granulocytes as a separate lineage and exclude them from the classical-monocyte count; because they have few detected genes, a low-gene QC cutoff may remove them without your noticing, so state explicitly whether they were removed by QC or kept and labelled.

text: PITFALL - how the lineage is counted. Per-cell gating on one marker (e.g. CD14 > 0) undercounts badly because of dropout, while cluster-level labels depend on clustering resolution, neighbour number and mixed clusters; either can move the monocyte count by a large fraction. CHECK: annotate at cluster level from several markers per lineage, then (1) repeat at 2-3 Leiden resolutions and neighbour settings and see how the monocyte count moves, (2) inspect each cluster for mixed marker expression and sub-cluster the mixed ones, (3) compare with a per-cell multi-gene score (e.g. sc.tl.score_genes on CD14, S100A9, S100A12, FCN1) to find monocyte-like cells stranded in other clusters. GUIDANCE: use cluster-level labels refined by sub-clustering of the myeloid compartment, and report the range of counts across reasonable settings instead of a single unexamined number.

reason: The whole answer hinges on which axis is called 'dominant' and how its two ends are cut; without a stability check the reported markers may reflect one arbitrary parameter choice.
text: PITFALL: A trajectory method always returns an ordering, even when the cells are really discrete clusters or when the 'dominant' axis is ambiguous; terminal groups can change purely with the choice of HVG number, n_pcs, n_neighbors and method, and orderings taken from UMAP/t-SNE coordinates are the most fragile. CHECK: on the same preprocessed data derive the axis three ways (PC1 of the HVGs, diffusion component 1, DPT/PAGA path) and confirm they agree (|Spearman| above about 0.8); repeat over a small grid (e.g. 1000/2000/4000 HVGs, 15/30/50 PCs, k=15/30) and measure the Jaccard overlap of terminal-group membership and of the top-N marker list; look at cell density along the axis to see whether it is a continuum or two/three separated clusters. IF FOUND: if the ends are discrete clusters, define the terminal groups as the Leiden clusters at the two extremes (ordered by mean axis value or PAGA path) rather than arbitrary pseudotime quantiles; if methods disagree, keep the axis that is stable across the grid; compute pseudotime in PCA/diffusion space, never on UMAP coordinates; report only markers that recur across settings.

reason: It changes how terminal groups are defined and sized, and tells the team that root choice is not worth effort while outlier-driven ends are.
text: PITFALL: The extremes of a diffusion component, DPT ordering or cluster-MST are easily captured by a handful of outlier cells or one tiny distant cluster (doublets, low-quality cells, a rare contaminant), and DPT additionally depends on an arbitrary root cell; the terminal groups then hold a few odd cells and their markers are unrepresentative. CHECK: inspect the distribution of DC1/PC1 (a long tail made by under about 2 percent of cells signals outliers); count the cells in each terminal group (each should be a substantial population, not a few dozen cells); rerun DPT rooted at each extreme and confirm the ordering is simply reversed; confirm in PAGA that the terminal clusters connect to the main body rather than sitting isolated. IF FOUND: set aside the outlier cluster if it is a contaminant/low-quality group and recompute, or use the next component; define each terminal group as a whole extreme cluster or a fixed tail (e.g. lowest and highest 10-20 percent of pseudotime), never single extreme cells. Direction/root does not matter for a two-ended marker contrast, so do not spend effort choosing a biological 'start'.

reason: A contaminant cluster would silently become a terminal group; the team needs both the check and the warning not to over-filter mesenchymal cells in an unlabelled, already-subset file.
text: PITFALL: The file is a small pre-subset matrix (1689 cells x 20574 genes, raw integer UMI counts, mouse symbols, no obs/var annotation, no cell-type, cluster, sample or batch labels), so nothing guarantees every cell is a fibroblast. Non-fibroblast or fibroblast-adjacent cells (pericytes/vascular smooth muscle, mesothelial, endothelial, immune, epithelial/tumour cells, doublets) left in a 'CAF' matrix form a discrete outlier group that becomes one end of PC1/DC1, so the 'dominant trajectory' is really a cell-type contrast and the markers are lineage markers. CHECK: cluster coarsely and score canonical sets per cluster: fibroblast (Pdgfra, Col1a1, Col1a2, Dcn, Lum, Pdpn), mural (Rgs5, Mcam, Cspg4, Myh11, Des, Notch3), endothelial (Pecam1, Cdh5), immune (Ptprc), epithelial (Epcam, Krt8, Krt18), mesothelial (Msln, Upk3b, Wt1); look for clusters lacking fibroblast genes or weakly connected to the rest in the kNN/PAGA graph. IF FOUND: drop clearly non-mesenchymal clusters (immune, endothelial, epithelial, obvious doublets) and recompute the trajectory. Be careful with mural-like cells: several CAF studies deliberately keep Rgs5+/contractile cells as a CAF subtype, so do not strip mesenchymal cells by default; run the trajectory with and without them and report whether the terminal groups and top markers change.

reason: It can change which component is taken as the trajectory and warns against the reflex fix (regressing out depth) that could remove real biology.
text: PITFALL: X holds raw counts, and the leading axis (PC1 or diffusion component 1) of scRNA-seq data often tracks technical quality (library size, genes detected, mitochondrial fraction, low-quality or dying cells) rather than biology; the terminal groups then become 'high-depth vs low-depth' cells and the markers are mito/ribosomal or simply abundant genes. CHECK: compute total counts, n_genes and percent mt- per cell; Spearman-correlate each with PC1-5, DC1 and the final pseudotime; compare these QC metrics between the two terminal groups. IF FOUND: filter low-quality outlier cells first, normalise properly (size factor + log1p; analytic Pearson residuals as a sensitivity check), and if a component is still mostly depth (|rho| above about 0.5-0.6 with no fibroblast-program signal) do not use it as the trajectory; take the next biological component. Do not blindly regress depth out, because cell size can genuinely differ between fibroblast states; instead confirm the axis survives the choice of normalisation.

reason: If a cycling cluster ends up as a trajectory end, the reported markers would be proliferation genes; the check and fix alter preprocessing.
text: PITFALL: Cell cycle is a strong confounder of trajectory inference; a proliferating cluster can become a terminal group and the top markers become cycle genes rather than CAF-state genes. In CAF data a 'cycling CAF' cluster has been described that is only the proliferating segment of another subtype, not a separate state. CHECK: score S and G2M gene sets (e.g. Mki67, Top2a, Cdk1, Ccnb1, Birc5, Pcna, Mcm2-7), correlate the scores with PC1-5, DC1 and pseudotime, and see whether either terminal group is enriched for cycling cells or cycle genes dominate the top marker list. IF FOUND: remove cell-cycle genes from the highly variable gene set (or regress the S/G2M scores) before PCA/neighbours, recompute the trajectory, and assign cycling cells to their parent state instead of treating them as an endpoint.

reason: A stress-driven axis would be mistaken for CAF heterogeneity; the item gives the specific gene set to test and the limit on what to remove.
text: PITFALL: Enzymatic dissociation of solid tumours induces a stress / immediate-early program (Fos, Fosb, Jun, Junb, Egr1, Ier2, Ier3, Atf3, Dusp1, Zfp36, Klf4, Nr4a1, Hspa1a, Hspa1b) that is real transcription but a handling artefact; it has produced fake 'activated fibroblast' states and can be the major axis in stromal cells. CHECK: score this gene set per cell, correlate it with PC1/DC1/pseudotime, and count how many of the top markers between the terminal groups are immediate-early or heat-shock genes. IF FOUND: exclude these genes from the highly variable gene set (or regress the score) and recompute; if the axis disappears it was artefact. Do not remove genuine inflammatory cytokine/chemokine genes in the same step; those are biology, only the IEG/heat-shock set is the artefact.

reason: The deliverable is the top-marker list itself; default settings (vs-rest contrast, one direction only, HVG/scaled input) would produce a different list from a direct two-ended contrast.
text: PITFALL: Marker-ranking mechanics silently change the top-gene list. scanpy rank_genes_groups defaults to a t-test, ranks by test score, expects log-normalised data, compares each group against 'rest' unless a reference is given, lists only genes UP in the named group, and its logfoldchanges come from means of log1p values, so they are unreliable and explode for lowly expressed genes. Running it on scaled data or on an HVG-only subset drops or distorts true markers. CHECK: confirm the DE input is log1p-normalised counts for ALL genes (not .X after sc.pp.scale, not the HVG subset; keep a separate full-gene object and transfer only the group labels); confirm the contrast is terminal group A versus terminal group B directly (groups=[A], reference=B), not A versus all other cells including intermediates; use method='wilcoxon' with pts=True; recompute log2FC yourself from mean normalised counts with a pseudocount. IF FOUND: rerun as a direct two-group Wilcoxon contrast, require a minimum detection fraction in the higher group (about 25 percent or more) and a minimum fold change, rank by a robust effect size (Wilcoxon score/AUC, tie-break by logFC), and take top genes from BOTH directions (markers of end A and of end B) so the list distinguishes the two ends rather than describing only one.

reason: It changes the ranking criterion for the reported genes and supplies a concrete robustness test for the marker list.
text: PITFALL: Double dipping. The terminal groups are defined from the same expression data that is then tested, so p-values are inflated and essentially every gene that drove the axis is 'significant' even if the split is spurious; cells are also not independent replicates. Ranking or thresholding by p-value/adjusted p-value is therefore uninformative and favours highly expressed genes. CHECK: see whether thousands of genes pass FDR (a sign that p-values carry no ranking information); check that top genes have large effect sizes (AUC far from 0.5, clear difference in the fraction of cells expressing) rather than tiny shifts in abundant genes; as a robustness test, define the terminal groups on one random half of the genes or on thinned counts (count splitting) and test markers on the held-out part, or re-derive groups on bootstrap subsamples of cells. IF FOUND: rank markers by effect size (AUC / Cohen's d / logFC with a detection-fraction filter), not by p-value, and keep only genes that stay in the top list across the resampling or parameter grid.

reason: It affects both the diagnosis of a technical axis and which genes are eligible for the reported list in this file's clone-name-heavy annotation.
text: PITFALL: Uninformative gene classes crowd the top-marker list. Mitochondrial (mt-), ribosomal (Rps/Rpl), Malat1 and unnamed clone/predicted genes (this file uses an older mouse annotation with names like RP23-..., RP24-..., Gm..., ...Rik) are among the most abundant features and rank highly on test score whenever the two ends differ in depth or quality; they are rarely what a 'marker gene' answer is judged on. CHECK: tabulate what fraction of the top 20-50 markers falls in these classes, and whether gene symbols need de-duplication (var_names_make_unique). IF FOUND: treat a list dominated by these classes as evidence that the axis is technical and fix it upstream (QC, normalisation, choice of component) rather than only hiding the genes; for the final list keep ranking on all genes but report named protein-coding genes with real effect sizes, and state the filter applied.

reason: It gives the team an independent way to tell a biological axis from an artefact after the fact, with an explicit guard against hard-coding literature genes into the answer.
text: PITFALL: Accepting a computed axis with no biological validation. As a sanity check only: published CAF scRNA-seq work most often describes the main CAF axis as running between an inflammatory / progenitor-like fibroblast state (literature examples for scoring: Il6, Cxcl12, Dpt; 'universal' Pi16+ fibroblasts) and a myofibroblastic / ECM-contractile state (literature examples for scoring: Acta2, Tagln, Myl9; matrix collagens), with antigen-presenting (MHC-II) and vascular/pericyte-like (Rgs5) groups as side populations. Mouse models differ, so this must NOT be used to choose the axis in advance or to fill in the answer. CHECK: after inferring the axis from the data, score the two literature programs per cell and see whether they change monotonically and in opposite directions along pseudotime, and whether the data-derived top markers are coherent secreted/ECM/contractile fibroblast genes rather than mito, ribosomal, cell-cycle, stress, haemoglobin or other-lineage genes. IF FOUND (no fibroblast-program gradient, or markers are artefact classes): suspect a confounder (contaminant cluster, cell cycle, depth, dissociation stress), fix it and recompute. If the data-derived axis is biologically coherent but differs from the literature expectation, trust the data and say so. The reported marker genes must come from the data contrast, never from these example genes.

reason: An attribute-style existence check gives the same result regardless of the data, so it would silently fix the answer to one branch of the rule instead of letting the data decide.

reason: The file has raw counts only, so the team must pick a normalization; the default choice can shift gates differently in myeloid and lymphoid cells and change label fractions.
text: CLR normalization (the Mosaic default: per-cell centred log ratio across the antibody panel) is compositional. A cell bright for many markers (myeloid cells, blasts) gets a large geometric mean, which pushes its other markers down, while lymphocytes with few bright markers have their background pushed up. The CLR negative peak is therefore not at zero and sits at different values in different cell types. Check: plot lineage markers (CD3, CD19, CD14, CD56, CD123, CD11c) under CLR and under asinh or log of library-scaled counts, and see whether the negative peak moves between cell groups; re-run the labelling under a second normalization and compare label fractions. Do not gate on one global CLR cut-off. Treat any label whose >=1% status flips between normalizations as unresolved and settle it with explicit multi-marker gating.

reason: A pooled threshold can mislabel whole samples' worth of cells, which changes pooled label fractions.
text: The five samples were stained and sequenced separately, so the negative and positive peaks of the same marker can sit at different values in each sample. Normalizing or thresholding the pooled matrix can make one sample's background look like another sample's positive population; Mosaic's NSP normalization also fits its background/signal model to total reads within a run. Check: overlay per-sample densities of CD3, CD19, CD14, CD4, CD8, CD56, CD123 and of total antibody reads per cell, and look for shifted peaks or very different depth. If found: normalize and set thresholds per sample (or align peaks across samples) before pooling labels, and check that clusters are not simply samples.

reason: Sticky cells and doublets can add false members to small labels; a few hundred such cells is enough to matter at a 1% cut-off.
text: Some cells carry a cell-wide technical signal (antibody aggregates, dead or sticky cells, Fc-receptor binding on monocytes and other myeloid cells, doublets) and look positive for everything, including mutually exclusive lineage markers; they get mis-gated into T, B, NK or DC labels. Check: per cell, compare summed isotype counts (IgG1+IgG2a+IgG2b) and total antibody counts with the rest of the sample; count cells positive for exclusive pairs (CD3 with CD19, CD3 with CD14, CD19 with CD14) and see whether they are the high-isotype or high-total cells; check whether isotype signal is higher in CD14/CD64-positive cells. If found: require a marker to exceed the cell's own isotype/background level, label cross-lineage and high-isotype cells Other/Unassigned, and keep them in the denominator.

reason: All three reported numbers come from this metric code and from the choice of how many clusters to make; a counting error or an over-clustered solution changes the answer directly, and using labels inside the clustering would invalidate it.
text: PITFALL (purity is inflatable, and the metric code is easy to get wrong): cluster purity rises trivially with the number of clusters (one cell per cluster gives 100%), and the task's 'average purity' is an unweighted mean over clusters, so many tiny pure clusters raise it while hiding large mixed ones. A resolution chosen only to maximise purity is over-clustered and not a meaningful result. CHECK: over a resolution sweep tabulate n_clusters, distinct types captured, unweighted mean purity, cell-weighted purity, minimum cluster size and the purity of the 5 largest clusters, and see whether purity gains come only from cluster count. Verify the metric code: purity on a 0-100 scale; captured = number of DISTINCT dominant cell types (not number of clusters); total_clusters = exactly the clusters used to compute purity (the final labelling, including any sub-clusters); no empty/unused categories and no NaN labels in the type-by-cluster crosstab. IF FOUND: among solutions that reach at least 17 captured types with stable purity, prefer the one with the fewest clusters, and state cluster count and cell-weighted purity next to the reported figure. Never feed the cell_type labels into the clustering itself: labels may only score or choose among unsupervised partitions, and any such label-guided tuning must be disclosed.

reason: Single-marker gates move monocytes, pDC and blasts into CD4_T or NK and move NK into CD8_T, which changes the fractions of exactly the labels being tested.
text: No single marker in this panel is lineage-restricted for CD4_T, CD8_T or NK. CD4 is dim on monocytes and present on pDC; CD8 is dim on a subset of NK cells; CD56 is on NK-like T cells, on aberrant monocytes and on some AML blasts; CD16 is on non-classical monocytes and neutrophils as well as NK. Check: cross-tabulate CD3 against CD4, CD8, CD56 and CD16; within CD3-negative CD56+ or CD16+ cells check CD7 (NK are CD7+) and CD14/CD33/CD64/CD11b (myeloid); count CD3+ cells that are CD4+CD8+ or CD4-CD8-. Suggested rule: require CD3+ for both T labels (supported by CD5/CD2/CD7); define NK as CD3-negative, CD19-negative, CD14/CD64/CD33-negative with CD56+ and/or CD16+ and CD7+; send CD3+CD56+ cells to their T label; fix and state a rule for double-positive and double-negative T cells.

reason: The cDC/monocyte boundary is set by the rule chosen, so whether cDC reaches 1% can depend on the definition; the team should know this and report both.
text: cDC and monocytes share CD11c, HLA-DR, CD33 and dim CD4, so a bare 'CD11c+ HLA-DR+' rule labels monocytes as cDC (or all cDC as Myelomonocytic), and the cDC fraction then depends entirely on that rule. FcεRIα marks both cDC2 and basophils; CD1c is also found on some B cells and CD141 can be low-positive on monocytes (these last two are general immunology knowledge supplied by the library, not taken from its cited source). Check: within HLA-DR+ CD11c+ cells that are CD3/CD19/CD56-negative, split by CD14 and CD64 and look at CD1c, CD141 and FcεRIα; confirm CD1c+ cells labelled cDC are CD19/CD22-negative and CD123-low. Suggested rule: cDC = HLA-DR+ CD11c+ with CD1c+ (cDC2) or CD141-high (cDC1), CD14-negative, CD64-low, CD123-negative/dim, lineage-negative; CD14+ or CD64-high cells go to Myelomonocytic. reason: pDC is a small population whose size is very sensitive to the definition, so the gate, not the data, could decide its 1% status unless the team uses a multi-marker rule and reports both variants.
text: Calling pDC from CD123 alone over-counts. Basophils are CD123-bright but HLA-DR-negative and FcεRIα-positive; monocytes can be CD123/HLA-DR bright; myeloid or monocytic blasts can be CD123-bright. pDC are also CD4-positive and CD3-negative, so a CD4 gate without CD3 puts them (and monocytes) into CD4_T. Check: among CD123-high cells, tabulate HLA-DR, CD303, CD304, FcεRIα, CD34, CD64, CD14, CD11c, CD3, CD19, and count how many are HLA-DR+ with CD303 and/or CD304 and negative for CD3/CD19/CD14/CD64/CD34. Suggested rule: pDC = CD123-high AND HLA-DR+ AND (CD303+ or CD304+) AND lineage-negative (CD3, CD19, CD14, CD64 negative, CD11c low, CD34 negative); send CD123+ HLA-DR-negative FcεRIα+ cells (basophils) and CD123+ CD34+ cells (blasts) elsewhere. reason: The goal is 17 of 18 types, so the rare types decide success; this tells the team why a plain resolution sweep can stall below 17 and what to do instead.
text: PITFALL (resolution limit hides rare types): modularity-based Leiden/Louvain merges communities smaller than a scale set by total graph size. In a graph of about 100,000 cells at default resolution (~1.0), rare PBMC types (the library names HSPC, ILC, pDC, Plasmablast, cDC, NK CD56bright as the likely ones) can be absorbed into neighbours and never be the plurality of any cluster. Raising global resolution does not fix this cleanly: it shatters the large populations at the same time. CHECK: for every run build an 18-row capture table (one row per cell type: type size, the cluster holding most of that type, share of the type in that cluster, whether the type is dominant in any cluster) and run it across resolutions (e.g. 0.5 to 5); note which types remain uncaptured. IF FOUND: sub-cluster only the parent cluster(s) that contain the missing type (sc.tl.leiden with restrict_to, or re-run HVG + PCA + neighbours on that subset) instead of cranking global resolution; the CPM quality function is an alternative without this limit.

reason: Normalisation state and number of PCs are set before any clustering and determine whether rare types can be separated at all; an error here cannot be repaired by tuning resolution later.
text: PITFALL (preprocessing can silently drop rare-type signal): clustering raw counts, log-transforming twice, or keeping too few PCs removes it, because the PCs that separate rare populations explain little total variance and fall below an elbow-plot cut-off. Log-normalisation and Pearson residuals perform similarly overall, but Pearson residuals give marker genes of small populations high variance. CHECK: confirm X holds integer counts before normalising (X.data equals its rounded self; look at the maximum) and that it is not already logged; compare 30 vs 50 PCs and log1p-CP10k vs analytic Pearson residuals (scanpy.experimental.pp) on the per-type capture table (for each of the 18 types: is it dominant in any cluster). IF FOUND: normalise from raw counts exactly once, keep about 50 PCs rather than cutting at the elbow, and switch to Pearson-residual HVG/PCA if it captures a rare type that log-normalisation misses.

reason: A team that only sweeps resolution leaves an equally strong parameter untested; k decides whether the smallest types can form a cluster of their own.
text: PITFALL (the kNN graph matters as much as resolution): the neighbour graph is fixed before Leiden runs. A larger n_neighbors gives a more global view and merges small populations into neighbours; going from k=15 to k=50 usually changes the cluster count more than a resolution change does. A population with fewer cells than a few multiples of k cannot hold its own neighbourhood. CHECK: note the size of the smallest cell type and compare it with k; rebuild neighbours at k=10, 15 and 30 on the same PCs and compare, at a matched number of clusters, which of the 18 types are dominant in at least one cluster. IF FOUND: use the smaller k (10-15) for the global graph or for the sub-clustering step aimed at the rare type, and record k, number of PCs and distance metric alongside resolution.

reason: The choice between per-cell gating and cluster-level labelling, and the clustering resolution, directly changes the reported percentages, especially for the smallest compartment.
text: Annotate at cluster level, not cell by cell from a single marker. reason: Tells the team to test for a condition/donor structure that would otherwise be mistaken for cell-type structure, and gives a decision rule for whether to integrate.
text: PITFALL (donor and stimulation can drive the clusters): this dataset is multi-donor, stimulated-vs-control PBMC (12 donors x 91 cytokine conditions, with a PBS control). Stimulation (interferon-type cytokines change hundreds of genes in every cell, monocytes most strongly) and donor identity can drive the top PCs, so cells group by condition or donor rather than by type. Splitting one type by state only adds clusters, but a shared response programme can also pull different types together, lowering purity or losing a captured type. CHECK: for each cluster compute the largest donor share and the largest cytokine share (and PBS vs cytokine share) and compare with the global shares; correlate the top PCs with donor and treatment; flag mixed-type clusters dominated by one cytokine or donor. IF FOUND: select HVGs batch-aware (batch_key = donor or sample), integrate the PCs with Harmony on donor (optionally also cytokine), re-cluster, and compare the per-type capture table against the unintegrated run; keep whichever captures more types at an equal number of clusters.

reason: Counterweight to the donor/stimulation item: integration is the standard reflex for multi-donor data and here it can cost the rare-type captures the goal depends on.
text: PITFALL (batch integration can over-correct and erase rare types): Harmony's objective is biased toward major cell types, so small populations can be blended into large neighbours; MNN, scVI and LIGER can alter the data considerably. Integrating by default may lose exactly the rare types needed to reach 17 of 18. CHECK: before vs after integration, at the same number of clusters, compare which of the 18 types are dominant in at least one cluster and the purity of the clusters dominated by rare types (HSPC, ILC, pDC, Plasmablast, cDC, NK CD56bright). A rare type that was dominant somewhere before integration and nowhere after is over-correction. IF FOUND: use the uncorrected PCA, or integrate on donor only with a weaker setting. Treat integration as an option that must be justified by the capture comparison, not as a required step.

reason: Score-argmax is the most common shortcut for a three-compartment split and can shift the percentages without any visible error.
text: Do not assign cells by the highest of three gene-set scores (argmax of sc.tl.score_genes or similar). Such scores are uncalibrated: they depend on signature size, on the expression level of the signature genes (control-gene binning biases highly expressed markers) and on the matrix used (a scaled X makes it worse), so comparing three scores is biased and low-count cells are assigned almost at random. Check: cross-tabulate score-argmax labels against cluster-level marker labels and look at score distributions per cluster. Use scores only as a per-cluster summary computed on log-normalised data, take the final label from the cluster's dominant marker programme, and if the two approaches disagree by more than a few percent of cells inspect the disagreeing clusters by hand.

reason: Gives a specific cause and remedy for a low-purity mixed cluster that resolution tuning alone would not explain or fix.
text: PITFALL (a mixed 'cycling' cluster): proliferating cells from different lineages (activated T, NK, B) share a cell-cycle programme that can be stronger than their type markers, so they form one cycling cluster. Cytokine-stimulated PBMC are likely to contain such cells, and the 18 labels have no 'proliferating' class, so that cluster would be a low-purity mix. CHECK: score S and G2M phases (sc.tl.score_genes_cell_cycle) or look at MKI67/TOP2A per cluster, and inspect the label composition of any cluster with high cycling scores. IF FOUND: sub-cluster that cluster on an HVG set with cell-cycle genes removed (or regress S/G2M scores before PCA) so that it splits by lineage, and compare the result with the original. Do not regress cell cycle blindly across the whole dataset, since regression can remove other biology.

reason: The pass mark is a threshold (17 of 18); the team should know whether its count is stable or an accident of one seed before reporting it.
text: PITFALL (seed dependence): Leiden is stochastic and has no null model; a different random seed changes the partition, so a result of 17 or 18 captured types that rests on one small borderline cluster can flip between runs, and the reported cluster count and purity move with it. CHECK: re-run the chosen configuration with 3-5 random_state values (and, if cheap, on an 80% subsample) and record captured types, n_clusters and mean purity each time. IF FOUND: prefer a configuration whose capture count is the same across seeds, fix and report random_state, and report the range across seeds rather than the best seed.

reason: The marker panel chosen for CAF versus cancer cells determines where a mesenchymal-like cancer line lands; a wrong panel moves cells between two of the three reported compartments.
text: Common 'CAF/mesenchymal' markers are not fibroblast-specific: Vim, S100a4 (FSP1), Acta2, Fn1, Sparc, Thy1 and EMT signatures are also expressed by EMT-like carcinoma cells, macrophages, T cells (Thy1), pericytes and smooth muscle. 4T1 cancer cells are a hybrid epithelial/mesenchymal line that keeps Cdh1, Epcam and keratins (Krt8, Krt18) while expressing vimentin, so a Vim/S100a4/EMT-based rule moves cancer cells and myeloid cells into CAF and inflates it. Check: for putative CAF clusters require a fibroblast matrix programme (Col1a1, Col1a2, Col3a1, Dcn, Lum, Pdgfra, Pdgfrb, Pdpn, Fap) together with absence of Ptprc and of Epcam/Krt8/Krt18/Cdh1 at cluster level; cross-tabulate Vim-high cells against Epcam/Krt and Ptprc. Define CAF by collagen/Pdgfr genes with negative selection for immune and epithelial markers, define Epithelial/Cancer by Epcam/Krt8/Krt18/Cdh1 (not by absence of Vim), and never use Vim, S100a4 or Acta2 alone.

reason: A mixed cycling cluster or an MHC-II-based immune call would move whole clusters to the wrong compartment.
text: Two sources of false lineage calls. (1) Cell-cycle genes can dominate clustering and produce a 'proliferating' cluster (Mki67, Top2a, Birc5, Cdk1 high) that mixes cycling cancer cells with cycling immune or stromal cells; labelling the whole cluster as cancer misassigns the others. (2) MHC class II genes (H2-Aa, H2-Ab1, Cd74) and interferon-response genes are induced in cancer cells and fibroblasts and are not valid Immune markers. Check: inside any Mki67/Top2a-high cluster look at Ptprc, Epcam/Krt8/Krt18 and Col1a1/Dcn separately and sub-cluster it (or regress cell-cycle scores), assigning each part to its own compartment; confirm Immune clusters with lineage-restricted genes (Ptprc, Lyz2, Csf1r, Cd3e, Cd79a, Nkg7, S100a8) rather than MHC-II/IFN genes.

text: Pitfall, naming the axis from gene-family names: gene families in a loadings list do not by themselves identify the axis. Ribosomal protein (RPL/RPS) genes differ strongly between hematopoietic cell types, so their presence can reflect cell-type identity rather than a translation/ribosome-biogenesis program; likewise a few immediate-early genes (FOS, JUN, DUSP1) or a few cell-cycle genes do not by themselves make a stress or proliferation axis. A handling/stress signature can also be real without being PC1 of the whole dataset: in published PBMC scRNA-seq, sampling-time stress correlated with PC1 only when PCA was run within each cell subtype, while across all PBMC cell type was the largest driver of variance. Check: count how many of the top 20 fall in each class (RPL/RPS, lineage/surface markers, IEG/heat-shock, cell-cycle such as MKI67/TOP2A); see whether any IEG/stress genes load on the same pole as lineage markers of one cell class; then test what PC1 actually separates by grouping PC1 scores by obs['popv_prediction'] and computing between-cell-type vs within-cell-type variance (eta-squared / one-way ANOVA R2). Decision rule: if PC1 variance is mostly between annotated cell types, name the axis by which cell types sit at each pole; if it is mostly within cell types, a program-type axis (translation, stress, cell cycle) is supported. Call PC1 a stress axis only if it varies mainly within cell types and the top loadings are dominated by IEG/heat-shock genes on one pole with no lineage markers.

text: Reference composition biases label transfer. A PBMC benchmark of five label-transfer methods found that the number of reference cells per type changes the result, and rare types (DC, pDC, plasma cells, cycling NK) are an imbalanced-classification problem that neighbour voting and unweighted classifiers under-call in favour of abundant T cells and monocytes. Check: tabulate reference cells per label; rerun the transfer with a class-balanced reference (down-sample each type to a cap, or use class_weight='balanced') and compare the five percentages with the full-reference run. text: Assigning one label per coarse cluster (the query ships with 20 Seurat clusters at resolution 1), or majority voting over clusters, erases rare populations that sit inside a larger cluster (DCs inside monocytes, pDCs or plasma cells inside B cells, NK inside cytotoxic T). Pure per-cell labels, on the other hand, are noisy from dropout, and majority voting depends on the clustering and latent space it is run on. Check: cross-tabulate per-cell predicted labels against clusters and flag any cluster where the top five-category label is below about 80-90 percent; compare the five percentages from per-cell labels with those from cluster-majority labels. If per-cell and cluster-level percentages differ materially for a category, that difference is the uncertainty to report.

reason: The axis and formula of CLR change the PCA input and therefore the clusters; common library defaults (Seurat, muon) use the other axis.
text: PITFALL ('CLR' is not one formula). The original CITE-seq CLR is per cell: each cell's antibody counts relative to that cell's geometric mean across antibodies. Seurat's default (margin=1) instead normalises each antibody across cells, with log1p(x / exp(sum(log1p(x[x>0]))/n)), which is always >= 0; muon.prot.pp.clr defaults to axis=0 with flavor='seurat'. reason: Whether treatments are confounded with or spread across well positions is the first fork in this decision, and it can only be read off the cytokine x well crosstab; a team that assumes either layout will reason from the wrong design.
text: PITFALL - establish the treatment-to-well layout from the data before anything else; do not assume it. In split-pool (ParseBio/SPLiT-seq) data the round-1 well (bc1_well) acts as the sample barcode, so a treatment may sit in its own fixed wells (position and treatment nested/confounded, in which case no normalization can separate a position effect from a treatment effect) or may be spread over many wells. CHECK: crosstab cytokine x bc1_well and donor x bc1_well; count how many distinct wells each cytokine (and PBS) uses, whether any well holds more than one cytokine, and whether each treatment's wells cover both edge and interior positions; quantify the association (chi-square or Cramer's V on edge/interior x treatment). GUIDANCE: state the observed layout as a fact about the design, then judge separately whether any position effect is large enough to matter. Confounding alone does not settle whether a correction is warranted, and a balanced layout alone does not prove there is no position effect.

reason: The decision depends on the measured size of the position effect, and the wrong unit of analysis (cells instead of wells) would make any effect look significant and mislead the conclusion.
text: PITFALL - judge the position effect by effect size at well level, not by a p-value at cell level. The experimental unit for cell recovery is the well; testing with each cell as an observation (e.g. chi-square over all cells) is pseudoreplication and will be 'significant' for trivially small effects. CHECK: aggregate to one row per bc1_well (cells per well, optionally per well x donor); confirm n in the test is the number of wells (<=96 per plate), not the number of cells; define edge (rows A/H or columns 1/12 of a 96-well plate) vs interior; fit cells_per_well ~ edge and ~ row + column; report R-squared and the edge-vs-interior percent difference in recovery, with its direction and consistency. GUIDANCE: rough yardsticks from plate-assay literature are that an R-squared near zero (about <0.02) with a small edge/interior difference is negligible, while R-squared above about 0.3 or consistently ~20-35% lower edge recovery is substantial. Report the measured numbers and let them decide; do not pick a conclusion before computing them.

reason: Without holding treatment fixed the team cannot tell plate bias from treatment-driven count differences, which leads to opposite conclusions about whether normalization is justified.
text: PITFALL - a raw association between well position and cell count can be produced by treatment biology rather than plate bias: cytokines that kill or expand cells change per-well counts, so the association may only reflect which treatments happen to sit at the edge. CHECK: compare edge vs interior per-well cell counts within PBS control wells only (if PBS occupies both kinds of position), and/or remove per-cytokine means and re-test position on the residuals where cytokines span both edge and interior wells. GUIDANCE: only a position difference that survives holding treatment fixed is evidence of systematic plate bias; if it vanishes, the count differences are attributable to treatment.

reason: A variance comparison is an obvious thing to compute here and is uninterpretable under an aliased layout; the team needs to know when it is invalid.
text: PITFALL - comparing 'variance in cell counts across positions' against 'variance across treatments' is circular when treatments map close to one-to-one onto wells, because the two groupings are then nearly the same partition and both variances measure the same differences. CHECK: count cytokines per well and wells per cytokine; if the mapping is near 1:1 the two decompositions are aliased. GUIDANCE: in that case do not use 'position variance exceeds treatment variance' as an argument either way; summarise position with a low-dimensional descriptor (edge vs interior, row, column) and use its R-squared instead.

reason: Testing only an edge indicator could miss or mischaracterise a real positional pattern, changing how the position effect is quantified.
text: PITFALL - edge vs interior is not the only possible spatial pattern; row or column gradients (pipetting order, multichannel loading) or second-ring effects can exist while the edge contrast looks null, and vice versa. CHECK: parse bc1_well into row letter and column number, view per-well cell counts as an 8x12 plate heatmap, and fit counts ~ row + column alongside counts ~ edge, comparing R-squared. GUIDANCE: describe the pattern actually present (edge, row, column, or none) and still decide on its effect size.

text: Normalisation pitfall. A CellTypist model stores per-gene mean/sd learned on log1p of counts normalised to 10,000 per cell and re-applies them to the query. Feeding raw counts, another target sum (median, 1e6), SCT/Pearson residuals or z-scored data gives wrong scores or an 'Invalid expression matrix' / '.raw' error. Check X is integer before normalising; then run sc.pp.normalize_total(adata, target_sum=1e4) and sc.pp.log1p(adata) exactly once on ALL 40,352 genes and verify np.expm1(adata.X[:10]).sum(axis=1) equals 10000 for every row. CellTypist silently uses only genes shared between query and model, so any gene filter or rename before prediction (HVG subset, min_cells filter, dropping MT/ribosomal/lncRNA or ENSG-named genes, symbol conversion) removes model features and changes scores without an error. Here all 888 model features exist in the raw var names (including ENSG-style ones), so nothing needs converting. reason: The choice of label column directly changes the rare-class percentages (DC, progenitor), which are separate fields in the answer.
text: Two label columns pitfall. CellTypist can return per-cell 'predicted_labels' (deterministic, depends only on expression) and 'majority_voting' (each Leiden over-cluster takes its dominant label). Their proportions differ, mostly for rare classes (DC, Progenitor cell, ILC), which get absorbed into the dominant neighbouring label under voting. Majority voting also depends on the neighbour graph (CellTypist builds it itself here, since none exists), Leiden version/seed and resolution (default 25 for 100k-200k cells), so it is not reproducible across environments and is memory-heavy at 100k cells. Per-cell labels are the direct output of the provided model; majority voting is an optional refinement. If you run both, cross-tabulate them and compare the six percentages; if any field differs by more than about 0.5 point, state which one is reported and why. Do not mix the two, and do not compute proportions from a custom clustering instead of the model's labels without saying so.

text: Prediction mode pitfall. CellTypist mode='prob match' (p_thres=0.5) can leave cells 'Unassigned' or give multi-labels joined by '|'; these do not map onto the six answer fields and change the denominator. The default mode='best match' always assigns exactly one of the 7 classes (the model's argmax). Use best match for the reported percentages; confirm the label set is exactly the 7 model classes with no 'Unassigned' or '|' labels. The fraction of cells with max sigmoid probability < 0.5 may be reported as a confidence diagnostic only; do not drop low-confidence cells from the denominator unless explicitly justified and reported.

text: ILC pitfall. The model predicts 7 classes including 'ILC', but the answer has 6 fields (T, monocyte, B, NK, DC, progenitor) that must sum to 100. Any cells predicted 'ILC' make the six sum to less than 100 unless a rule is chosen, and the rule changes the numbers. The task text does not specify the rule.
