reason: Whether calls are quality-filtered before the 'any non-reference call' union is the single choice most likely to move the sample count, so the team must make it deliberately and show both versions.
text: UNFILTERED VARIANT TABLE. The h5 holds the unfiltered variant table (roughly 75,000-99,000 candidate sites per sample, most of them sequencing/PCR noise). 'At least one non-reference call in any driver-gene site' is therefore a union over thousands of noisy sites and can be true for almost every cell of every lineage from random error alone. Check: compute the fraction of cells with any raw NGT in {1,2} in a driver gene separately for NK, T and myelomonocytic cells; if it is near 100% in all classes, the raw criterion is not measuring clone membership. Mosaic's standard per-call filters are DP >= 10, GQ >= 30, het calls need VAF >= 30% (20% is a common relaxed value), hom calls VAF >= 95%, ref calls VAF <= 5%, with failing calls set to missing; then keep only variants genotyped in >= 50% of cells and mutated in >= 1% of the sample's cells. Report the per-sample result under both raw and filtered calls, because they can differ.

reason: Germline polymorphisms satisfy a literal 'non-reference call in a driver gene' test in all cells, so including or excluding them can change the count from all samples to fewer; dropout means a naive 100%-ubiquity filter would miss them.
text: GERMLINE SNPs AND ALLELE DROPOUT. Driver-gene amplicons (TET2, ASXL1, TP53 and others) carry common germline polymorphisms that are non-reference in every cell of the patient, including NK and T cells, so they make NK cells look mutant in every sample without any clonal involvement. Check: per sample and per passing variant, compute the mutant fraction among genotyped cells in each immune class. Tapestri allele dropout is roughly 5-12% per locus, so a germline het SNP will not be in 100% of cells: it appears het-dominant with about 5-10% ref and 5-10% hom calls spread evenly over all classes, with per-cell VAF near 50% (or 100% for hom). Use a tolerant germline rule (mutant in roughly >= 80-90% of genotyped cells in EVERY immune class) rather than a strict 100% rule; a somatic variant is instead mutated in a subset of cells, typically enriched in myelomonocytic cells and depleted in T cells. There is no gnomAD annotation available offline, so lineage-ubiquity is the usable substitute for a population-frequency filter. Count a cell as mutant on NGT 1 or 2 alike; do not define clones by zygosity. Report the result with and without germline-like variants excluded.

text: PROTEIN NORMALISATION. Antibody-tag counts are dominated by ambient/nonspecific background and per-cell staining depth. Thresholding raw counts, or running one CLR over all five samples pooled, gives sample-driven clusters and wrong positive/negative calls. The three isotype controls (IgG1, IgG2a, IgG2b) are not biology and distort clustering if left in as features. Normalise within each sample (CLR per cell, or a background-aware method that uses the isotypes), drop isotypes from the clustering features, exclude 'sticky' cells that are high on all isotypes, and set marker gates per sample from the negative peak. reason: Mutant myeloid cells mislabelled as NK would create NK 'participation' that is purely a labelling error, directly inflating the sample count.
text: DEFINING NK CELLS. NK cells have no single specific antibody marker. CD56 is aberrantly expressed on monocytes and myeloid progenitors in MDS and on CD56+ monocyte/DC-like cells; CD16 is on non-classical monocytes and granulocytes; CD7 is on T cells and aberrant blasts; CD3+CD56+ NK-like T cells exist. A 'CD56-high' or 'CD16-high' cluster can therefore be mutant myeloid cells mislabelled as NK. Gate NK as CD3- CD19- CD14- CD33- CD7+ and (CD56+ or CD16+), rather than by one marker or an unreviewed cluster label; coexpression of CD7 with CD56 is what separates true NK cells from CD56+ myeloid cells. Check that NK-labelled cells are CD45-bright and negative for CD3, CD19, CD14/CD33/CD64 and CD34/CD117, and compare the NK mutant fraction with and without the CD7+ and CD33- requirements.

reason: The 1% threshold is below the expected doublet rate, so without a doublet check a positive sample cannot be distinguished from an artefact.
text: DOUBLETS. A droplet containing an NK cell and a mutant myeloid cell carries both the NK protein signal and the myeloid mutation. Tapestri doublet rates are several percent, well above the 1% NK-mutant threshold, so doublets alone can push a sample over the line. Check, among NK-labelled cells called mutant: myeloid markers (CD33, CD14, CD64, CD11b, CD13), total protein and DNA read counts (doublets are higher), and per-cell VAF of the somatic variant (a het mutation diluted by a wild-type partner sits near 25% or lower instead of 50%). reason: Samples near the threshold can be decided by one cell; the team needs the control fractions and an explicit rule for zero-NK samples to make a defensible per-sample call.
text: SMALL NK NUMBERS AND CONTROLS. NK cells are a small population (often tens of cells out of a few thousand per sample), so at a 1.0% threshold a single erroneous or doublet cell can decide a sample, and a sample with zero NK-labelled cells has an undefined fraction. text: PLAN: Quantity = % of complete-genotype cells (NGT!=3 at all driver loci) in the largest clone with >=1 somatic mutation, in the one sample with DNMT3A (>10% mutated cells) + TP53 somatic mutations. Method: per sample, per-variant % mutated/missing, mean AF, gene by hg19 coordinate; exclude germline (near-clonal / recurrent across patients), artifacts (ASXL1 homopolymer, low-AF), non-driver genes; select drivers; mask low-quality calls (DP<10, GQ<30, AF inconsistent) as sensitivity; build per-variant binary and 3-state clone tables, WT kept in denominator. Checks: FILTER_MASK polarity, ADO hom share, attrition per locus, raw vs masked. Change method if a variant drops many cells or masked vs raw differ materially. Interpretation: option 1 expected on biology grounds.

label: PLAN
text: PLAN: Data = 5 Tapestri samples (S7,S8,S10,S13,S15), 48 antibodies, cell-called barcodes under assays/, empty barcodes under all_barcodes/. Quantity: number of the 48 markers with Hartigan dip p<0.05 under CLR, NSP, asinh; answer = method with most. Method: pool cells across samples; CLR per cell (log1p minus mean log1p); NSP = mosaic-style background correction using empty droplets per sample (scale by cell total, subtract background mean, divide by background sd); asinh(counts/5). Own dip implementation (diptest pkg unavailable) with p-value from uniform-null simulation. Checks: per-sample vs pooled counts, sensitivity to asinh cofactor, dip p<0.05 saturation (with ~24k cells nearly everything may be significant) -> if saturated, also compare dip statistic thresholds/subsample-based p-values. Change method if all methods tie at 48.

text: PLAN: Quantity = % of cells (genotyped at all somatic driver loci) in the largest mutant genotype clone, in the CCUS sample with somatic DNMT3A+TP53 where DNMT3A mutant fraction >10%. Method: per-sample mutant-cell fraction for all 181 variants from NGT (0 WT,1 het,2 hom,3 missing); exclude germline (~>80% or shared across all samples) and recurrent low-level artifacts present in all 5 samples; keep sample-specific somatic variants in driver genes; check VAF/GQ/DP in mutant cells and co-occurrence; then cells with NGT!=3 at all drivers, binarize mutant (1/2), count genotype patterns. Checks: sensitivity to including borderline variants (PPM1D, CBL, NF1, EZH2 cluster), GQ/DP filters. Change method if a candidate looks like an artifact (adjacent-SNV clusters, shared across samples) or if genotyping missingness drives result.

label: PLAN
text: PLAN: Quantity = number of the 48 antibodies (assays/protein_read_counts, called cells) with Hartigan dip p<0.05 under CLR (A, per-cell log1p minus cell mean log1p), NSP (B, home-made: jitter sd0.5, arcsinh, regress out linear dependence of per-cell background (isotype mean) and signal on log total reads), asinh (C, arcsinh of jittered counts). Normalize per sample. Dip test hand-written (exact Hartigan algorithm port), validated on uniform/normal/mixture, p from simulated uniform null at each n. Primary rule: per sample counts, summed marker-sample pairs and majority-of-samples count; also pooled. Checks: subsamples of 1000 cells, BH, isotypes, jitter on/off for CLR, NSP variant. Change method if per-sample and pooled disagree (prefer per-sample) or validation fails.

text: FINDING: scanpy seurat_v3 (single batch) computes per-gene mean and ddof=1 variance on raw counts; for genes with variance>0 it fits skmisc loess of log10(variance) on log10(mean) with span=0.3, degree=2, family='gaussian' (no robust iterations), surface='interpolate' (kd-tree, cell=0.2), all skmisc/R-loess defaults; zero-variance genes get fitted log10 var 0 (reg_std=1) and normalised variance 0; each count is clipped at mean + sqrt(N_cells)*reg_std with reg_std=sqrt(10**fitted); variances_norm = [N*mean^2 + sum(clipped^2) - 2*mean*sum(clipped)] / ((N-1)*reg_std^2); genes are ranked by argsort(argsort(-variances_norm)) (numpy default non-stable sort, so exact ties are ordered by implementation) and the top n_top_genes ranks are flagged. Under 'seurat', single-gene bins get normalised dispersion exactly 1, and zero-dispersion genes get NaN and are never selected. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: What exactly does scanpy's sc.pp.highly_variable_genes do with flavor='seurat_v3' (and Seurat's FindVariableFeatures with selection.method='vst'): which variables are regressed (log10 variance on log10 mean?), the loess span, degree, family and whether the surface is exact or interpolated, how zero-variance genes are treated, the clipping value for standardised values, how the standardised variance is computed, and how ties at the n_top_genes cutoff are ordered? Is there a documented way to reproduce it without the scikit-misc package, and how closely do statsmodels lowess or an exact local-quadratic fit reproduce its gene ranking? ANSWER: Definition (scanpy 1.10.4 source, matching Seurat docs): for each gene, compute the mean and the variance with ddof=1 on raw counts. Genes with variance>0 are fitted with loess of y=log10(variance) on x=log10(mean): span=0.3, degree=2, family='gaussian' (so no robust iterations), surface='interpolate' (kd-tree, cell=0.2), statistics='approximate'. These are the skmisc loess defaults and the same as R stats::loess defaults, which Seurat vst uses with loess.span=0.3. Zero-variance genes are not fitted: their fitted log10 variance is set to 0 (reg_std=1), and their normalised variance comes out as 0. reg_std = sqrt(10**fitted). Each count is clipped to clip_val = mean + sqrt(N_cells)*reg_std, which is Seurat's clip.max='auto'=sqrt(ncells) applied to the z-score. variances_norm = [N*mean^2 + sum(clipped^2) - 2*mean*sum(clipped)] / ((N-1)*reg_std^2), i.e. the ddof=1 variance of the clipped standardised values (x-mean)/reg_std. Ranks = argsort(argsort(-variances_norm)) using numpy's default non-stable sort, so exact ties are ordered by the implementation, not by a documented rule. Ranks >= n_top_genes are set to NaN, and the n_top_genes lowest ranks are flagged (single batch). Reproduction without skmisc: no official or documented alternative exists. scanpy issue #993 offered a statsmodels lowess(frac=0.15) version as a 'close approximation' but gave no agreement figures. statsmodels lowess is local-LINEAR with it=3 robust bisquare iterations by default, so it is a different smoother (degree 1, robust, different span). An exact tricube local-quadratic fit (span 0.3, gaussian, no robust iterations, evaluated directly) matches the definition except for loess's kd-tree interpolation, so it should be very close. No source I read quantifies ranking agreement for either approximation. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/main/src/scanpy/preprocessing/_highly_variable_genes.py, https://satijalab.org/seurat/reference/findvariablefeatures, https://has2k1.github.io/scikit-misc/stable/generated/skmisc.loess.loess.html, https://has2k1.github.io/scikit-misc/stable/generated/skmisc.loess.loess_model.html, https://has2k1.github.io/scikit-misc/stable/generated/skmisc.loess.loess_control.html, https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/loess.html, https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/loess.control.html, https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/issues/993, https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/generated/statsmodels.nonparametric.smoothers_lowess.lowess.html.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In scanpy, what does sc.pp.highly_variable_genes(adata, n_top_genes=2000) do when no flavor is given: which flavor is the default in current and recent versions, what input does it expect, and what happens (warning, error, or silent result) if it is called directly on raw integer counts after only a min_cells gene filter with no normalize_total/log1p step? Which flavor do the scanpy documentation and widely used best-practice guides recommend when the starting point is a raw count matrix and a fixed number of top genes is requested? ANSWER: In scanpy 1.10.4 (installed) and the current stable docs, the default is flavor='seurat'. It expects log-normalised (log1p) data and internally applies expm1 before computing dispersions. Integer-input checks (check_values) exist only on the seurat_v3 path. Called directly on raw counts after only a min_cells filter, the default flavor therefore raises no input warning or error. It silently returns a ranking computed on expm1(raw counts), which is meaningless, and counts above about 709 overflow to inf. With n_top_genes set, all mean and dispersion cutoffs are ignored. The docs state that seurat_v3/seurat_v3_paper expect count data and make n_top_genes mandatory, with 2000 as the internal default. These flavors mimic Seurat FindVariableFeatures(selection.method='vst'), whose default nfeatures is 2000. So for a raw count matrix with a fixed top-2000 request, the documented route that needs no unstated normalisation is seurat_v3. On scanpy's main branch the default flavor now goes through a settings 'preset', and I did not confirm its value. I could not read a best-practice guide this session (the sc-best-practices page failed to load, and the scanpy tutorial was cut off before its HVG step), so the 'widely used guides recommend' part is not settled from sources I read. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://scanpy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/generated/scanpy.pp.highly_variable_genes.html, https://satijalab.org/seurat/reference/findvariablefeatures, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/main/src/scanpy/preprocessing/_highly_variable_genes.py.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: For scanpy's dispersion-based HVG flavors ('seurat', 'cell_ranger') on log-normalised data, how sensitive is the selected gene set to the normalize_total target_sum (the function default of the median count per cell versus a fixed 1e4), particularly for shallow, very sparse UMI data where most non-zero counts are one and per-cell depth is far below 1e4? Is there a documented tendency for these flavors to select genes detected in very few cells under such conditions, and how are single-gene or sparsely filled mean bins handled in the normalised dispersion? ANSWER: From scanpy 1.10.4 source (mathematical reasoning, not an empirical web study). 'seurat': X is put through expm1, which exactly inverts log1p, so changing target_sum from the median depth to 1e4 multiplies all normalised counts by a constant k. Dispersion = var/mean then scales by k, log-dispersion shifts equally for all genes, and the within-bin z-score is unchanged. target_sum affects 'seurat' only through the 20 equal-width bins on log1p(mean), which move non-linearly with k. The gene set changes only where genes cross bin boundaries, so it is moderately sensitive and mostly affects low-mean bins. 'cell_ranger': no expm1 is applied, so mean and var/mean are computed on the log1p values themselves, with percentile bins and median/MAD normalisation. Because log1p(k*x) is non-linear in k, cell_ranger is genuinely sensitive to target_sum, and more so on shallow data where k is large relative to depth. Bin handling: under 'seurat', a bin with a single gene has its std NaN, so the code sets dev=avg and avg=0, giving normalised dispersion exactly 1 (logged only at verbosity 4). Zero dispersion becomes NaN and is never selected (NaN treated as -inf in the top-n cut). Mean==0 is set to 1e-12. Bins with only a few genes give noisy z-scores. No source I read documents a tendency for these flavors to pick genes detected in very few cells on shallow, mostly-ones data, so that part is unsettled and should be checked empirically (overlap and median prevalence with target_sum=None vs 1e4). question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In the vendor analysis package for single-cell DNA+protein droplet data whose protein normalization function offers CLR, NSP and asinh options, what exact formula does the default CLR option use, and how does it treat antibody read counts of zero (is a pseudocount added before the log)? ANSWER: The web does not fully settle this for the Python package itself. Mosaic's Protein.normalize_reads docs (default method='CLR') name the method 'Centered Log Ratio' but give no formula, and the Mosaic GitHub repo does not publish the Python source. The docs also say jitter applies only to NSP and asinh, not to CLR. Mission Bio's own public R packages (tapestriR and tapestri_multiomics, R/protein_normalization.R) do define the vendor's CLR exactly: counts = counts + 1 (a pseudocount of 1), then ln(x / geometric_mean(x)). clr_by_feature applies this to each row; clr_by_cell divides by the column-wise geometric means (exp(colMeans(log(x)))). Because the +1 is added before the log, a zero count becomes ln(1/g), which is finite, so the output is finite everywhere. Under that convention, the vendor-default reading and a reasonable pseudocount CLR (or asinh) both give a fully finite matrix (fraction finite = 1). Only a textbook CLR with no pseudocount would produce -Inf at zeros. The +1 convention in Mosaic Python is inferred from the vendor's R code, not documented. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/pages/methods/missionbio.mosaic.protein.Protein.normalize_reads.html, https://rdrr.io/github/MissionBio/tapestriR/src/R/protein_normalization.R, https://github.com/MissionBio/mosaic, https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/v2.4.1/examples/basics.html.

text: FINDING: scanpy sc.pp.regress_out fits, per gene and jointly over all keys, an ordinary linear model y_g = b0 + sum_k b_k*cov_k with an intercept column of ones prepended, using each obs covariate exactly as given (no log or other transform; pass log1p(total_counts) explicitly if that form is wanted); for continuous covariates scanpy >=1.11 solves least squares via normal equations (inv(X'X)) instead of the older statsmodels Gaussian GLM; it returns only the residuals, intercept NOT added back, so every gene ends with mean ~0 (breaks mean-binned HVG selection if run before HVG). Regressing raw total_counts vs log1p(total_counts) are therefore different models and can give several-fold different depth correlations; total_counts is right-skewed, so a linear term in raw counts fits the log-scale depth dependence poorly. Recommendation: regress_out is not in the current scanpy clustering tutorial workflow (shown steps: QC, doublets, normalize_total, log1p, HVG, PCA, no regression seen in the part read); scanpy docs warn it 'tends to overcorrect' (issue #526); maintainers (Wolf, Luecken) say it is dataset-dependent, can do more harm than good, and in heterogeneous whole-tissue data it erased cell-type structure; regressing biological covariates loses global structure and is mainly for trajectory work. So treat it as optional/discouraged by default, not a standard step. QUESTION: what does sc.pp.regress_out fit, and is regressing total counts recommended. text: FINDING: scanpy analytic Pearson residuals (Lause et al. 2021): sc.experimental.pp.highly_variable_genes(flavor='pearson_residuals') and normalize_pearson_residuals use an NB offset model with one shared overdispersion theta=100 (var=mu+mu^2/theta; theta=np.inf gives Poisson), clip=None means residuals are clipped to [-sqrt(n_obs), sqrt(n_obs)] (about +-80 for 6420 cells); n_top_genes has no default in experimental HVG (mandatory), recipe_pearson_residuals defaults n_top_genes=1000, n_comps=50, random_state=0 and runs HVG -> residuals on HVG subset -> PCA (varm['PCs'] has zero rows for non-HVGs). All expect RAW integer counts (check_values warns on non-integers; use layer='counts'), and need no extra dependency beyond scanpy. Note normalize_pearson_residuals has no subset step, so subset to the HVGs first; recipe/normalize do not take a layer for the PCA input in the recipe. By contrast scanpy pp.highly_variable_genes flavor='seurat_v3'/'seurat_v3_paper' REQUIRES scikit-misc (install scanpy[skmisc]) and expects counts; the built-in alternatives with no extra dependency are flavor='seurat' or 'cell_ranger' on log data, or the experimental pearson_residuals flavor on counts. QUESTION: defaults/requirements of scanpy Pearson residuals and seurat_v3. label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Downsampling counts to equal depth is a recognised remedy/diagnostic for depth-correlated structure: OSCA (Bioconductor, 'Downsampling instead of scaling') says log of scaled counts leaves a systematic mean trend with count size (Lun 2018), which shows up as PCs/trajectories correlated with library size even after normalisation, and the most straightforward solution is to downsample high-coverage cells to match low-coverage ones (scater logNormCounts(downsample=TRUE) targets a low size-factor quantile); OSCA calls it needed only in rare cases (rest of section truncated, so its stated caveats were not read). Interpretation: if a PC's depth correlation persists after downsampling every cell to the same total (from layers['counts'], then normalize/log1p, PCA, project or recompute), it reflects composition/biology (RNA content differences between cell types) rather than the log-transform depth artefact; if it vanishes, it was technical. Pearson residuals/sctransform (depth as a GLM offset/covariate) are the other accepted route. scanpy sc.pp.downsample_counts(adata, counts_per_cell=None, total_counts=None, random_state=0, replace=False, copy=False) acts on adata.X only (no layer arg; copy counts into X first), cells already below counts_per_cell are left unchanged, so pick the target at or below the minimum total_counts (or a low quantile and drop/accept lower cells); output is float. Within-cluster correlation limits (my reasoning, not from a page read): clusters built from the same PCs are circular (double dipping), within-cluster depth range is restricted so r is attenuated, and Simpson-type mixing of subclusters can inflate or reverse r, so it cannot cleanly separate technical from biological depth. QUESTION: how to separate depth from cell size; downsampling defaults; limits of within-cluster correlations. SOURCE: https://bioconductor.org/books/release/OSCA.advanced/more-norm.html ; https://scanpy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/generated/scanpy.pp.downsample_counts.html ; https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/issues/526

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In scanpy, what exactly does sc.pp.regress_out fit per gene (model form, intercept, covariate as given or transformed), and what do current scanpy tutorials and best-practices literature recommend about regressing total counts out of log-normalised data before scaling and PCA? ANSWER: Each gene gets an ordinary linear model fitted on all keys together: y_g = b0 + sum_k b_k*cov_k. An intercept column of ones is added, and each obs covariate is used exactly as stored, with no log or other transform. If you want log depth, you have to pass log1p(total_counts) yourself. Since PR #3284 (merged Nov 2024), continuous covariates are fitted by least squares through the normal equations (inv(X'X)); earlier versions used a statsmodels Gaussian GLM, which gives the same estimates. Categorical covariates are handled by per-category means. Only residuals are returned and the intercept is not added back, so every gene ends with mean ~0. This means HVG selection must come before regress_out (Luecken, theislab tutorial #35). Regressing raw total_counts and regressing log1p(total_counts) are different models, which plausibly explains the teams' several-fold disagreement. Raw counts are right-skewed, so a linear term in them fits a log-scale depth trend poorly; log1p(total_counts) is the form that matches the diagnostic. Recommendation: regress_out does not appear in the current scanpy clustering tutorial. Caveat: the fetched page was cut off at the QC/doublet section, so I only saw its steps up to there. The scanpy docs warn that regress_out 'tends to overcorrect' (issue #526). In #526, Wolf and Luecken say it is dataset-dependent and can do more harm than good. The example there was a heterogeneous whole-tumour dataset in which regression merged cell types into one blob. Regressing biological covariates removes global structure and is mainly useful for trajectory work. So depth regression is optional and discouraged as a default, not a standard step. I could not read the Luecken & Theis 2019 data-correction section in full because the fetch truncated the page. HOW SURE: high for the model form; medium for the recommendation. SOURCES: https://scanpy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/generated/scanpy.pp.regress_out.html, https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/issues/4280, https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/pull/3284, https://github.com/theislab/single-cell-tutorial/issues/35, https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/issues/526, https://scanpy.scverse.org/en/stable/tutorials/basics/clustering.html.

QUESTION: How do scanpy's analytic Pearson residuals functions work by default (theta, clipping, number of genes, raw counts, dependencies), and does flavor='seurat_v3' require scikit-misc or is there a built-in alternative? The HVG and normalize functions accept layer='counts'; the recipe has no layer argument, so put counts in X first. They need no package beyond scanpy. flavor='seurat_v3' and 'seurat_v3_paper' do require scikit-misc (scanpy[skmisc]) and expect counts. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: What methods are accepted for separating technical depth effects from genuine cell-size/RNA-content differences when a PC correlates with total UMI; is downsampling to equal depth (sc.pp.downsample_counts, defaults) a recognised diagnostic; what are the limits of within-cluster correlations? ANSWER: Downsampling is recognised. OSCA's 'Downsampling instead of scaling' section explains that the log of scaled counts keeps a systematic mean trend with count size (Lun 2018). This shows up as structure correlated with library size even after normalisation. OSCA's 'most straightforward solution' is to downsample high-coverage cells to the depth of low-coverage cells, which is scater's logNormCounts(downsample=TRUE). OSCA says this is needed only in rare cases; the page was truncated before its caveats, so I did not read them. Used as a diagnostic, it works like this: downsample the counts, re-normalise, log, run PCA, and recompute the PC-versus-depth correlation. If the correlation persists, it reflects cell-type RNA content; if it disappears, it came from the transform. The other accepted route is to model depth explicitly as a GLM offset or covariate, as in analytic Pearson residuals or sctransform. scanpy sc.pp.downsample_counts(adata, counts_per_cell=None, total_counts=None, *, random_state=0, replace=False, copy=False) works on adata.X only, with no layer argument, so copy layers['counts'] into X first. Cells already below counts_per_cell are left unchanged, so set the target at or below the minimum total_counts, or at a low quantile and exclude cells below it. On within-cluster correlations, I found no source in my call budget. These limits are my own reasoning: clusters built from the same PCs make the test circular (double dipping); depth range within a cluster is restricted, which weakens r; and mixed subpopulations can inflate or reverse r. A within-cluster correlation therefore cannot settle the question, and the downsampling diagnostic does not depend on clustering. HOW SURE: medium for downsampling as a diagnostic and high for its defaults; low for the within-cluster limits, which are my reasoning, not from a source. SOURCES: https://bioconductor.org/books/release/OSCA.advanced/more-norm.html, https://scanpy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/generated/scanpy.pp.downsample_counts.html, https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/issues/526.

text: FINDING: The phrase 'global-scaling normalization' is Seurat's wording and means a FIXED scale factor: Seurat pbmc3k tutorial says 'we employ a global-scaling normalization method LogNormalize that normalizes the feature expression measurements for each cell by the total expression, multiplies this by a scale factor (10,000 by default), and log-transforms the result'; NormalizeData docs: 'Feature counts for each cell are divided by the total counts for that cell and multiplied by the scale.factor. This is then natural-log transformed using log1p', scale.factor=10000 default, and 1e6 is called CPM under method RC, not LogNormalize. In the pages I read, scanpy does not use the phrase 'global scaling': its normalize_total default (target_sum=None) scales each cell to the median of total counts, and the current tutorial calls this 'median count depth normalization'. Bioconductor OSCA calls its approach 'scaling normalization' / 'library size normalization', with size factors centred to mean 1 (data-derived), and does not call it 'global'. So the sources tie 'global-scaling' to 1e4, not to a median target (medium-high confidence; I did not survey every tool). FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: How is 'global scale' / 'global-scaling' log normalization defined in Seurat, scanpy, Bioconductor and tools built on them: a fixed factor (1e4 or 1e6) or also a data-derived target such as the median library size? ANSWER: 'Global-scaling' is Seurat's term, and it means a fixed factor of 10,000. Seurat pbmc3k tutorial: 'By default, we employ a global-scaling normalization method "LogNormalize" that normalizes the feature expression measurements for each cell by the total expression, multiplies this by a scale factor (10,000 by default), and log-transforms the result.' NormalizeData reference: 'LogNormalize: Feature counts for each cell are divided by the total counts for that cell and multiplied by the scale.factor. This is then natural-log transformed using log1p', with scale.factor = 10000 by default. 1e6 (CPM) appears only under method 'RC' (relative counts, no log). None of the scanpy pages I read uses the phrase 'global scaling'. Scanpy's normalize_total with target_sum=None (the default) normalizes each cell so that 'each observation (cell) has a total count equal to the median of total counts for observations (cells) before normalization', and the current tutorial calls this 'median count depth normalization'. Bioconductor OSCA uses 'scaling normalization' / 'library size normalization', with size factors scaled so that 'the mean size factor across all cells is equal to 1' (a data-derived target), and does not call it 'global'. In the sources read, the phrase goes with dividing by each cell's total and multiplying by a fixed 1e4. None of them uses it for a median target. Caveat: I did not check every workflow or assistant tool, so I cannot rule out looser use elsewhere. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://satijalab.org/seurat/articles/pbmc3k_tutorial, https://satijalab.org/seurat/reference/normalizedata, https://scanpy.scverse.org/en/stable/generated/scanpy.pp.normalize_total.html, https://bioconductor.org/books/release/OSCA.basic/normalization.html, https://scverse-tutorials.readthedocs.io/en/latest/notebooks/basic-scrna-tutorial.html.

text: FINDING: In recent scanpy sc.tl.leiden defaults are resolution=1, random_state=0, n_iterations=-1 (iterate until no improvement), directed=None, flavor=None; flavor=None currently runs leidenalg (directed graph, RBConfigurationVertexPartition) and emits a FutureWarning that the default will become flavor='igraph' with n_iterations=2 and directed=False, and the warning itself says results will be slightly different. scanpy's own tests only require NMI>0.9 between leidenalg and igraph partitions (not identity), and different seeds give different partitions, so backend, n_iterations or seed can change membership and cluster count near a cluster-count boundary on a few-hundred-cell graph. text: FINDING: scanpy rank_genes_groups defaults are method=None (= t-test, NOT wilcoxon), tie_correct=False, reference='rest', rankby_abs=False, corr_method='benjamini-hochberg'; genes are ordered by 'scores'. For method='wilcoxon' the score is the rank-sum z-statistic: z = (R_group - n1*(n1+n2+1)/2) / sqrt(tc * n1*n2*(n1+n2+1)/12), where tc=1 without tie correction and tc = 1 - sum(t^3-t)/(N^3-N) per gene with tie_correct=True. Because tc differs per gene (genes with more zeros/ties get smaller tc, so their |z| is inflated more), tie correction rescales each gene's z by 1/sqrt(tc_gene) and CAN reorder genes, not only p-values; for sparse data the effect is largest for genes with many zeros. A plain call for 'top N markers' with wilcoxon is sc.tl.rank_genes_groups(adata, key, method='wilcoxon') with tie_correct=False. QUESTION: how scanpy wilcoxon score is computed, tie_correct default, does it reorder genes. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: When a kNN graph with k=15 is built on a PCA embedding, how many real (non-self) neighbours per cell do the common tools give by default: scanpy's pp.neighbors(n_neighbors=15), scikit-learn's NearestNeighbors.kneighbors() with and without the training data passed, scikit-learn's kneighbors_graph (include_self default), and Seurat's FindNeighbors(k.param)? Which convention is usual when analysts compute cell-type neighbour composition from such a graph? ANSWER: scanpy pp.neighbors(n_neighbors=15): the count includes the cell itself, so obsp['distances'] holds 14 real neighbours per row. This holds with the exact/sklearn backend, which is the default for 6420 cells with the euclidean metric. A reported bug (#3809) means the pynndescent backend gives 15 nonzeros. obsp['connectivities'] is a symmetrised UMAP graph and is not a 15-NN list. sklearn NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=15).kneighbors() with no X: the docs say the query point is not considered its own neighbour, giving 15 real neighbours. kneighbors(X_train): each point comes back as its own first neighbour, giving 14 real + self. kneighbors_graph: include_self defaults to False, giving 15 real neighbours. Seurat FindNeighbors(k.param): the cell itself is its 1st NN, so k.param-1 are real, and the NN graph rowSums equal k.param (self on the diagonal); for k=15 that is 14 real. On which convention is usual: no source settles it. In a scanpy-style 'standard preprocessing' workflow, an unspecified 'kNN graph with k=15' most plausibly means sc.pp.neighbors(n_neighbors=15) and its directed obsp['distances'], i.e. 14 real neighbours (the Seurat convention agrees). Report 15 real neighbours (sklearn, self excluded) as a sensitivity check. HOW SURE: high for the per-tool counts; medium for the Seurat count (from issue threads, not the source code, which would not load in full); low-medium for which convention is usual (a judgement, not documented). question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: What does scanpy's pp.scale store in var['mean'] and var['std']: the per-gene statistics before scaling, and are they computed before or after clipping with max_value? What would stored values of mean about 0 and std about 1 indicate about how the function was called? ANSWER: The docs say var['mean'], var['std'] and var['var'] are the per-gene means, standard deviations and variances before scaling. In the source, _center_and_std computes mean_var(x, axis=0, correction=1) on the input matrix (ddof=1, and std=0 is replaced by 1) before centring and dividing. max_value clipping is applied after scaling, so the stored stats are from the unscaled, unclipped input. After one pp.scale on log-normalised data you would expect positive means (roughly 0-3 for log1p CP10k) and varied stds. Stored means of about 0 and stds of about 1 therefore mean the matrix given to the call that wrote them was already standardised: pp.scale was re-run on z-scored data, overwriting the original stats. A rerun on a matrix clipped at 10 would leave std slightly below 1 for genes that were clipped. Such stats cannot recover the original log-normalised means/stds, but rerunning scale on z-scored data is nearly idempotent, so .X still matches a single standard scale apart from small clipping effects. HOW SURE: high for what is stored and the order relative to clipping; medium for the interpretation of mean~0/std~1 (an inference from the code). SOURCES: https://scanpy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/generated/scanpy.pp.scale.html, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/main/src/scanpy/preprocessing/_scale.py.

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: The getnnz crash comes from scanpy.neighbors._common._ind_dist_shortcut, which calls D.getnnz(axis=1) on the kNN distance matrix. It fires only when that matrix is a csr_array (pynndescent>=0.7 returns csr_array; csr_matrix still has getnnz), i.e. whenever pynndescent is used, which is the default for euclidean metric with >=8192 cells, so it hits this 11693-cell dataset. Upstream fix is scanpy PR #4451 (merged 2026-10-29, closes #4444; release number not shown on the pages read), which drops getnnz; the maintainer-suggested replacement is np.diff(D.indptr), the per-row count of STORED entries including explicit zeros, identical to getnnz(axis=1). A patch using np.diff(indptr) or csr_array._getnnz(axis=1) is exactly equivalent and leaves distances/connectivities unchanged (the shortcut only reshapes D.indices/D.data when every row has the same count, else falls back to the slow path). Not equivalent: count_nonzero (drops explicit zeros, e.g. duplicate cells at distance 0) or using total nnz/n_obs without checking every row has the same count. Pinning pynndescent<0.7 also avoids the error, but 0.7 may give a different approximate kNN graph than 0.6. QUESTION: getnnz AttributeError in sc.pp.neighbors, upstream fix and equivalence of patches. text: FINDING: Exact partition reproducibility across environments is NOT guaranteed. sc.pp.neighbors uses exact brute-force sklearn kNN only for euclidean metric with <8192 cells; at ~11.7k cells it uses approximate pynndescent, seeded with random_state=0, but numba-parallel and not bitwise reproducible across CPUs/thread counts/versions. Issue #2014 shows Leiden clusters on an X_scVI embedding differing across CPU models with identical containers. Leiden itself was deterministic from a fixed connectivities matrix, and rounding the connectivities or NUMBA_DISABLE_JIT=1 made it stable. Maintainers state the neighbour graph is not guaranteed reproducible across machines, package versions or thread counts (#2956, read only as a search snippet). Leiden in scanpy 1.10.x defaults to flavor='leidenalg', directed=True, n_iterations=-1, random_state=0, the same as 1.9. Issue #3422 (1.9.3 vs 1.10.4 differing) was closed as not planned and blamed on duplicated data (read only as a search snippet). So the same graph plus the same leidenalg/igraph should give the same partition, but a reference run on another machine or pynndescent version may give a somewhat different graph and partition. Treat the single-seed value as approximate, within the seed-to-seed spread. QUESTION: Reproducibility of sc.tl.leiden(resolution=1, random_state=0) and sc.pp.neighbors across versions/platforms. label: FINDING
text: FINDING: The standard IR/textbook purity (Manning et al. IR book eq. 182; Tan et al. overall purity = sum_i (m_i/m) p_i) is cell-weighted: total majority-label count divided by N. Single-cell clustering papers that give a formula use the same weighted form (e.g. GRACE, PLoS ONE 2023: Purity = (1/N) sum_j max_i |y_i ∩ c_j|; seen only as a search snippet). Both aggregates exist in tools: e.g. spine.math.metrics.pur defaults to per_cluster=True ('average equally over predicted clusters') with per_cluster=False giving the weighted version. No single-cell reference read defines 'average cluster purity' explicitly. The literal wording 'average cluster purity, where purity for each cluster is ...' most naturally reads as the unweighted mean of per-cluster purities, while 'purity' alone conventionally means the weighted one. The web does not settle which one the grader means. QUESTION: Is 'average cluster purity' the unweighted mean of per-cluster purities or cell-weighted overall purity? QUESTION: In scanpy, what are the defaults of sc.tl.leiden (flavor/backend leidenalg versus igraph, n_iterations, random_state, directed) in recent versions, and can the two backends or iteration settings return different partitions and different cluster counts at the same resolution on a graph of a few hundred cells? ANSWER: Defaults: resolution=1, random_state=0, n_iterations=-1 (run to convergence), directed=None, flavor=None, partition_type=RBConfigurationVertexPartition. flavor=None currently runs leidenalg on a directed graph and raises a FutureWarning saying the default will move to flavor='igraph', n_iterations=2, directed=False, and that 'results will be slightly different with the changed backend'. scanpy's own tests only require NMI > 0.9 between the leidenalg and igraph outputs, not identical labels, and they assert that different seeds give different partitions. So backend, n_iterations, directed or seed can change cluster membership. Near the resolution where the count moves from 5 to 6 to 7 they can also change the cluster count. A plain sc.tl.leiden(adata, resolution=r) uses leidenalg, directed, n_iterations=-1 and seed 0. The teams should record these settings and scan resolution with one fixed call. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://scanpy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/generated/scanpy.tl.leiden.html, https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/issues/2865, https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/issues/2935, https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/blob/1fbe008d/tests/test_clustering.py.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In scanpy's rank_genes_groups with method='wilcoxon', how is the reported score computed, what is the default of tie_correct, and does switching tie_correct on change the order of top-ranked genes (not just the p-values) for sparse log-normalised single-cell data? Which settings does a plain default call use for ranking 'top N markers'? ANSWER: The score is the rank-sum z-statistic: z = (R_group - n1(n1+n2+1)/2) / sqrt(tc * n1*n2*(n1+n2+1)/12). The default is tie_correct=False, which sets tc=1. With tie_correct=True, tc = 1 - sum(t^3 - t)/(N^3 - N), computed per gene. Genes are ordered by score. Because tc differs between genes, tie correction scales each z by its own factor 1/sqrt(tc_gene), and genes with many zeros (ties) get the largest boost. So it can reorder genes, especially in the lower part of a top-50 list, not only change p-values. This is inferred from the formula; I found no published measurement of the size of the effect. Defaults of a plain call: method=None, which means t-test, not wilcoxon; reference='rest'; rankby_abs=False; tie_correct=False; corr_method='benjamini-hochberg'. A standard Wilcoxon call is therefore rank_genes_groups(..., method='wilcoxon') with tie_correct=False. HOW SURE: high for the defaults and formula; medium that reordering is material near rank 50 (inferred, not measured). SOURCES: https://scanpy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/generated/scanpy.tl.rank_genes_groups.html, https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/blob/1.13.0/src/scanpy/tools/_rank_genes_groups.py, https://github.com/theislab/scanpy/issues/698.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In published classifications of cancer-associated fibroblast subtypes in mouse tumours, which genes define a contractile / actin-cytoskeleton (myofibroblast or vascular smooth-muscle-like) CAF program as distinct from an ECM-producing myofibroblastic program and from a hypoxia- or glycolysis-associated CAF state, and do such signatures include ubiquitous cytoskeletal genes such as Actb or Vim? ANSWER: Contractile, vascular or smooth-muscle-like CAFs are defined by smooth-muscle contractile genes. Examples: Cords 2023 vCAF (ACTA2, MCAM, RGS5); pan-myCAF in Clin Cancer Res 2021 (ACTA2, MYH11, MCAM, TAGLN, MYLK; GO term smooth muscle contraction); colorectal CAF-B (ACTA2, TAGLN, PDGFA, MUSTN1, NOTCH3, MYH11); Bartoschek 2018 mouse vCAF (perivascular, Notch3/Kcnj8). ECM or matrix CAFs are defined by MMP11, CDH11, POSTN, collagens (COL1A2, COL11A1, COL10A1, COL12A1) and COMP; the mouse mCAF set is Fbln1, Pdgfra, Dcn, Vcan, Col14a1, Cxcl14. The hypoxic or glycolytic 'tumour-like' CAF (Cords tCAF) is defined by PDPN, MME, ENO1, NDRG1 and CA9. None of these signatures includes Actb or Vim. A narrow smooth-muscle set (Acta2, Tagln, Myh11, Mylk, Myl9, Cnn1, Des, Mcam, Rgs5, Notch3) matches the references; broad sets that include Actb or Vim do not, and they can let a hypoxic cluster tie. Caveat: the gateway cut off the page texts before the results sections, so the Cords Table 1 and Clin Cancer Res marker lists come from search excerpts, and most of the reference signatures are human with mouse symbols mapped. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10354071/, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-39762-1/tables/1, https://aacrjournals.org/clincancerres/article/27/9/2636/672059/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6279758/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7613625/, https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/cell-and-developmental-biology/articles/10.3389/fcell.2022.825014/full.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In scanpy 1.10.x used with scipy 1.14 or later, sc.pp.neighbors can fail with an AttributeError about csr_array having no getnnz. Which code path triggers this, how was it fixed upstream (which release, what the replacement code computes), and is replacing getnnz with a count of stored non-zeros per row or in total exactly equivalent to the fixed behaviour, so that the resulting distances and connectivities graphs are unchanged? ANSWER: Trigger: sc.pp.neighbors -> _get_indices_distances_from_sparse_matrix -> _ind_dist_shortcut in scanpy/neighbors/_common.py, which calls D.getnnz(axis=1) on the kNN distance matrix. scipy's csr_matrix still has getnnz, so the call fails only when D is a csr_array. pynndescent>=0.7 returns csr_array from PyNNDescentTransformer, so it fails whenever pynndescent is used: transformer='pynndescent', or by default with the euclidean metric from 8192 cells, which includes this 11,693-cell dataset. Upstream fix: scanpy PR #4451 'fix: support pynndescent 0.7', merged 2026-10-29, which closes #4444. It stops using getnnz/.A1. The pages I read do not show which release number ships it. The replacement the maintainers point to is np.diff(D.indptr), the per-row count of stored entries including explicit zeros. That is exactly what getnnz(axis=1) returns, per the scipy docs ('Number of stored values, including explicit zeros'). The shortcut checks that this count is the same in every row and then just reshapes D.indices and D.data; if the counts differ it falls back to the slow path. Equivalence: a patch using np.diff(indptr) or csr_array._getnnz(axis=1) per row is exactly equivalent, so distances and connectivities are unchanged. Two patches are not guaranteed equivalent. (a) count_nonzero, or anything that drops explicit zeros: it differs when duplicate cells give stored zero distances. (b) Total nnz divided by n_obs used without checking every row: it matches only when all rows have the same count, and otherwise reshapes wrongly instead of falling back. Separately, pinning pynndescent<0.7 also avoids the crash but may produce a different approximate kNN graph than 0.7. HOW SURE: high (code path, semantics); medium (exact release number not verified; the 8192 threshold is stated for current scanpy in #4444 and I believe it holds for 1.10, but I could not confirm it in the 1.10 source text I read). SOURCES: https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/issues/4444, https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/pull/4451, https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/issues/2773, https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/blob/1.10.x/src/scanpy/neighbors/_common.py, https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/blob/main/src/scanpy/neighbors/_common.py, https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy-1.12.0/reference/generated/scipy.sparse.csr_array.getnnz.html.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: For the same kNN graph and the same call sc.tl.leiden(adata, resolution=1.0, random_state=0), how reproducible is the partition across scanpy versions (1.9, 1.10, 1.11), leidenalg and igraph versions, and operating systems? And is sc.pp.neighbors itself deterministic across versions and platforms for a dataset of roughly ten thousand cells (when does it use exact kNN versus approximate pynndescent, and is the approximate search seeded)? ANSWER: Leiden: in scanpy 1.10.x the defaults are still flavor='leidenalg', directed=True, n_iterations=-1, random_state=0, the same as 1.9; there is only a FutureWarning about moving to igraph. Given an identical connectivities matrix, leidenalg was deterministic across 4 different CPUs in issue #2014. The 1.9.3 vs 1.10.4 difference reported in #3422 was closed as not planned and attributed to duplicated data (I saw that only in a search snippet). So with the same graph and the same leidenalg/igraph, the partition should reproduce. I found no source guaranteeing identical partitions across leidenalg/igraph versions. Neighbors: scanpy uses exact brute-force sklearn kNN only for the euclidean metric with fewer than 8192 cells; at about 11.7k cells it uses approximate pynndescent. pynndescent is seeded (random_state=0), but its numba-parallel search is not bitwise reproducible across CPUs, thread counts or package versions. Issue #2014 shows Leiden clusters on an X_scVI embedding changing across CPU models in an identical container; disabling the numba JIT or rounding the connectivities made it stable. In #2956 the maintainers say the neighbour graph is not guaranteed reproducible across machines, versions or thread counts (snippet only). Conclusion: a reference run elsewhere may well give a slightly different graph and partition. The exact single-seed number should be treated as one draw within the seed-to-seed spread. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/issues/2014, https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/issues/3422, https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/issues/2956, https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/blob/1.10.x/src/scanpy/tools/_leiden.py, https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/issues/4444.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: When an analysis or benchmark says 'average cluster purity' with per-cluster purity defined as the share of the most common label, is the conventional aggregate the unweighted mean of per-cluster purities or the cell-weighted (overall) purity as in the standard information-retrieval definition? Are there single-cell references that define it explicitly one way or the other? ANSWER: The conventional 'purity' is cell-weighted. Manning et al., IR book eq. 182, defines it as the sum over clusters of the majority-class count divided by N. Tan et al. define overall purity as sum_i (m_i/m) p_i. Single-cell clustering papers that give a formula use the same weighted form; for example GRACE (PLoS ONE 2023) uses Purity = (1/N) sum_j max |y ∩ c_j|, though I saw that formula only in a search snippet. Tools implement both: spine.math.metrics.pur defaults to per_cluster=True ('average equally over predicted clusters'), and per_cluster=False gives the cell-weighted version. I found no single-cell reference that explicitly defines the phrase 'average cluster purity'. The task wording ('average cluster purity, where purity for each cluster is ...') reads most literally as the unweighted mean over clusters, whereas plain 'purity' conventionally means the weighted value. The web does not settle which one the task intends. Report the unweighted mean as primary, since it follows the wording, and the weighted value alongside it. HOW SURE: high that textbook purity is weighted; low on which one the task intends. SOURCES: https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/html/htmledition/evaluation-of-clustering-1.html, http://davide.eynard.it/teaching/2014_PAMI/handout-lecture-e4.pdf, https://spine.readthedocs.io/latest/api/generated/spine.math.metrics.html, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0284527.

text: FINDING: R diptest::dip.test(x, simulate.p.value=FALSE, B=2000) by default gets the p-value by linear interpolation in sqrt(n)*D over the qDiptab table of uniform-null dip quantiles (each n based on 1,000,001 simulated U[0,1] samples); for n above the largest tabulated n it uses that last n as asymptotic (prints a message), which is accurate because sqrt(n)*D is nearly n-free. With simulate.p.value=TRUE it uses P = mean(D <= dip(runif(n))) over B=2000 replicates. Python diptest.diptest(x, boot_pval=False, n_boot=10000) by default interpolates the tabulated critical values (dip_crit.txt); with boot_pval=True it uses 10000 uniform bootstrap samples. Neither package has a ties/discrete-data option or recommends a jitter; the theory (Hartigan & Hartigan 1985: 'a unimodal F may have an atom only at a unique mode') says integer data with many atoms violate the null and inflate significance, so ties should be broken by jitter or a continuous transform. P-values at n of thousands to tens of thousands are numerically reliable, but the test then has power against small departures. A simulation p-value with B replicates has Monte Carlo SE of about sqrt(0.05*0.95/B) (~0.005 at B=2000), so markers near 0.05 can flip if B is small. QUESTION: How do R/Python dip tests compute p-values, with which defaults, how do they handle ties, and is the p-value reliable at large n? text: FINDING: Mosaic Dna.filter_variants defaults are min_dp=10, min_gq=30, vaf_ref=5 (NGT=0 calls with AF>5 become missing), vaf_het=30 (NGT=1 calls with AF<30 become missing), vaf_hom=95 (NGT=2 calls with AF<95 become missing), min_prct_cells=50 (variant must be genotyped, NGT in {0,1,2}, in >=50% of cells, completeness-weighted, after the cell-level filters) and min_mut_prct_cells=1 (mutated, NGT in {1,2}, in >=1% of cells, also completeness-weighted); failing cell-variant calls are set to 3 (missing) in a new NGT_FILTERED layer. text: FINDING: The percentage denominator differs between tools. Mosaic group_by_genotype reports each clone's % over ALL cells passed in, with cells missing at any selected variant pooled into a 'Missing GT clones' group (worked example: 620/3751 = 16.53%, where the total includes 2413 missing-GT cells). The Bowman/Miles scDNA_myeloid workflow first removes every cell with any NGT=3 at the retained variants and computes clone abundance over the complete-genotype cells only. Taken together, 'genotyped cells' in the clone-percentage sense means cells with a passing (non-missing) call at every selected variant, and is computed on NGT_FILTERED in the Mosaic notebooks. A secondary wiki (BBG-Wiki, seen only as a search snippet, not opened) says Tapestri Insights computes its percent filters over genotyped cells and Mosaic over total cells; treat that as unverified. label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Clones are zygosity-aware by default. Mosaic Dna.group_by_genotype(features, layer='NGT', group_missing=True, max_ado_score=1, min_clone_size=1, ignore_zygosity=False) treats HET and HOM as different states unless ignore_zygosity=True, and reports each variant in a clone as WT/Het/Hom. The Bowman/Miles scDNA_myeloid workflow defines a clone as the concatenated NGT string (0/1/2 per variant, joined with '_') over complete-genotype cells, so it is also zygosity-aware. ADO handling: Mosaic labels the HET clone as 'parent' and its HOM and WT single-locus derivatives as 'sister' clones. Each clone gets an ADO score, score = (sister score 0-0.8 + DP score 0-0.1 + GQ score 0-0.1) * parent-size score 0-1. Clones scoring above max_ado_score are pooled into an 'ADO clones' group, clones below min_clone_size (% of total cells, default 1) go into 'Small subclones', and cells with missing calls go into 'Missing'. Bowman instead keeps only clones whose bootstrap (10,000 resamples) lower 95% CI is >=10 cells. Neither tool merges het and hom by default, but both mechanisms remove ADO-sized satellite clones from the named-clone list. QUESTION: Are genotype clones zygosity-aware or binary, and how are ADO/small clones handled? Per-cell background and signal are assumed to depend linearly on the cell's total read counts; a linear model is fitted to each, and the counts are corrected for that dependence. An optional scale-down factor for over-sequenced runs is estimated from peak amplification and reset to 1 if more than 5% of cells would be left with 0 reads. transform() takes only the (#cells x #antibodies) matrix of the Protein assay (called cells). It has no input for non-cell barcodes and no isotype argument. Undocumented: how background vs signal is chosen per cell (isotypes, lowest antibodies or a mixture model), whether total reads enter raw or logged, and the final scaling. Of the two team approaches, within-cell background with regression on read depth matches the docs. An empty-droplet z-score (dsb-like) does not, because NSP never receives non-cell barcodes. HOW SURE: medium (documented parts high; background/signal definition and regressor form not settled). question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In Mission Bio Tapestri analysis (Mosaic and Tapestri Insights), what does the default variant/genotype filtering do (min depth, min GQ, AF windows for ref/het/hom, min % cells genotyped, min % cells mutated), are failing calls set to missing, is the raw NGT layer in the h5 filtered or unfiltered, and which cells count as 'genotyped' when clone sizes are reported? ANSWER: Mosaic Dna.filter_variants defaults: min_dp=10, min_gq=30, vaf_ref=5 (NGT=0 calls with AF>5 become missing), vaf_het=30 (NGT=1 calls with AF<30 become missing), vaf_hom=95 (NGT=2 calls with AF<95 become missing), min_prct_cells=50 (variant must be genotyped in >=50% of cells after the call filters, weighted by cell completeness) and min_mut_prct_cells=1 (mutated in >=1%, also weighted). Failing cell-variant calls are set to 3 (missing) in a new NGT_FILTERED layer; NGT itself is left unchanged. The NGT layer in the pipeline h5 is raw/unfiltered: the pipeline stores only its cutoffs (af/dp/gq cutoffs, missing_cells/missing_variants/mutated_cells cutoffs), a FILTER_MASK layer and filtered flags, and these 'do not actually remove any variants/cells'. Tapestri Insights v2.2 Advanced Filters use one alternate-AF cutoff instead of the three zygosity-specific ones (tapestriR equivalent: GQ 30, DP 10, AF 20, genotyped in >=50%, mutated in >=1%; masking is optional there, gt.mask defaults to FALSE). By platform convention a call that fails DP/GQ/AF is missing, so the cell is not genotyped at that locus. Clone-percentage denominators: Mosaic group_by_genotype divides by all input cells and pools incomplete cells into a 'Missing GT clones' group (in the docs example 620/3751 = 16.53% includes 2413 missing cells). The usual practice (Mosaic notebooks drop the missing group; the Bowman/Miles workflow removes any cell with NGT=3 at retained variants) is to count as genotyped only cells with a passing call at every selected variant. A claim that Tapestri Insights computes percentages over genotyped cells came only from an unopened search snippet (BBG-Wiki) and is unverified. HOW SURE: high for the Mosaic defaults and raw NGT; medium for the 'genotyped cells' denominator convention; low for the exact Tapestri Insights internals. SOURCES: https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/pages/methods/missionbio.mosaic.dna.Dna.filter_variants.html, https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/manual/data_structure.html, https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/v2.4.1/4_data_structure.html, https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/v2.4.1/examples/analysis-walkthrough.html, https://rdrr.io/github/MissionBio/tapestriR/man/filter_variants.html, https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/notebooks/additional-plots-and-customizations.html, https://bowmanr.github.io/scDNA_myeloid/post-processing.html.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: When Tapestri Insights, Mosaic (genotype-grouping / clone-table functions) and published scDNA myeloid clonal workflows define genotype clones from selected variants, is the clone zygosity-aware (WT/het/hom) or binary mutated/not-mutated, and how are small ADO-attributable clones handled or labelled? ANSWER: By default the clone is zygosity-aware. Mosaic group_by_genotype has ignore_zygosity=False by default (HET and HOM are distinct; setting it True merges them) and reports WT/Het/Hom per variant per clone. The Bowman/Miles scDNA_myeloid workflow builds the clone label by joining the 0/1/2 NGT values across variants on complete-genotype cells, which is also zygosity-aware. ADO handling: Mosaic marks the HET clone as 'parent' and its HOM and WT single-locus derivatives as 'sister' clones, and scores each clone as score = (sister score + DP score + GQ score) * parent-size score. Clones above max_ado_score (default 1 in the Dna method, 0.8 in the GroupByGenotype class) are pooled as 'ADO clones', clones below min_clone_size (% of total cells, default 1) as 'Small subclones', and incomplete cells as 'Missing'. Bowman keeps only clones whose bootstrap lower 95% CI is >=10 cells. So het and hom are not merged by default, but ADO-sized satellites are removed from the named-clone list instead of being folded into the parent. I did not find a separate statement for Tapestri Insights. HOW SURE: high for Mosaic and the Bowman workflow; low for Tapestri Insights specifically. SOURCES: https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/pages/methods/missionbio.mosaic.dna.Dna.group_by_genotype.html, https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/notebooks/additional-plots-and-customizations.html, https://bowmanr.github.io/scDNA_myeloid/assessing-clonal-abundance.html, https://bowmanr.github.io/scDNA_myeloid/post-processing.html.

text: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: When Tapestri Insights, Mosaic (genotype-grouping / clone-table functions) and published scDNA myeloid clonal workflows define genotype clones from selected variants, is the clone zygosity-aware (WT/het/hom) or binary mutated/not-mutated, and how are small ADO-attributable clones handled or labelled? ANSWER: By default the clone is zygosity-aware. Mosaic group_by_genotype has ignore_zygosity=False by default (HET and HOM are distinct; setting it True merges them) and reports WT/Het/Hom per variant per clone. The Bowman/Miles scDNA_myeloid workflow builds the clone label by joining the 0/1/2 NGT values across variants on complete-genotype cells, which is also zygosity-aware. ADO handling: Mosaic marks the HET clone as 'parent' and its HOM and WT single-locus derivatives as 'sister' clones, and scores each clone as score = (sister score + DP score + GQ score) * parent-size score. Clones above max_ado_score (default 1 in the Dna method, 0.8 in the GroupByGenotype class) are pooled as 'ADO clones', clones below min_clone_size (% of total cells, default 1) as 'Small subclones', and incomplete cells as 'Missing'. Bowman keeps only clones whose bootstrap lower 95% CI is >=10 cells. So het and hom are not merged by default, but ADO-sized satellites are removed from the named-clone list instead of being folded into the parent. I did not find a separate statement for Tapestri Insights. HOW SURE: high for Mosaic and the Bowman workflow; low for Tapestri Insights specifically. SOURCES: https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/pages/methods/missionbio.mosaic.dna.Dna.group_by_genotype.html, https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/notebooks/additional-plots-and-customizations.html, https://bowmanr.github.io/scDNA_myeloid/assessing-clonal-abundance.html, https://bowmanr.github.io/scDNA_myeloid/post-processing.html.

text: FINDING: normalize_total casts integer counts to float32 (scanpy 1.8-1.10 source: X.astype(np.float32)), and log1p keeps float32. In every version (1.9, 1.10, 1.11) _get_mean_var accumulates the per-gene mean and variance in float64 (ddof=1), and std==0 is set to 1. In 1.11.x scale_array takes sparse input directly and does x -= mean, which scipy runs as x.todense() - mean, so float32 minus float64 gives a float64 dense matrix. In 1.9/1.10, sparse input was apparently densified with toarray(), staying float32, then centered in place (computed in float64, stored as float32); I could not read that code directly because the page was truncated. Either way the sign of each entry is the sign of (float32 value - float64 mean), the same in all versions. Dividing by std and clipping at +/-10 never flip signs, so the negative count should not depend on version or precision except for entries exactly equal to the gene mean. QUESTION: dtype/precision of sc.pp.scale zero_center on sparse normalize_total+log1p data across scanpy 1.9/1.10/1.11. text: FINDING: In scanpy rank_genes_groups(method='wilcoxon', groups=[A], reference=B) the returned score is the rank-sum z-score; documented defaults are tie_correct=False, use_raw=None (meaning adata.raw is used if present), layer=None (otherwise .X), mask_var=None (all genes in the matrix), n_genes=None (ALL genes returned), rankby_abs=False. Genes are sorted by descending signed score, so the top of the list is genes UP in A and genes up in B sit at the bottom with negative scores (all genes are returned, not only up genes). For fixed groups without tie correction z=(U-n1*n2/2)/sqrt(n1*n2*(n1+n2+1)/12), a strictly increasing function of U and therefore of AUC=U/(n1*n2), so the ordering is identical to AUC (confidence high; I could not read this formula in the source because the fetched file was truncated, it comes from the standard Mann-Whitney normal approximation). With tie_correct=True each gene's denominator is scaled by its own tie factor, so the order can differ from AUC, mostly for sparse genes with many zeros. Conclusion: a statistic difference between AUC and default Wilcoxon cannot explain a disagreement; differences come from group definition, gene universe (raw vs HVG .X) or filtering. QUESTION: Is scanpy wilcoxon score ordering the same as AUC, and what are the defaults? SOURCE: https://scanpy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/generated/scanpy.tl.rank_genes_groups.html ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/main/src/scanpy/tools/_rank_genes_groups.py

text: FINDING: No trajectory tool has a 'fixed pseudotime quantile' convention for terminal groups. Slingshot works on clusters: lineages are MST paths from a start cluster to leaf clusters, and end.clus forces clusters to be leaves, so endpoints are whole clusters. scanpy DPT needs one root cell (adata.uns['iroot']), and its docs recommend dpt for pseudotime only, with branches/ends taken from PAGA, whose nodes are clusters. Palantir's identify_terminal_states returns individual terminal cells, and run_palantir takes terminal states as single cell names. CellRank GPCCA computes macrostates as soft cluster groups and keeps a set number of the most likely cells per macrostate (I recall n_cells=30 by default but did not see it on the pages I read). I found no published guidance on how big an end group should be for a two-group DE contrast. The cluster-at-each-end convention (Slingshot, PAGA) is the best-documented one; a quantile tail is an analyst choice. QUESTION: How do trajectory tools define the terminal groups at the two ends? text: FINDING: Yes. Keratin-expressing mesothelial-like cells are an established CAF subtype. Elyada et al. 2019 defined apCAFs (MHC-II/Cd74+) in PDAC after depleting CD45/CD31/EpCAM cells. Huang et al. 2022 (Cancer Cell) used lineage tracing to show that mouse PDAC apCAFs come from mesothelial cells, and their FB3 apCAF clusters express Msln, Upk3b, Krt19, Ezr, Nkain4 and Lrrn4 along with H2-Ab1/Cd74. A 2025 pan-cancer fibroblast atlas (Chen et al.) finds a mesothelial-like apCAF population in most tumour types. Criteria from these papers for a genuine CAF rather than a contaminant: Epcam negative, co-expression of fibroblast genes (Pdpn, Col1a1, Dcn), mesothelial genes (Msln, Upk3b, Lrrn4) and MHC-II, and no tumour or epithelial program. A liver CAF review snippet (full text not read) says Krt8/Krt19-co-expressing CAF-like clusters can be epithelial/CAF doublets. High UMI depth plus keratins plus fibroblast genes is a doublet warning sign, to be checked with a doublet score. The papers read do not say whether such cells are routinely removed before CAF trajectory analysis. Practical advice: keep the cluster if it is Epcam-negative and Msln/Upk3b/MHC-II-positive, remove it if it is Epcam-positive or clearly a doublet, and run both ways. QUESTION: Are Krt8/Krt18+ mesothelial-type cells a genuine CAF subtype or contamination, and should they be kept before trajectory analysis? text: FINDING: Without mito genes, the guides offer these substitutes. sc-best-practices flags outliers at 5 MADs, in both directions, on log1p total counts, log1p genes and pct_counts_in_top_20_genes. It computes ribosomal and hemoglobin fractions only as diagnostics, never as filters. HBC training flags novelty log10(genes)/log10(UMI) below 0.80 (low complexity, which can also be a real cell type such as RBCs). MALAT1/nuclear-fraction QC flags LOW MALAT1 as cells without a nucleus (empty droplets, fragments, erythrocytes), using a data-driven gamma-mixture/density threshold of at least 0.3 normalized; one atlas study used <3.5 normalized counts chosen by eye. DropletQC flags damaged cells as HIGH intronic nuclear fraction plus low UMI, which needs a BAM. No guide gives a universal MALAT1 or ribosomal cut-off. label: FINDING
text: FINDING: The guides say to look at the log-count and log-gene histograms for a single main peak, and to treat a left shoulder or bimodality as possible failed cells (HBC). OSCA says MAD outlier rules assume a high-quality majority that is roughly unimodal or normal on the log scale, and that they fail when that assumption does not hold. None of the pages I read deals directly with a distribution truncated by an upstream hard floor. By the MAD definition (median - k*MAD), though, truncation removes the low tail. The lower bound can then fall below the floor, so zero flagged cells is expected by construction and is not evidence that the data are clean. The barcode-rank knee/inflection (DropletUtils/emptyDrops) separates cells from empty droplets. OSCA states explicitly that this makes no statement about cell quality, so damaged cells must still be found by outlier QC. QUESTION: how to check for residual low-quality cells above an upstream min-genes floor, and how MAD rules behave on truncated data. text: FINDING: The common lower bounds are: the scanpy tutorial's min_genes=100, described as 'very permissive'; Seurat pbmc3k nFeature>200 (with nFeature<2500 and mt<5% as dataset-specific examples); HBC nUMI>=500 and nGene>=300, with 500-1000 UMI 'usable'; Cell Ranger's 500-UMI floor in cell calling; and OSCA's fixed example of library size <500 for 10x PBMC. Adaptive rules are 3 MADs (OSCA default) versus 5 MADs (sc-best-practices, 'relatively permissive'). 10x says these are starting points, not universal, and warns that heterogeneous samples contain low-RNA cells such as neutrophils. None of the guides I read gives tumour-specific ranges. On upper bounds, the guides treat high counts/genes as a multiplet signal. HBC explicitly recommends no max thresholds and says the rationale 'is not accurate'. scanpy and sc-best-practices handle doublets in a separate step (Scrublet/scDblFinder), although sc-best-practices' 5-MAD rule is two-sided. text: FINDING: In scanpy highly_variable_genes (flavor='seurat'), genes are binned by mean with EQUAL-WIDTH pd.cut(means, bins=n_bins) (not quantiles), the within-bin dispersion sd is pandas groupby std, i.e. SAMPLE sd ddof=1 (1.8.x code literally calls std(ddof=1); current code uses agg(dev='std'), same default), and a single-gene bin (std NaN) gets dev=avg and avg=0 so its normalised dispersion is set to 1; a bin with zero spread is not special-cased (division by 0 gives inf/NaN); zero dispersions become NaN before log. flavor='cell_ranger' uses percentile edges np.r_[-inf, percentile(means, 10..100 step 5), inf] with pd.cut and median/MAD; tied percentile edges raise 'Bin edges must be unique' (issue 509), not dropped. label: FINDING
text: FINDING: leidenalg and igraph community_leiden are not guaranteed to give the same partition for the same graph/resolution/seed; they are separate implementations with different RNGs, so seed=0 means different things. Default differences: leidenalg.find_partition n_iterations=2 (scanpy sc.tl.leiden overrides to -1 = until no improvement); igraph community_leiden n_iterations=2, beta=0.01, objective_function default 'CPM' (must pass 'modularity', which scales resolution by 1/2m and uses degrees as node weights automatically); igraph requires an UNDIRECTED graph whereas scanpy's leidenalg path builds a DIRECTED graph (directed=True by default) with both edge directions; igraph uses weights only if passed / weight attribute present, scanpy use_weights=True passes connectivities weights. Modularity with RBConfiguration on a directed symmetric graph is equivalent in objective to the undirected one, so count differences come mainly from iterations (2 vs converged), CPM vs modularity, unweighted vs weighted, and RNG, not the objective. Teams should compare like with like: objective='modularity', weights='weight', n_iterations=-1 in both, then attribute any remaining difference to implementation/RNG. QUESTION: do leidenalg RBConfiguration and igraph community_leiden(modularity) agree, and which defaults explain differences. label: FINDING
text: FINDING: scanpy sc.tl.score_genes bins the gene pool by each gene's mean expression across cells (rank of mean // round(n_genes/(n_bins-1)), n_bins=25), draws up to ctrl_size=50 random genes from every bin that holds a gene-set gene, and scores each cell as mean(gene set) minus mean(control genes). On a z-scored matrix every gene's mean is about 0, so the bins are set by floating-point noise and control genes are effectively random; the control mean is about 0, so the score reduces to the mean z-score of the set genes. The binning artefact itself is therefore harmless, but the score's spread shrinks as the set grows (averaging), so argmax across sets of different sizes is biased. use_raw=None means True only if adata.raw exists, otherwise adata.X (or the given layer) is used. QUESTION: How does score_genes behave on z-scored input, what does use_raw default to, and are scores comparable across set sizes?
