question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In scanpy's sc.pp.scale with zero_center=True applied to a sparse matrix that came from integer counts through normalize_total and log1p, what floating-point dtype does the densified matrix have, and in what precision are the per-gene mean and standard deviation computed and subtracted? Has this changed between scanpy 1.9, 1.10 and 1.11+? ANSWER: normalize_total casts integer counts to float32 (X.astype(np.float32)), and log1p keeps float32. In 1.9, 1.10 and 1.11, _get_mean_var accumulates the per-gene mean and variance in float64 (sparse kernels and dense np.mean use dtype=np.float64; variance is ddof=1; std==0 is set to 1). In 1.11.x, scale_array accepts CSR/CSC directly and does `x -= mean` on the sparse matrix. scipy runs that as x.todense() - mean, so float32 minus float64 gives a float64 dense result (dematrix turns it into an ndarray). For 1.9/1.10, the sparse path is believed to densify with toarray() (staying float32) and then subtract the float64 mean in place, computing in float64 and storing in float32. I could not read that branch directly because the fetched pages were truncated. So the densified dtype does change: float32 in 1.9/1.10, likely; float64 in 1.11+, from the source I read. In every version, though, the sign of each scaled entry is the sign of (float32 log value - float64 mean), because a nonzero float64 difference does not round to zero in float32. Dividing by std and clipping at +/-10 cannot flip a sign. The count of negatives should therefore be the same across versions and precisions, except for entries exactly equal to their gene mean, which are vanishingly rare. A shift at the second decimal should not come from this source. HOW SURE: medium (high for float64 mean/var and float32 normalize_total; medium for the exact 1.9/1.10 densify path, which I saw only partly). SOURCES: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/1.11.x/src/scanpy/preprocessing/_scale.py, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/1.10.x/src/scanpy/preprocessing/_scale.py, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/1.9.x/scanpy/preprocessing/_utils.py, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/1.11.x/src/scanpy/preprocessing/_utils.py, https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/blob/1.10.x/src/scanpy/preprocessing/%5Fnormalization.py, https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/v1.16.0/scipy/sparse/_base.py.

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Cook's handling, read from source code. Both DESeq2 and PyDESeq2 use the cutoff F.ppf(0.99, p, m-p), where p = number of design-matrix columns and m = number of samples. P-value flagging only looks at samples whose exact design-matrix row occurs at least 3 times (nOrMoreInCell n=3 / n_or_more_replicates). Count replacement plus refitting needs at least 7 copies of the row (minReplicatesForReplace=7 / min_replicates=7). Replacement value = int(trimmed mean (trim=0.2) of normalised counts over ALL samples x size factor), applied only to replaceable samples. In ~donor + condition, every donor x condition row is unique (1 sample each), so no sample is eligible: no p-values are set to NA, no counts are replaced, nothing is refit. In R, recordMaxCooks gives maxCooks=NA. In PyDESeq2, use_for_max is all False, so cooks_outlier is all False, and _replace_outliers returns early with replaced=False. Under ~condition with 7 or more donors per arm, both flagging and replacement/refit happen. Differences: R applies the 'do not flag if 3 or more samples have larger counts than the max-Cook's sample' rule only when the design has one 2-level factor; PyDESeq2 applies it to every design. R's Cook's distance is computed on dispModelMatrix with a robust trimmed-moment dispersion (minDisp 0.04); PyDESeq2 does the same via robust_method_of_moments_disp. So any count change under a donor-blocked design is not reference behaviour. QUESTION: DESeq2/PyDESeq2 default Cook's outlier cutoff, replicate requirements, and behaviour in a blocked design. QUESTION: When a task specifies only library-size normalization, log1p and per-gene z-score scaling for a single-cell matrix whose cells come from several samples, is the scanpy convention (sc.pp.scale) to scale each gene over all cells pooled, and does any standard scanpy or Seurat workflow scale within sample by default? Neither default workflow scales within sample, so the pooled reading is the conventional one. I did not check how Seurat v5 handles split layers. HOW SURE: high. text: FINDING: Independent filtering, read from source code. The filter statistic is baseMean (mean of normalised counts over all genes, including all-zero genes). lower = mean(baseMean==0); upper = 0.95 if lower<0.95 else 1; theta = 50 evenly spaced values from lower to upper (np.linspace / seq length.out=50); cutoffs = quantile(baseMean, theta), linear (R type 7 = numpy default). For each cutoff, keep genes with baseMean >= cutoff and run BH on their non-NA p-values (PyDESeq2 drops NaN explicitly; R p.adjust ignores NA). Genes below the cutoff, Cook's-flagged genes and NA p-values get padj = NA. numRej = count of padj < alpha. Fit lowess(theta, numRej, f=1/5, 3 robustness iterations). If max(numRej) <= 10, use j = first theta (no filtering). Otherwise thresh = max(lowess fit) - sqrt(mean((numRej - fit)^2 over points with numRej>0)), and j = the first theta with numRej > thresh. R adds fallbacks (first numRej > 0.9*maxFit, then > 0.8*maxFit, else the first theta); PyDESeq2 falls back straight to the first theta. Default alpha: PyDESeq2 DeseqStats alpha=0.05; R results() alpha=0.1, so set alpha=0.05 in R to match the padj<0.05 cutoff. pAdjustMethod is BH. PyDESeq2 uses its own lowess, which approximates R's but is not bit-identical. QUESTION: Default independent-filtering algorithm and alpha in PyDESeq2 DeseqStats and in DESeq2 results(). text: FINDING: Dispersion defaults, read from source code. Gene-wise: min_disp=1e-8, max_disp=max(10, n_samples). Both packages use a Cox-Reid adjusted NB likelihood on log(alpha), starting from moment/rough estimates. PyDESeq2 optimises with scipy L-BFGS-B bounded to [log 1e-8, log max_disp] and falls back to a grid search if it fails; R uses C++ backtracking line search (kappa_0=1, dispTol=1e-6, maxit=100) with a grid fallback; results are clipped to [minDisp, maxDisp]. Mu for the gene-wise fit is a linear model when #unique design rows == #columns, otherwise IRLS (PyDESeq2; minmu 0.5). Trend: alpha(mu) = a0 + a1/mu, fitted by an iterated Gamma-family identity-link GLM. R starts at (0.1, 1), keeps genes with dispGeneEst > 100*minDisp, and refits each iteration on genes with ratio disp/fit in (1e-4, 15). It stops when sum(log(new/old)^2) < 1e-6 and the GLM has converged; if any coefficient <= 0 or there are more than 10 iterations it raises an error, and DESeq2 switches to fitType='local' (locfit). PyDESeq2 instead fits by L-BFGS-B on all non-zero genes, starting at (1,1), drops genes with ratio < 1e-4 or >= 15 before the next fit, and falls back to a MEAN trend (trimmed mean, 0.001, of gene-wise dispersions > 10*min_disp), not local. Prior: varLogDispEsts = MAD(log gene-wise disp - log trend)^2 over genes with gene-wise disp >= 100*minDisp; R mad uses constant 1.4826, PyDESeq2 uses 1/norm.ppf(0.75). prior var = max(varLogDispEsts - trigamma((m-p)/2), 0.25); R alone switches to a simulation/KL estimate when 1 <= m-p <= 3. MAP: Cox-Reid likelihood + Gaussian log-prior centred on log(trend). Genes are not shrunk (they keep the gene-wise value) if log(genewise) > log(trend) + 2*sqrt(varLogDispEsts) (outlierSD=2). LFC: DESeq2 betaPrior=FALSE by default and PyDESeq2 has no prior, so the Wald test uses MLE LFCs with only a tiny ridge (1e-6) on each coefficient; prior_LFC_var=None, lfc_null=0, and apeglm shrinkage does not change p-values. QUESTION: Default dispersion estimation details in PyDESeq2/DESeq2 and whether an LFC prior is used before the Wald test. QUESTION: In scanpy's rank_genes_groups with method='wilcoxon' and an explicit reference group, is ordering by score the same as ordering by AUC, with and without tie correction? Does it list only up genes; which gene universe/matrix (use_raw, layers) and how many genes by default? ANSWER: Without tie correction (the default, tie_correct=False), yes. For fixed groups the score is the Mann-Whitney z=(U-n1*n2/2)/sqrt(n1*n2*(n1+n2+1)/12), a strictly increasing function of U and therefore of AUC=U/(n1*n2), so both give the same gene order. With tie_correct=True each gene's denominator is scaled by its own tie factor, so the order can differ from AUC, mainly for sparse genes with many zeros. The formula is the standard normal approximation: the fetched source file was truncated before the scoring code, and the docs only say the score is the z-score behind the p-value. Defaults: use_raw=None (uses adata.raw if present, else .X), layer=None, mask_var=None (all genes in the matrix used), n_genes=None (all genes returned), rankby_abs=False. Genes are sorted by descending signed score, so genes up in the tested group come first and genes up in the reference come last with negative scores. Not only up genes are returned, but the top-N of one call describes only the tested group. The statistic cannot explain the teams' disagreement; group definition, gene universe (raw/all genes vs HVG-subset .X) and filtering can. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://scanpy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/generated/scanpy.tl.rank_genes_groups.html, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/main/src/scanpy/tools/_rank_genes_groups.py, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/1.9.8/scanpy/tools/_rank_genes_groups.py.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: How are terminal cell groups at the two ends of a single dominant trajectory defined by default/convention in DPT, PAGA, Slingshot, Palantir, CellRank; is there guidance on end-group size for a two-group DE contrast? ANSWER: No tool I read defines ends as a fixed pseudotime quantile. Slingshot: lineages are MST paths from a start cluster to leaf clusters, and end.clus forces chosen clusters to be leaves, so ends are whole clusters. scanpy DPT: needs one root cell (uns['iroot']); its docs recommend dpt for pseudotime only and PAGA (nodes are clusters) for branch structure. Palantir: identify_terminal_states returns individual terminal cells, and run_palantir takes terminal states as single cell names. CellRank GPCCA: terminal states are macrostates (soft cluster groups) restricted to a set number of the most likely cells. I recall the default as n_cells=30 but did not see it on the pages read. I found no published guidance on how large an end group should be for a DE contrast. The cluster-at-each-end convention (Slingshot/PAGA) is the best documented; a quantile tail is an analyst's choice. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://github.com/kstreet13/slingshot/blob/main/man/getLineages.Rd, https://scanpy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/generated/scanpy.tl.dpt.html, https://palantir.readthedocs.io/en/stable/core.html, https://cellrank.readthedocs.io/en/latest/notebooks/tutorials/estimators/600_initial_terminal.html, https://cellrank.readthedocs.io/en/latest/api/_autosummary/estimators/cellrank.estimators.GPCCA.html.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In scanpy's highly_variable_genes with the dispersion-based flavors, when dispersions are normalised within mean-expression bins, which degrees-of-freedom convention does the within-bin standard deviation use (sample or population), how are genes binned by mean (equal-width cut or quantile cut, and how are tied bin edges handled), and how is a bin with a single gene or zero spread treated? ANSWER: Within-bin SD is the pandas groupby std, i.e. sample SD with ddof=1 (the 1.8.x code calls disp_grouped.std(ddof=1); current scanpy/rapids code uses agg(avg='mean', dev='std'), which has the same default). flavor='seurat' bins by EQUAL-WIDTH pd.cut(means, bins=n_bins=20), not quantiles. flavor='cell_ranger' uses percentile edges np.r_[-inf, np.percentile(means, arange(10,105,5)), inf] passed to pd.cut and normalises with median/MAD. Tied percentile edges (e.g. many zero-mean genes) raise 'ValueError: Bin edges must be unique' (issue 509); they are not dropped or rank-broken. In a single-gene bin the std is NaN, so scanpy sets dev=avg and avg=0, which makes that gene's normalised dispersion exactly 1. A bin with zero spread but more than one gene is not special-cased, so the division by 0 gives inf/NaN. In seurat flavor zero dispersions are set to NaN before the log, and zero means are set to 1e-12. So scanpy has no equal-frequency precedent for the task's rule; the only convention it supplies is ddof=1 for the within-bin SD. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/theislab/scanpy/1.8.x/scanpy/preprocessing/_deprecated/highly_variable_genes.py, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/rapids_singlecell/81167a7c/src/rapids_singlecell/preprocessing/_hvg.py, https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/issues/509.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: How does scanpy's sc.tl.score_genes behave when the expression matrix it is given is already z-scored per gene (every gene has mean 0 and unit variance): how are the control genes binned and sampled in that case, what does the use_raw default do when no raw attribute exists, and is the resulting score still comparable between gene sets of different sizes? ANSWER: From the source code: genes in the pool are binned by mean expression across cells. The bin is rank(mean, method='min') // round(n_genes/(n_bins-1)), with n_bins=25. For each bin containing a set gene, up to ctrl_size=50 random genes are drawn (set genes are removed from the controls). The score is mean(set genes) minus mean(control genes) per cell. On z-scored input every gene's mean is about 0, so the bins come from floating-point noise and the control genes are effectively a random sample of all genes. Their per-cell mean is about 0, so the score reduces to the mean z-score of the set genes. The degenerate binning therefore adds little artefact by itself. However, the scores are not well comparable between sets of different sizes: averaging more genes shrinks the spread of the score, and every gene gets equal weight whatever its real expression level, so argmax across sets is biased. use_raw=None resolves to True only if adata.raw exists. Otherwise adata.X (or the given layer) is used, so with no raw the scaled X is scored. This last point comes from the docs and the check_use_raw call, not from reading check_use_raw itself. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/1.9.6/scanpy/tools/_score_genes.py, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/main/src/scanpy/tools/_score_genes.py, https://scanpy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/generated/scanpy.tl.score_genes.html.

text: FINDING: popv_prediction_score is an integer vote count: how many of popV's classifiers (eight in the paper) agree with the consensus label popv_prediction. When the Cell Ontology is used, each method's vote is spread along the ontology path from the root to its predicted term and majority voting is done on these spread votes, so the score is the number of agreeing votes for the chosen term. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In DESeq2 and in PyDESeq2, how exactly are Cook's-distance outliers handled by default: what is the cutoff (which F quantile and degrees of freedom), how many replicates per unique design-matrix row are required for a sample to be eligible for p-value flagging and for count replacement with refitting, and what happens in a blocked design such as ~donor + condition where every unique design row has a single sample? Do DESeq2 and PyDESeq2 differ here? ANSWER: Cutoff in both packages: F quantile 0.99 with df (p, m-p), where p = number of design-matrix columns and m = number of samples (qf(.99,p,m-p) / scipy f.ppf(0.99,p,m-p)). P-value flagging: only samples whose exact design-matrix row appears at least 3 times are used for maxCooks (nOrMoreInCell n=3 / n_or_more_replicates(...,3)); a gene whose max Cook's distance over those samples exceeds the cutoff gets pvalue=NA. Replacement and refit: samples need at least 7 copies of their design row (DESeq minReplicatesForReplace=7 / DeseqDataSet min_replicates=7, refit_cooks=True). Flagged counts in those samples are replaced by int(trimmed mean (trim=0.2) of normalised counts over all samples x size factor), then dispersions and LFCs are refit for the replaced genes. Under ~donor + condition with one pseudobulk per donor x condition, every row is unique (count 1), so no sample is eligible for either step: nothing is flagged (R maxCooks=NA; PyDESeq2 use_for_max all False, so cooks_outlier is all False), nothing is replaced, and nothing is refit (R sufficientReps=FALSE; PyDESeq2 _replace_outliers returns early with replaced=False). Cook's handling should therefore change nothing in the donor-blocked design. Under ~condition with 7 or more donors per arm, both flagging and replacement/refit apply. Differences: (a) R applies the heuristic 'do not flag if 3 or more samples have counts larger than the max-Cook's sample's count' only when the design is a single 2-level factor; PyDESeq2 applies it to every design. (b) R replaceOutliers returns early if m <= p. Both compute Cook's distance using a robust trimmed method-of-moments dispersion (floor 0.04) and the hat diagonals of the final fit. HOW SURE: high. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: What is the exact default independent-filtering algorithm in PyDESeq2's DeseqStats and in DESeq2's results(): which quantile grid of the mean normalised count is tried, how is the threshold chosen (lowess fit of rejections and the rule relative to the maximum), which alpha is used by default in each, and how are genes with missing p-values treated in the BH adjustment? ANSWER: Filter statistic: baseMean over all genes. lower = mean(baseMean == 0); upper = 0.95 if lower < 0.95 else 1; theta = 50 equally spaced values from lower to upper; cutoffs = quantile(baseMean, theta), linear interpolation (R type 7 = numpy default). For each cutoff, BH is applied to the p-values of genes with baseMean >= cutoff (>=, not >). NA p-values (e.g. Cook's-flagged) are excluded from the BH count n: PyDESeq2 drops them explicitly and R p.adjust ignores NAs. They and all genes below the cutoff get padj = NA. numRej[i] = number of padj < alpha. Fit lowess(theta, numRej, f=1/5, 3 robustness iterations). If max(numRej) <= 10, use the first theta (effectively no filtering). Otherwise residual = numRej - fit over points with numRej > 0, thresh = max(fit) - sqrt(mean(residual^2)), and the chosen theta is the FIRST with numRej > thresh. R adds fallbacks (first numRej > 0.9*maxFit, then > 0.8*maxFit, else the first theta); PyDESeq2 goes straight to the first theta. Final padj = the BH column at that theta. Default alpha: PyDESeq2 DeseqStats alpha=0.05; DESeq2 results() alpha=0.1, so R must be called with alpha=0.05 to match a padj<0.05 cutoff. The method is BH in both. PyDESeq2 uses its own Python lowess, which approximates R's C lowess but is not guaranteed bit-identical. NaN padj should be counted as not significant. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/PyDESeq2/main/src/pydeseq2/ds.py, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/PyDESeq2/main/src/pydeseq2/stats.py, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/thelovelab/DESeq2/devel/R/results.R.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In PyDESeq2 (and where it differs, DESeq2), what are the default details of dispersion estimation that a hand-written reimplementation must match: bounds (min/max dispersion) and optimiser for gene-wise Cox-Reid estimates, the iterative parametric gamma-GLM trend fit and its fallback when it fails, how the prior variance is estimated, the rule for genes whose gene-wise dispersion is far above the trend (not shrunk), and whether any prior is placed on the log fold change before the Wald test? ANSWER: Bounds: min_disp=1e-8; max_disp = max(10, n_samples) in both. Gene-wise step: maximise NB log-likelihood + Cox-Reid term (-0.5*logdet(X'WX), W = mu/(1+mu*alpha)) over log(alpha). The start value comes from rough/moment estimates, and mu comes from a linear model if #unique design rows == #columns, otherwise IRLS (minmu 0.5). PyDESeq2 uses scipy L-BFGS-B with bounds [log 1e-8, log max_disp] and an analytic gradient, plus a grid-search fallback if it fails. R uses a C++ backtracking line search (kappa_0=1, dispTol=1e-6, maxit=100) with grid refit for non-converged genes. Both clip results to [minDisp, maxDisp]. Trend (parametric): disp = a0 + a1/baseMean, fitted by a Gamma-family identity-link GLM. In R (parametricDispersionFit), only genes with dispGeneEst > 100*minDisp are used, start coefs are (0.1, 1), and each iteration fits only genes whose disp/fit ratio is in (1e-4, 15). It stops when sum(log(new/old)^2) < 1e-6 and the GLM converged. It errors if any coefficient <= 0 or there are more than 10 iterations, and DESeq() then falls back to fitType='local' (locfit on log scale, weighted by mean). PyDESeq2 minimises the gamma deviance-like loss mean(y/mu + log mu) with L-BFGS-B, starting at (1,1). Its first fit uses all non-zero genes (no 100*minDisp filter); genes with ratio < 1e-4 or >= 15 are dropped before the next iteration, with the same 1e-6 stopping rule. If the fit fails to converge or any coefficient is <= 1e-10, it falls back to a MEAN trend (trimmed mean, proportiontocut=0.001, of gene-wise dispersions > 10*min_disp), not local. Prior variance: varLogDispEsts = MAD(log genewise - log trend)^2 over non-zero genes with genewise >= 100*minDisp (MAD scaled to normal: 1.4826 in R, 1/norm.ppf(0.75) in PyDESeq2). prior_var = max(varLogDispEsts - trigamma((m-p)/2), 0.25). R alone switches to a Monte Carlo KL-matching estimate when 1 <= m-p <= 3; PyDESeq2 only warns. MAP step: Cox-Reid likelihood + (log alpha - log trend)^2/(2*prior_var), same optimiser and bounds. Shrinkage exception: if log(genewise) > log(trend) + 2*sqrt(varLogDispEsts) (outlierSD=2; uses varLogDispEsts, not prior_var), the final dispersion is the gene-wise estimate. LFC prior: none by default. DESeq2 betaPrior=FALSE; PyDESeq2 fits MLE LFCs by IRLS with only a negligible ridge of 1e-6 per coefficient (prior_LFC_var=None) and runs the Wald test (normal null, lfc_null=0) on these unshrunken LFCs. apeglm shrinkage (lfc_shrink) is optional and does not change p-values. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/PyDESeq2/main/src/pydeseq2/dds.py, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/PyDESeq2/main/src/pydeseq2/dispersions.py, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/PyDESeq2/main/src/pydeseq2/default_inference.py, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/PyDESeq2/main/src/pydeseq2/ds.py, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/PyDESeq2/main/src/pydeseq2/stats.py, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/thelovelab/DESeq2/devel/R/core.R, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/thelovelab/DESeq2/devel/R/methods.R.

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: edgeR filterByExpr and decoupler filter_by_expr share defaults min_count=10, min_total_count=15, large_n=10, min_prop=0.7. The rule is depth-aware: CPM cutoff = min_count/median(library size)*1e6, and a gene is kept if CPM>=cutoff in at least n samples AND its total raw count >=15. n is the smallest group size when group is given. With a design and no group it is 1/max(hat value); for a balanced ~donor+condition design with 7 pairs that is 14/8=1.75, so effectively 2 samples. With neither group nor design (decoupler group=None) it is all samples. If n>10, n is relaxed to 10+(n-10)*0.7, so 14 samples become 12.8. The DESeq2 vignette's pre-filter is keep <- rowSums(counts(dds) >= 10) >= smallestGroupSize. It uses raw counts, so it is not depth-aware, and it is optional because independent filtering exists. For 7 vs 7 this is >=10 raw counts in >=7 samples. QUESTION: default low-expression filters in pseudobulk DE workflows. label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Neither DESeq2 nor PyDESeq2 sets the p-value of a gene to NA because the reference condition is all zero. Only rows that are zero in every sample get NA (R) or have it set (Cook's outliers aside), so such genes keep a finite, bounded MLE LFC plus a Wald p-value and padj, unless independent filtering removes them for low baseMean. Ridge penalty: R uses lambda=1e-6 on the log2 scale (converted as lambda/log(2)^2); PyDESeq2 uses ridge_factor=1e-6 on the natural-log scale. R: IRLS runs up to maxit=100 with betaTol=1e-8. Rows that do not converge or are unstable are refit with optim L-BFGS-B, with bounds -30..30 on the LOG2 scale (large <- 30). PyDESeq2: irls_solver has min_beta=-30 and max_beta=30 on the NATURAL-LOG scale (about +-43.3 in log2) and maxiter=250. If any |beta|>30 or maxiter is reached, it switches to L-BFGS-B with those bounds; when there are <=2 variables and that fails, it falls back to grid search. min_mu is 0.5 in both. The reported log2FoldChange is beta/ln2. So the two tools can give different LFC values for zero-baseline genes, and those values sit near the bounds and depend on the optimizer. The web did not settle whether such genes end up significant; that depends on the fitted SE. QUESTION: MLE LFC and p-value for a gene with zero counts in every reference sample. label: FINDING
text: FINDING: The independent filter statistic is baseMean, the mean of normalized counts. theta is 50 evenly spaced quantiles from lowerQuantile=mean(baseMean==0) to 0.95, or to 1 if lowerQuantile>=0.95. At each quantile cutoff, BH is applied to genes with baseMean>=cutoff and non-NA p-values, and rejections are counted at padj<alpha. alpha is 0.1 in R and 0.05 in PyDESeq2. A lowess curve (f=1/5) is fitted to rejections against theta. If max rejections<=10, no filtering is done. Otherwise thresh = max(lowess fit) - RMSE of residuals (residuals only where rejections>0), and the first theta whose rejections exceed thresh is chosen. R has extra fallbacks at 90% and then 80% of max fit; PyDESeq2 falls back to the first theta. Genes below the cutoff get padj=NA. Cook's handling in a paired ~donor+condition design with no replicates within a donor-by-condition cell: Cook's flagging only uses samples whose design-matrix row occurs >=3 times. Replacement needs >=7 samples with an identical design-matrix row (minReplicatesForReplace=7 / min_replicates=7). Every sample is its own design cell here, so by default no gene is flagged as a Cook's outlier and no counts are replaced. Cook's settings therefore do not change the result in this design. The cutoff, if it were used, is the F(0.99; p, m-p) quantile. QUESTION: independent filtering threshold rule and Cook's defaults for a paired design. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In scanpy, which highly-variable-gene flavors operate on raw counts and which of them run without the scikit-misc package (for example the experimental Pearson-residuals HVG function), and how closely do their gene sets usually agree with flavor='seurat_v3'? ANSWER: sc.pp.highly_variable_genes expects log-normalized data for 'seurat' and 'cell_ranger', and raw counts only for 'seurat_v3'/'seurat_v3_paper'. The docs say those two count flavors require scikit-misc. The dependency-free count-based option is sc.experimental.pp.highly_variable_genes(flavor='pearson_residuals', n_top_genes=..., layer='counts'). It expects raw counts and ranks genes by the variance of analytic NB Pearson residuals (theta=100, clipping at sqrt(n_obs)); its docs list no scikit-misc requirement. The pages read give no numeric overlap with seurat_v3. A 2023 preprint (seen as a search snippet only) says SCTransform and scanpy Pearson residuals usually rank the same genes highest, but scores within the top 2000 can be unstable. The teams should therefore measure the overlap (Jaccard) and the agreement of the PC1 top-20 directly rather than assume a value. HOW SURE: high for flavor inputs and dependencies; low for the overlap (not settled by the pages read). SOURCES: https://scanpy.scverse.org/en/latest/api/generated/scanpy.pp.highly_variable_genes.html, https://scanpy.scverse.org/en/stable/generated/scanpy.experimental.pp.highly_variable_genes.html, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13059-021-02451-7, https://scanpy.scverse.org/en/stable/tutorials/experimental/pearson_residuals.html.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In the popV cell-type annotation tool, what does the integer prediction score stored alongside the consensus prediction mean (how is it computed, what is its range), and which score values are conventionally treated as reliable annotations? ANSWER: popv_prediction_score counts how many of popV's classifiers (eight in the paper) agree with the consensus label. With the Cell Ontology, each method's vote is spread along the ontology path from the root to its predicted term, majority voting is done on these spread votes, and the score is the vote count for the chosen term. Its range runs up to the number of methods used; the 1-6 seen in this file suggests six methods or fast mode, which is an inference. The popV docs say one dissenting classifier is still highly reliable, while more than two dissenting classifiers means less reliable results. So scores of N or N-1 (here 6 and 5) are reliable, and restricting to high-score cells is a valid confidence filter. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://popv.readthedocs.io/en/stable/, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-024-01993-3/figures/4, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-024-01993-3.

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: The plate edge effect is conventionally the outer ring of wells (row A/H, col 1/12 on a 96-well plate), but culture studies show it can reach rows 2-3 (VWR plates: outer -35%, row 2 -25%, row 3 -10% vs centre; Greiner: -16%, -7%, -1%); HTS literature models spatial bias as row and column effects (B-score/median polish, Loess), with edge effect a special case; no standard R2 cut-off exists, so magnitude is judged as percent difference vs centre wells or as row/column bias size relative to signal, and the R2 thresholds such as 0.02 or 0.3 are analyst choices, not field conventions. QUESTION: How is a plate edge effect conventionally defined and quantified, and with what thresholds? SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8024881/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4653387/ ; https://www.quantics.co.uk/blog/plate-layout/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4318693/

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Plate-design references say that putting controls on the plate edge or in outer columns makes them sensitive to edge effects, and that control-based normalization can then introduce bias; positional normalization (B-score, Loess) works poorly when actives are dense or clustered (above about 20% hit rate, the B-score normalizes incorrectly); scattered or randomized layouts are recommended so that plate effects can be estimated and corrected; when treatment is fully aliased with position, a position correction cannot separate plate bias from treatment and can remove real signal, so the evidence needed is an independent estimate of the position effect (uniformity/blank plates, or the same condition replicated across positions); none of the sources read explicitly says to normalize anyway. QUESTION: Is positional normalization warranted when treatment is fully aliased with well position and controls sit on one edge? SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4653387/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4318693/ ; https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ailsci.2023.100073 ; https://www.quantics.co.uk/blog/plate-layout/

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: A CSR matrix in h5ad can hold repeated column indices within a row, because the anndata format stores the raw data/indices/indptr arrays as they are in memory and scipy allows duplicates (the (data, indices, indptr) constructor does not merge them, while the (data,(i,j)) constructor does). scipy getnnz(axis=1) is np.diff(indptr), so it counts each stored entry separately, duplicates and explicit zeros included. count_nonzero calls sum_duplicates first. (X > 0) uses _scalar_binopt, which calls self.sum_duplicates() in place before comparing, so (X > 0).sum(axis=1) counts distinct genes after summing. scanpy filter_cells(min_genes) computes sum(X > 0, axis=1), so duplicates are merged first and the count can be lower than a per-entry count. normalize_total divides every stored value by a per-row total from a row sum, which adds duplicates together, so CP10K totals come out right either way. An elementwise log1p on X.data would be wrong for split duplicates (log1p(a)+log1p(b) != log1p(a+b)). CHECK: compare np.diff(indptr) with the per-row count of unique indices, or test X.has_canonical_format after sum_duplicates on a copy. QUESTION: Can an h5ad CSR contain repeated column indices in a row, and do getnnz, (X>0).sum, filter_cells and normalize_total count them separately or sum them first? SOURCE: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scipy/scipy/main/scipy/sparse/_compressed.py ; https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/v1.17.0/scipy/sparse/_compressed.py (_scalar_binopt, read only as a search excerpt) ; https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/5807 ; https://anndata.readthedocs.io/en/latest/fileformat-prose.html ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/1.10.4/src/scanpy/preprocessing/_simple.py ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/1.10.4/src/scanpy/preprocessing/_normalization.py.

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: scanpy sc.pp.filter_cells(min_genes=N) is inclusive. It keeps cells with n_genes >= N, where n_genes = sum(X > 0, axis=1); the code is cell_subset = number_per_cell >= min_number, and the docstring example says filter_cells(adata, min_genes=3) matches adata[adata.obs['n_genes'] >= 3]. There is no strict option. The usual way to get '> N' is to mask directly, e.g. adata[adata.obs['n_genes'] > N] or a mask of (X > 0).sum(1) > N, or for integer counts to call filter_cells(min_genes=N+1). So the task's 'n_genes > 1000' equals min_genes=1001, and a default min_genes=1000 pipeline would also keep nuclei with exactly 1000 genes. QUESTION: Is filter_cells(min_genes=N) inclusive (>= N), and how do you express a strict > N filter? SOURCE: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/1.10.4/src/scanpy/preprocessing/_simple.py ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/main/src/scanpy/preprocessing/_simple.py.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In Mission Bio's mosaic Python package, when a Tapestri multi-sample .h5 file is loaded with ms.load() using default arguments, how is the DNA variant assay assembled (union/intersection of per-sample ca/filtered==0 variants, cell concatenation, genotype for absent/failing variants), and what do 'single' and 'raw' change? ANSWER: Defaults are single=False, filter_variants=True, raw=False, filter_cells=False. load() returns a SampleGroup with one Sample/Dna object per sample. It does not concatenate cells. You get one cells-by-variants matrix only from SampleGroup.merge()/merge_assay(), which concatenate cells and rename barcodes to include sample names, or from single=True, which returns one merged Sample object. With filter_variants=True, load() keeps the variants that pass the stored 'filtered' column attribute (ca/filtered); it does not re-run filter_variants(). The SampleGroup class (match_ids=True) requires assay ids to be the same in every sample. Mission Bio's multisample notebooks then subset every sample to the UNION of the per-sample passing variants (sample.dna[:, var_union]), which points to union as the vendor's convention. The docs do not say how load() itself reconciles different per-sample passing sets, or what genotype a sample gets for a variant it lacks, so union versus intersection at load time and the fill value are NOT settled by the web. raw=True loads all barcodes instead of only cell-associated ones, plus the raw counts (cnv_raw/protein_raw). HOW SURE: medium for object structure and arguments; low for the combination rule and fill value (not documented). SOURCES: https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/pages/functions/missionbio.mosaic.io.load.html, https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/pages/missionbio.mosaic.samplegroup.SampleGroup.html, https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/pages/methods/missionbio.mosaic.samplegroup.SampleGroup.merge_assay.html, https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/notebooks/multi-sample-analysis.html, https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/notebooks/curated_notebooks/dna-multisample.html.

Does load() by default run Dna.filter_variants() so the variant set differs from ca/filtered==0? ANSWER: load() does not re-run filter_variants() by default. With variant_filter_config=None it loads the 'default pre-filtered data', i.e. the variants passing the stored ca/filtered flag (plus any whitelist); only passing variant_filter_config triggers recomputation. So the loaded set equals ca/filtered==0. The docs say the stored gq/dp/af cutoffs are used to compute FILTER_MASK and the 'filtered' row and column attributes, and that they 'do not actually remove' anything. The masked layer NGT_FILTERED is added by Dna.filter_variants() as a copy of NGT with failing cell-variant entries set to 3. Together these imply that the loaded NGT is the stored, unmasked NGT. No page I read states outright that load() leaves NGT unchanged: the data-structure page's layer table was cut off. This part is an inference. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/pages/functions/missionbio.mosaic.io.load.html, https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/manual/data_structure.html, https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/pages/methods/missionbio.mosaic.dna.Dna.filter_variants.html, https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/v2.4.1/4_data_structure.html, https://bbglab.github.io/bbgwiki/Methods/Sequencing/singleCell/Mosaic/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In Tapestri pipeline / Tapestri Insights, how is 'genotyped'/'missing' defined for 'remove variants genotyped in < X% of cells' and 'remove cells with < X% of genotypes present'; do low GQ/DP/out-of-range AF genotypes count as missing; is 'call rate' or 'completeness' used for masked or unmasked genotypes? ANSWER: Mission Bio's own filter code uses quality-masked genotypes. In tapestriR filter_variants, a genotype counts as 'known' only if NGT<3 AND GQ>=30 AND DP>=10 AND, for mutated calls, AF>=20. The mv (variant) and mc (cell) percentage filters are computed on that mask, so low-GQ, low-DP and low-AF genotypes count as missing. mosaic filter_variants likewise counts a variant as present (NGT in {0,1,2}) 'after the filters are applied'. It defines cell 'completeness' as the fraction of variants with a high-quality call, weighted, over all cells. tapestriR writes the mask into NGT only if gt.mask=TRUE (default FALSE), so the stored NGT is unmasked. A Mission Bio support answer quoted on the BBG wiki says Tapestri Insights computes these percentages over genotyped cells, while mosaic uses all cells. The term 'call rate' did not appear in any page I read; 'completeness' is the vendor's term, and it refers to quality-masked calls. I could not read the Tapestri Insights 'Advanced Filtering Explained' PDF, so the Insights GUI wording itself is unconfirmed. HOW SURE: medium-high that the platform's genotyped/missing filters use quality-masked genotypes; low on any 'call rate' terminology. SOURCES: https://rdrr.io/github/MissionBio/tapestriR/src/R/filter_variants.R, https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/pages/methods/missionbio.mosaic.dna.Dna.filter_variants.html, https://bbglab.github.io/bbgwiki/Methods/Sequencing/singleCell/Mosaic/, https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/v2.4.1/4_data_structure.html.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In standard pseudobulk differential-expression workflows built on DESeq2/PyDESeq2 or edgeR, what low-expression gene filter is applied by default before fitting, with exact default parameter values (edgeR filterByExpr and decoupler's filter_by_expr: min_count, min_total_count, large_n, min_prop; the DESeq2 vignette's recommended pre-filter and its 'smallest group size' variant)? How does each rule account for samples with very different library sizes and for the size of the smallest group? ANSWER: edgeR filterByExpr and decoupler filter_by_expr use the same defaults: min_count=10, min_total_count=15, large_n=10, min_prop=0.7. decoupler says it is adapted from edgeR. The edgeR source shows the rule is depth-aware. CPM cutoff = min_count / median(library size) * 1e6, and a gene is kept if CPM >= cutoff in at least n samples AND its total raw count across samples >= 15. A sample with a small library therefore needs fewer raw reads to count as expressing the gene. How n is set: (1) If group is given, n is the smallest group size. (2) If a design is given and no group, n = 1/max(hat value); for a balanced ~donor+condition design with 7 pairs this is 14/8 = 1.75, so effectively 2 samples. (3) With neither, which is decoupler's default group=None, all samples count as one group, so n = the number of samples. If n > large_n, it is relaxed to 10 + (n-10)*0.7; for 14 samples that is 12.8. The DESeq2 vignette's pre-filter is keep <- rowSums(counts(dds) >= 10) >= smallestGroupSize: a raw count of at least 10 in at least as many samples as the smallest group (7 for 7 vs 7). Without discrete groups it uses the minimal number of samples where non-zero counts would be interesting. This rule works on raw counts, so it is not depth-aware. The vignette calls it optional, since results() runs independent filtering anyway. A plain row-sum filter is not the default of any of these tools. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://rdrr.io/bioc/edgeR/src/R/filterByExpr.R, https://rdrr.io/bioc/edgeR/man/filterByExpr.html, https://decoupler.readthedocs.io/en/latest/api/generated/decoupler.pp.filter_by_expr.html, https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/DESeq2/inst/doc/DESeq2.html.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: For a gene with zero counts in every sample of the reference condition and non-zero counts in the treated condition, what maximum-likelihood log2FoldChange do DESeq2 and PyDESeq2 report under default settings (coefficient bounds, ridge penalty in the IRLS step, fallback optimizer when IRLS does not converge), and is that gene's Wald p-value and adjusted p-value kept or set to NA? ANSWER: Both tools report a finite but bounded MLE, and the bounds differ between them. R DESeq2 (betaPrior=FALSE): the ridge is lambda=1e-6 per coefficient on the log2 scale, passed to IRLS as lambda/log(2)^2, with betaTol=1e-8 and maxit=100. Rows that do not converge, are unstable (NA betas) or have non-positive variance are refit by optim L-BFGS-B with bounds lower=-30, upper=30 on the LOG2 scale. A NEWS snippet, which I did not open as a full page, says rows with |beta|>=30 also take this path. PyDESeq2 irls_solver: ridge_factor=1e-6 on the natural-log scale, maxiter=250, min_beta=-30 and max_beta=30 on the NATURAL-LOG scale. If any |beta| > 30 or maxiter is reached, it switches to L-BFGS-B bounded to [-30, 30] natural log, about +-43.3 in log2. If that fails and there are <=2 variables, it uses grid search. log2FoldChange is reported as beta/ln(2). min_mu is 0.5 in both. So for zero-baseline genes the reported LFC is large, sits near or on the bounds, depends on the optimizer, and can differ between R and Python. P-values: neither tool sets a gene's p-value to NA because the reference group is all zero. In R, only rows that are zero in every sample get NA for LFC, p and padj. Otherwise p is set to NA only for Cook's outliers, and padj only by independent filtering for low baseMean. PyDESeq2 likewise keeps the Wald p-value. The web did not settle whether such genes actually reach padj<0.05; that depends on their fitted SE. HOW SURE: high for bounds/ridge/optimizer and NA rules; low on whether such genes are significant. SOURCES: https://rdrr.io/bioc/DESeq2/src/R/fitNbinomGLMs.R, https://github.com/thelovelab/DESeq2/blob/devel/R/core.R, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/PyDESeq2/v0.5.4/pydeseq2/utils.py, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/PyDESeq2/v0.5.4/pydeseq2/ds.py, https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/DESeq2/inst/doc/DESeq2.html.

QUESTION: For a gene with zero counts in every sample of the reference condition and non-zero counts in the treated condition, what maximum-likelihood log2FoldChange do DESeq2 and PyDESeq2 report under default settings (coefficient bounds, ridge penalty in the IRLS step, fallback optimizer when IRLS does not converge), and is that gene's Wald p-value and adjusted p-value kept or set to NA? ANSWER: Both tools report a finite but bounded MLE, and the bounds differ between them. R DESeq2 (betaPrior=FALSE): the ridge is lambda=1e-6 per coefficient on the log2 scale, passed to IRLS as lambda/log(2)^2, with betaTol=1e-8 and maxit=100. Rows that do not converge, are unstable (NA betas) or have non-positive variance are refit by optim L-BFGS-B with bounds lower=-30, upper=30 on the LOG2 scale. A NEWS snippet, which I did not open as a full page, says rows with |beta|>=30 also take this path. PyDESeq2 irls_solver: ridge_factor=1e-6 on the natural-log scale, maxiter=250, min_beta=-30 and max_beta=30 on the NATURAL-LOG scale. If any |beta| > 30 or maxiter is reached, it switches to L-BFGS-B bounded to [-30, 30] natural log, about +-43.3 in log2. If that fails and there are <=2 variables, it uses grid search. log2FoldChange is reported as beta/ln(2). min_mu is 0.5 in both. So for zero-baseline genes the reported LFC is large, sits near or on the bounds, depends on the optimizer, and can differ between R and Python. P-values: neither tool sets a gene's p-value to NA because the reference group is all zero. In R, only rows that are zero in every sample get NA for LFC, p and padj. Otherwise p is set to NA only for Cook's outliers, and padj only by independent filtering for low baseMean. PyDESeq2 likewise keeps the Wald p-value. The web did not settle whether such genes actually reach padj<0.05; that depends on their fitted SE. HOW SURE: high for bounds/ridge/optimizer and NA rules; low on whether such genes are significant. SOURCES: https://rdrr.io/bioc/DESeq2/src/R/fitNbinomGLMs.R, https://github.com/thelovelab/DESeq2/blob/devel/R/core.R, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/PyDESeq2/v0.5.4/pydeseq2/utils.py, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/PyDESeq2/v0.5.4/pydeseq2/ds.py, https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/DESeq2/inst/doc/DESeq2.html.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: How exactly do DESeq2 and PyDESeq2 choose the mean-normalized-count threshold in independent filtering (the grid of quantiles, the lowess fit of rejections against quantile, and the rule for picking the threshold), and with a paired design of about seven samples per condition and no replicates within a donor-by-condition cell, do Cook's-distance outlier filtering and count replacement apply by default? ANSWER: Independent filtering is the same in both tools. The filter is baseMean. theta = 50 equally spaced quantiles from lowerQuantile = fraction of genes with baseMean==0 up to 0.95, or up to 1 if lowerQuantile >= 0.95. For each quantile cutoff, BH is applied to genes with baseMean >= cutoff and a non-NA p-value, and rejections are counted at padj < alpha. alpha defaults to 0.1 in R results() and 0.05 in PyDESeq2. A lowess curve (f=1/5) is fitted to the rejections against theta. If max rejections <= 10, the first theta is used, which means no filtering. Otherwise thresh = max(lowess fit) - RMSE of the residuals (only where rejections > 0), and the threshold is the first theta whose rejections exceed thresh. R falls back to 90% and then 80% of the max fit before using the first theta; PyDESeq2 goes straight to the first theta. Genes below the chosen cutoff get padj=NA; their p-values are kept. Cook's handling: flagging uses only samples whose design-matrix row occurs >= 3 times. R's vignette says flagging needs 3 or more replicates; PyDESeq2 uses n_or_more_replicates(design_matrix, 3), noted in its code as 'As in DESeq2'. The cutoff is the F(0.99; p, m-p) quantile. Replacement requires >= 7 samples sharing an identical design-matrix row (minReplicatesForReplace=7, nOrMoreInCell on the model matrix; PyDESeq2 min_replicates=7). With ~donor+condition and one sample per donor-by-condition cell, every design row is unique. So by default no gene is flagged as a Cook's outlier and no counts are replaced, and skipping Cook's handling changes nothing for this design. One caveat: I confirmed the R side of the >=3 rule from the vignette and the PyDESeq2 code comment, not from R's recordMaxCooks source. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://github.com/thelovelab/DESeq2/blob/devel/R/results.R, https://github.com/thelovelab/DESeq2/blob/devel/R/core.R, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/PyDESeq2/v0.5.4/pydeseq2/ds.py, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/PyDESeq2/v0.5.4/pydeseq2/dds.py, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/PyDESeq2/v0.5.4/pydeseq2/utils.py, https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/DESeq2/inst/doc/DESeq2.html.

text: FINDING: In BD Rhapsody pipeline v2.x-4.0 the prebuilt analysis objects (Seurat .rds, and h5ad/Cellismo-MuData, added in v2.0) hold RSEC-adjusted molecules as the main count matrix (obj@assays[['RNA']]$counts and mdata.mod['rna'].X are labelled RSEC); DBEC counts are only in the separate DBEC_MolsPerCell table (MEX in v2+, CSV in v1.x), so an analyst loading the default object gets RSEC, not DBEC. The pipeline docs fetched did not show which layer the Metrics_Summary 'genes per cell' metric uses (page truncated), and I found no documented version change in the object's layer; both points are unsettled. BD's own FAQ recommends RSEC at mean RSEC depth <2, DBEC (or RSEC with caveats) at 2-6, and DBEC at >6. QUESTION: Which count is the main matrix in BD Rhapsody standard outputs, does it vary by version, and which count does the metrics 'genes per cell' use? label: FINDING
text: FINDING: DBEC is fitted per bioproduct (gene) on that pipeline run's distribution of RSEC-adjusted read depth per molecule, pooled across all cells. It fits two negative binomials to the bimodal depth distribution and discards molecules in the low-depth mode. A gene is DBEC-corrected only if its mean non-singleton RSEC depth is >=4; otherwise it is flagged low depth and keeps its RSEC counts. Each pipeline run (cartridge) is fitted separately, so two cartridges sequenced to different depths can have different sets of genes corrected and different cutoffs. BD's FAQ warns that genes with inconsistent DBEC status can produce an apparent batch effect on tSNE, and that RSEC noise molecules grow with depth. BD advises using DBEC only after removing genes that did not pass in every sample (status is in Bioproduct_Stats.csv) when comparing across samples. QUESTION: How does DBEC decide which molecules to remove, and is it run- and depth-dependent so that it causes batch differences? SOURCE: https://bd-rhapsody-bioinfo-docs.genomics.bd.com/steps/steps%5Ferror%5Fcorrection.html ; https://scomix.bd.com/hc/en-us/articles/360044971032-Bioinformatics-Primary-Analysis

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In split-pool combinatorial barcoding scRNA-seq where the round-1 well is the sample ID, are cells cultured/treated in that plate or are fixed cells only loaded into it? Are edge effects documented for the round-1 plate and how are they assessed? ANSWER: Cells are not cultured or treated there. In the Parse Evercode protocols, cells are fixed and permeabilized beforehand, then thawed and only loaded into the Round 1 plate (e.g. ~37,500 cells/well) for a short in situ reverse-transcription step in a thermocycler. Evaporation edge effects come from long incubations, e.g. 72 h at 37 C in culture, so they are not physically expected in this plate. The protocols I read document no Round 1 edge effect. Any position artefact would come from cell input at loading (pipetting, settling), so it would show as a row or column pattern rather than an outer ring. That is checked with an 8x12 heatmap and a row+column fit of cells per well. Whether the 91-cytokine treatment itself happened in some other plate is not settled by these sources. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://support.parsebiosciences.com/hc/en-us/article_attachments/31841833600532, https://www.protocols.io/view/evercode-wt-mega-v2-2-1-cysrxwd6.pdf, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8024881/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: How is a plate edge effect conventionally defined and quantified (outer ring vs two rings, binary edge vs row/column terms, effect-size measure and cut-offs)? ANSWER: The edge effect is conventionally the outer ring of wells (rows A/H, columns 1/12). In culture plates it can reach rows 2-3: on VWR plates, outer wells were -35%, row 2 -25% and row 3 -10% versus centre wells; on Greiner plates the figures were -16%, -7% and -1%. HTS work models spatial bias with row and column terms (B-score/median polish, Loess) and treats the edge effect as a special case. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: When treatment is fully aliased with well position and controls sit on one edge, is positional/edge normalization warranted, not estimable, or harmful, and what evidence is expected? ANSWER: Partly settled. The sources warn that controls placed on edge columns are sensitive to edge effects and that control-based normalization can then add bias. Positional normalization breaks down when actives are dense or clustered: above about a 20% hit rate the B-score normalizes incorrectly. They recommend scattered or randomized layouts so that plate effects can be estimated. When treatment and position are fully aliased, a position correction cannot tell plate bias from treatment effect and risks removing real signal. In that case a position effect has to be estimated independently, from uniformity/blank plates or from the same condition repeated across positions, before any correction. None of the sources I read recommends normalizing anyway under full aliasing, though none states this exact case word for word. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4653387/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4318693/, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ailsci.2023.100073, https://www.quantics.co.uk/blog/plate-layout/.

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: For an undirected graph, igraph community_leiden(objective_function='modularity', resolution=g) optimises Q=1/(2m) sum_ij (A_ij - g k_i k_j/2m) delta, and leidenalg RBConfigurationVertexPartition optimises the same sum without the 1/(2m) factor, so at equal resolution on the SAME graph they target the same partition (Traag, scanpy issue 1053: igraph modularity is 'the equivalent of' RBConfiguration); the resolution is a multiplier on the configuration null model and is graph-relative, not an absolute scale. What differs between the teams' set-ups is the graph: scanpy igraph flavour runs undirected on the symmetrised, weighted UMAP connectivities (weights in (0,1], k_i are strengths), while leidenalg via scanpy defaults to directed=True and a raw sklearn kNN graph is directed (each cell has exactly k out-edges); the directed modularity is Q=1/m sum (A_ij - g k_out_i k_in_j/m), a different objective. Weights, symmetrisation (union/max vs sum), directedness and k change degrees, m and community density, so the same resolution gives different cluster counts across set-ups; resolutions are only comparable within one graph construction, and a gap in required resolution/cluster count between teams is mostly tooling/graph, not data. Compare set-ups at matched cluster count, not matched resolution. QUESTION: How does scanpy igraph Leiden resolution (weighted UMAP connectivities) relate to leidenalg RBConfiguration resolution on an sklearn kNN graph; do weights/symmetrisation/directedness change cluster counts; are resolutions comparable? SOURCE: https://igraph.org/c/html/0.10.15/igraph-Community.html ; https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/issues/1053 ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/main/src/scanpy/tools/_leiden.py ; https://scanpy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/generated/scanpy.tl.leiden.html ; https://leidenalg.readthedocs.io/en/stable/intro.html

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Recognised label-free rules for choosing which clusters to sub-cluster exist: (a) silhouette-based heterogeneity, where clusters with low silhouette are re-clustered (SCISSORS; CHOIR maximises silhouette to define parent clusters then sub-clusters each one); (b) iterate over EVERY cluster and accept a split only if the children differ significantly, by DE thresholds such as log2FC, adjusted P and fraction expressing, recursing until no interpretable split remains (IDclust; iterClust), or by a permutation-tested classifier accuracy (CHOIR, alpha 0.05 Bonferroni); (c) iterative re-PCA of subsets (PanoView). Choosing parents because annotation labels show a missing type is not unsupervised and must be disclosed as label-guided; a legitimate equivalent is to apply one rule (e.g. sub-cluster all clusters, or all clusters above a size or below a silhouette cut-off) uniformly. scanpy sc.tl.leiden restrict_to=(obs_key, [categories]) slices the existing adjacency (connectivities) to rows and columns of cells in those categories - it does NOT recompute HVGs, PCA or neighbours - runs Leiden on that subgraph, and writes labels to key 'leiden_R' by default, renaming sub-clusters as 'parent,0', 'parent,1' (prefix = joined parent names plus comma) while all other cells keep their original label. QUESTION: What label-free criteria decide which clusters to sub-cluster for rare populations, and what does scanpy restrict_to do? SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10412410/ ; https://www.choirclustering.com/articles/CHOIR.html ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11655290/ ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/main/src/scanpy/tools/_utils_clustering.py ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/main/src/scanpy/tools/_leiden.py

text: FINDING: Fine innate/T lymphocyte labels in PBMC are generally not expected to form their own clusters from RNA alone: Hao et al. 2021 (Seurat v4 WNN, 211k PBMC CITE-seq) state that effector, regulatory, gamma-delta and MAIT T cells often cannot be separated by scRNA-seq alone and built their fine annotation with protein (in the related atlas MAIT were defined by CD3/CD8/Va7.2/CD161 protein plus TRAV1-2 and iNKT by Va24Ja18), and Gutierrez-Arcelus et al. 2019 show MAIT, iNKT, gamma-delta T and NK lie on a continuous transcriptional 'innateness gradient' between adaptive T and NK cells rather than as discrete clusters. Labels such as NKT and ILC in a fine PBMC annotation are therefore likely reference-mapped (e.g. Azimuth) and expected to be split across CD8 memory/MAIT/NK clusters under global clustering; recovering them typically needs T/NK sub-clustering with subset-specific HVGs, or is not achievable. Preprocessing advice (from earlier library facts, not re-verified here): ~50 PCs rather than an elbow cut, smaller k (10-15), HVGs recomputed within the T/NK subset, and excluding TR*V/IG*/HLA/ribo/mito genes from HVGs help; larger k and too few PCs/HVGs hurt. Web reading did not give a quantitative HVG-number recommendation for these subsets. QUESTION: Are NKT/ILC separable from CD8 memory/MAIT/NK by unsupervised RNA clustering in PBMC, and which preprocessing helps? SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8238499/ ; https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-019-08604-4 ; https://www.cell.com/cms/10.1016/j.cell.2022.01.012/attachment/1638b222-42b4-4487-8755-ea211a28ff1a/mmc2.pdf

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In the BD Rhapsody sequence analysis pipeline for targeted mRNA panels, which molecule count (raw, RSEC-adjusted or DBEC-adjusted) is written as the main expression matrix in its standard per-cell outputs (MolsPerCell tables, h5ad and Seurat objects), does this differ between pipeline versions, and which count does the pipeline's own metrics summary use when it reports 'genes detected per cell'? ANSWER: The pipeline writes both RSEC_MolsPerCell and DBEC_MolsPerCell tables (CSV in v1.x, MEX in v2+). The prebuilt single-file objects (Seurat .rds and ScanPy h5ad, added in v2.0; Cellismo/MuData in later versions) contain the RSEC molecules-per-cell table: obj@assays[['RNA']]$counts and mdata.mod['rna'].X are labelled 'mRNA Expression (RSEC)' in the v4.0 docs, and the datatables step says 'RSEC molecule counts per cell are also preloaded' into Seurat/Cellismo/Scanpy. So an analyst who loads the default object gets RSEC, not DBEC. BD's FAQ recommends RSEC when mean RSEC depth is <2, either DBEC with non-passing genes removed or RSEC with caveats when depth is 2-6, and DBEC when depth is >6. I found no documented change between versions in which layer the objects use, but the release notes were truncated, so this is unconfirmed. Which count the Metrics_Summary 'genes per cell' metric uses was NOT settled: the metrics page was cut off before the cell-metric definitions. The visible molecule metrics are all Raw or RSEC (Total_RSEC_Molecules, Mean_RSEC_Sequencing_Depth, Sequencing_Saturation on RSEC), which suggests but does not prove RSEC. HOW SURE: high for objects holding RSEC (v4.0 docs); medium for this applying to all v2+ versions; low/unsettled for the metrics genes-per-cell layer. SOURCES: https://bd-rhapsody-bioinfo-docs.genomics.bd.com/outputs/outputs_sctools.html, https://bd-rhapsody-bioinfo-docs.genomics.bd.com/steps/steps_datatables.html, https://scomix.bd.com/hc/en-us/articles/360044971032-Bioinformatics-Primary-Analysis, https://bd-rhapsody-bioinfo-docs.genomics.bd.com/outputs/outputs_metrics_summary.html, https://bd-rhapsody-bioinfo-docs.genomics.bd.com/release_notes.html.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: How exactly does DBEC (distribution-based error correction) decide which molecules to remove: is it fitted separately per gene and per sequencing run, does it skip genes below a sequencing-depth threshold, and is it known to produce run-to-run (batch) differences in which gene-cell entries are set to zero when two cartridges are sequenced to different depths? ANSWER: DBEC runs per bioproduct (gene). It looks only at the distribution of RSEC-adjusted read depth per molecule, pooled across all cells in the run, and ignores UMI sequence. It assumes that true molecules of a gene share amplification efficiency, so the depth distribution is bimodal. It fits two negative binomial distributions, keeps molecules in the upper mode, and discards the lower mode (late-PCR artifacts such as chimeras). The cutoff between the modes is reported as the DBEC minimum depth. DBEC is applied only to genes with mean non-singleton RSEC depth >=4. Genes below that are marked 'low depth' and keep their RSEC counts. Status and metrics per gene are in <sample>_Bioproduct_Stats.csv. Because each pipeline run is fitted on its own reads, cartridges sequenced to different depths can differ in which genes pass and where the cutoffs fall. BD's FAQ says that at mean RSEC depth 2-6, genes with inconsistent adjustment status 'can lead to an apparent batch effect when plotted on tSNE'. It also says noise molecules in RSEC grow with depth. For cross-sample comparison BD recommends DBEC with non-passing genes removed, or RSEC only across samples of similar depth. HOW SURE: high for the algorithm and depth threshold; high that the vendor warns of batch effects from inconsistent DBEC status (fitting per run follows from it running per pipeline run on that run's depth distribution). SOURCES: https://bd-rhapsody-bioinfo-docs.genomics.bd.com/steps/steps%5Ferror%5Fcorrection.html, https://scomix.bd.com/hc/en-us/articles/360044971032-Bioinformatics-Primary-Analysis.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: For targeted-panel single-cell RNA-seq with a few hundred genes and no mitochondrial genes, what cell-level QC do vendor guidance and published analyses conventionally apply after the pipeline's own cell calling (fixed minimum genes or molecules, MAD outliers, upper cutoffs, or none), and is same-sample-tag doublet removal conventionally treated as part of QC when a retained-cell count is reported? ANSWER: Not settled by the web within the call budget. The BD workflow paper (Current Protocols 2024) and a 534-gene targeted-panel paper (Wellcome Open Res 2022) were both truncated before their cell-QC methods, and no BD page I read gives a post-cell-calling threshold for targeted panels. The Current Protocols text does state that sample multiplexing and informatic doublet inference are imperfect and 'not all doublets can be removed', which treats doublet handling as a separate, optional consideration. My reading, not settled by any source: there is no single convention. Teams should explicitly state and defend (i) whether any cut is applied beyond BD cell calling, (ii) lower-only versus two-sided cuts, and (iii) whether same-tag doublet removal is included in the reported retained count. HOW SURE: low. SOURCES: https://currentprotocols.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/cpz1.963, https://doi.org/10.12688/wellcomeopenres.16883.2.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In flow-cytometric and single-cell protein studies of myeloid neoplasms, what immunophenotype defines plasmacytoid dendritic cells, and can genuine pDCs in these patients be CD34-positive, CD117-partial, CD11c-dim, CD33/CD13-dim or CD56/CD7-positive? Is CD123-bright plus HLA-DR plus CD303 and/or CD304 regarded as sufficient to count a cell as pDC, or are CD34 and CD11c negativity required? ANSWER: The standard definition is CD123-bright, HLA-DR+ (low SSC, CD45-dim), with no lineage markers (CD3, CD19, CD56, CD14, CD11c, MPO). CD303 and CD304 are expected but can be missing on immature pDCs. CD64 is used to exclude monocytes, which can also be CD123/HLA-DR bright. In myeloid neoplasms, genuine pDCs can be CD34+ and CD117+ because they sit at early or intermediate maturation stages. In pDC-AML, pDCs are CD4+, CD56-negative and most often CD303+, CD304+ and CD34+, and some cases also carry CD7, CD5 or CD22. CD56 is rare in pDC-AML but typical of BPDCN. So CD34 negativity is not strictly required: CD34+ cells that are CD123-bright, HLA-DR+ and CD303/CD304+ can count as immature pDCs. Blasts are CD123-bright in about 14% of AML, and one lab separates blasts from pDCs using CD34 versus CD123. CD11c negativity is part of the standard definition. I found no source that accepts CD11c-dim or CD33/CD13-dim pDCs, although the sources I read did not discuss CD33 or CD13 on pDCs at all. In short, CD123-bright + HLA-DR + CD303/CD304 + lineage-negative (CD3/CD19/CD14/CD64/CD11c) counts as pDC. Normal marrow has about 0.29% pDCs and most AML about 0.03%. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13748365/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11171351/, https://haematologica.org/article/view/haematol.2020.253740, https://ashpublications.org/blood/article/146/Supplement%201/6925/555469/Plasmacytoid-dendritic-cell-associated-acute, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7955409/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: What does the Mission Bio Mosaic documented protein workflow do to assign cell-type labels: which normalization is the default, which clustering method and default parameters are used, are labels given per cluster or per cell, and how does the vendor's guidance for its heme-oncology antibody panel identify dendritic-cell subsets and handle cells that match no lineage? ANSWER: Protein.normalize_reads defaults to CLR (asinh, NSP and ANSP are the alternatives). The curated notebooks use NSP with random_state=42, then PCA (10 components) and UMAP (defaults n_neighbors=50, cosine metric, min_dist=0, taken only from a search snippet of the run_umap page, which I did not open). They then cluster the UMAP with graph-community, which is Louvain on a shared-nearest-neighbour graph, with k=5. The user reads a per-cluster heatmap and renames clusters by hand, so labels are per cluster. The automated cluster_and_label also works per cluster: graph-community k=5, random_state=42, merge='labeled', min_prob_diff=0.9, with the IgG1/IgG2a/IgG2b isotypes used to flag sticky cells. It gives each cluster the most likely type from a hierarchical 'truth' tree, which by default is a built-in PBMC tree, using NSP values clipped to 0-1 and a beta likelihood. The 'probability' method can call 'Unassigned' for cells that match nothing, and doublet clusters become 'Mixed'. The 'likelihood' method forces every cell into a truth type. assign_from_truth does the same labelling per cell. The web did not settle the vendor part: I found no Mission Bio or BioLegend guidance on identifying pDC or cDC subsets with the Heme Oncology panel, or on handling cells that match no lineage. BioLegend only says clusters were identified from protein expression on a UMAP. HOW SURE: high for the Mosaic defaults and labelling mechanics; low for the vendor guidance on DC subsets, which I did not find. SOURCES: https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/pages/methods/missionbio.mosaic.protein.Protein.normalize_reads.html, https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/pages/methods/missionbio.mosaic.protein.Protein.cluster_and_label.html, https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/pages/methods/missionbio.mosaic.protein.Protein.assign_from_truth.html, https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/pages/methods/missionbio.mosaic.assay._Assay.cluster.html, https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/notebooks/curated_notebooks/ge-protein.html, https://www.biolegend.com/en-us/products/totalseq-d-human-heme-oncology-cocktail-v10-20465.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: How does the resolution parameter of scanpy's Leiden clustering with the igraph flavour (modularity objective on the weighted UMAP-connectivity graph) relate to the resolution parameter of leidenalg's RBConfigurationVertexPartition run on an unweighted or distance-weighted k-nearest-neighbour graph built with scikit-learn? Do edge weights, symmetrisation and directedness of the graph change the number of clusters obtained at a given resolution, and are resolutions comparable between the two set-ups? ANSWER: On the same undirected graph they are the same objective. igraph's modularity with resolution g is Q = 1/(2m) sum_ij (A_ij - g k_i k_j/2m) delta(c_i,c_j). RBConfiguration is the same sum without the 1/(2m) prefactor, so it has the same optimum; Traag (scanpy issue 1053) calls igraph modularity 'the equivalent of' RBConfigurationVertexPartition. The resolution multiplies the configuration null model, so it is relative to the graph, not an absolute scale. The two teams' graphs differ. scanpy's igraph flavour runs undirected on the symmetrised, weighted UMAP connectivities, where k_i are weighted strengths. scanpy's leidenalg flavour defaults to directed=True, and a raw scikit-learn kNN graph is directed (k out-edges per cell). The directed objective is a different function: Q = 1/m sum (A_ij - g k_out_i k_in_j/m). Edge weights, how the graph is symmetrised, directedness and k all change degrees, total weight m and within-community density, so the same resolution gives different cluster counts. Resolutions are only comparable within one graph construction. The teams' gap in resolution and cluster count is therefore largely a tooling and graph effect, not a property of the data. Compare set-ups at a matched number of clusters. The docs I read do not state the exact size of the effect; I inferred it from the formulas. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://igraph.org/c/html/0.10.15/igraph-Community.html, https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/issues/1053, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/main/src/scanpy/tools/_leiden.py, https://scanpy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/generated/scanpy.tl.leiden.html, https://leidenalg.readthedocs.io/en/stable/intro.html.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In single-cell RNA-seq clustering practice, what label-free criteria are used to decide which clusters to sub-cluster in order to recover rare cell populations (for example iterative or hierarchical sub-clustering of every cluster, or rules based on cluster size, within-cluster variance or silhouette), and what does scanpy's restrict_to option in Leiden do to the graph and to the cluster labels? ANSWER: Published label-free rules exist. (1) Silhouette-based heterogeneity: SCISSORS uses silhouette scores to find heterogeneous clusters and re-clusters them. CHOIR maximises silhouette to define parent clusters, then sub-clusters them. (2) Recursive splitting of every cluster, keeping a split only if the sub-clusters differ significantly. IDclust uses DE thresholds (log2FC, adjusted P, fraction of cells expressing, number of DE genes) and stops when no interpretable split remains; iterClust works similarly. CHOIR instead uses a permutation-tested classifier (alpha 0.05, Bonferroni). (3) Iterative re-PCA on subsets (PanoView, which picks clusters with the lowest variance). Picking parent clusters because the annotation shows a type is missing is label-guided, not unsupervised, and must be disclosed. A defensible alternative is one rule applied uniformly, e.g. sub-cluster every cluster, or every cluster below a silhouette or above a size cut-off. scanpy's restrict_to=(obs_key, categories) only slices the existing connectivities to the rows and columns of cells in those categories. It does not recompute HVGs, PCA or neighbours. It then runs Leiden on that subgraph and writes labels to 'leiden_R' by default. Sub-clusters are named 'parent,0', 'parent,1', ... (the joined parent names plus a comma), and all other cells keep their original labels. HOW SURE: high for restrict_to behaviour; medium for the criteria (SCISSORS details only partly read). SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10412410/, https://www.choirclustering.com/articles/CHOIR.html, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11655290/, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/main/src/scanpy/tools/_utils_clustering.py, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/main/src/scanpy/tools/_leiden.py.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In human PBMC single-cell RNA-seq with fine-grained annotation, are populations such as NKT cells and innate lymphoid cells generally separable from CD8 memory T, MAIT and NK cells by unsupervised graph clustering on a standard log-normalised HVG PCA, or do they usually require protein markers, reference mapping or sub-clustering of the T/NK compartment? Which preprocessing choices (number of HVGs, scaling, number of PCs, neighbours) are reported to help or hurt the recovery of such rare or continuous lymphocyte subsets? ANSWER: Generally not separable by RNA alone. Hao et al. 2021 (CITE-seq of 211k PBMC) state that effector, regulatory, gamma-delta and MAIT T cells often cannot be separated by scRNA-seq alone, and they used protein (WNN) to define fine states. Gutierrez-Arcelus et al. 2019 show that MAIT, iNKT, gamma-delta T and NK cells sit on a continuous transcriptional 'innateness gradient' between adaptive T and NK cells, not in discrete clusters. Fine labels such as NKT and ILC are therefore likely protein- or reference-derived. Expect them to be spread across CD8 memory, MAIT and NK clusters in global clustering. Recovering them needs sub-clustering of the T/NK compartment with HVGs re-selected inside it, and may not be possible at all. On preprocessing, the reading did not settle the question quantitatively, and no source gave an HVG number for these subsets. Earlier library facts (not re-verified here) point to about 50 PCs rather than an elbow cut, smaller k (10-15), HVGs recomputed within the subset, and removing TCR, Ig, HLA, ribosomal and mitochondrial genes from the HVGs. Large k and too few PCs or HVGs hurt. HOW SURE: medium on separability; low on preprocessing specifics. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8238499/, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-019-08604-4.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: Is there published guidance, from systematic analyses across many single-cell RNA-seq datasets, on which mitochondrial-percentage cut-off is appropriate for human cells versus mouse cells and across tissues, and what default do those analyses recommend for human tissue when the tissue is not known? ANSWER: Yes. Osorio & Cai (Bioinformatics 2021; 37(7):963) looked at 5,530,106 cells from 1,349 PanglaoDB datasets. Human tissues have significantly higher mito% than mouse tissues, and this is not explained by platform. They give reference values for 121 mouse and 44 human tissues. A 5% cut works for mouse tissues but fails to separate healthy from low-quality cells in 13 of 44 (29.5%) human tissues. The pages I opened (PMC, bioRxiv PDF, OUP, GitHub) were cut off after the abstract and introduction, so I did not read the default they recommend for human tissue. A search-result summary of the paper says it recommends 10% as the standard threshold for human samples, with 5% kept for mouse. 10x Genomics cites this paper and says mito expression varies by sample and cell type (for example cardiomyocytes) and that data-driven cuts (3-5 MAD/SD from the median) are also common. Summary: 5% for mouse, about 10% for human when the tissue is unknown, tissue-specific values where available. HOW SURE: high that human needs a higher cut than the 5% that suits mouse; medium that the human default is exactly 10%, because the pages I opened were truncated and that figure comes from a search snippet. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8599307/, https://www.biorxiv.org/content/biorxiv/early/2020/08/19/2020.02.20.958793.full.pdf, https://academic.oup.com/bioinformatics/article/37/7/963/5896986, https://www.10xgenomics.com/analysis-guides/common-considerations-for-quality-control-filters-for-single-cell-rna-seq-data.
