question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: What exactly is the MAD-based outlier rule for cell QC in the scverse single-cell best-practices chapter (which metrics, how many MADs for each, whether metrics are log1p-transformed, two-sided or one-sided, and whether a fixed mitochondrial-percentage cut is added), and what are the defaults of the Bioconductor equivalents (scuttle/scater isOutlier and perCellQCFilters: nmads, log, type, batch)? ANSWER: Bioconductor, read from the docs and source: isOutlier(metric, nmads=3, type=c('both','lower','higher') so 'both' by default, log=FALSE (log2 when TRUE), subset=NULL, batch=NULL so the median and MAD are pooled unless a batch is given, min.diff=NA). perCellQCFilters(x, sum.field='sum', detected.field='detected', sub.fields=NULL, ...) calls isOutlier with log=TRUE and type='lower' on library size and on detected features, and with type='higher' and no log on each sub.fields column. nmads stays at 3 and batch at NULL unless passed through '...'. Because sub.fields defaults to NULL, mito is only filtered if you pass sub.fields (or TRUE to pick up subsets_*_percent columns). The function is now deprecated in favour of scrapper::suggestRnaQcThresholds. scverse best practices: the chapter page was cut off before its MAD section, so I could not confirm it from the source. From lab memory and recall, the rule is a two-sided is_outlier (outside median ± n*MAD) at 5 MADs on log1p_total_counts, log1p_n_genes_by_counts and pct_counts_in_top_20_genes, plus a mito rule of 3 MADs on pct_counts_mt (not log-transformed) OR pct_counts_mt > 8. The main differences: scverse uses 5 MADs, two-sided, with a top-20-genes metric and a fixed 8% mito cut; scuttle uses 3 MADs, lower tail only for counts and genes, and no fixed mito cut. HOW SURE: high for the scuttle defaults; medium for the scverse rule, because the page was truncated and it rests on prior memory. SOURCES: https://rdrr.io/bioc/scuttle/man/isOutlier.html, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LTLA/scuttle/master/R/perCellQCFilters.R, https://www.sc-best-practices.org/preprocessing-visualization/quality-control/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In the Seurat guided clustering tutorial and the scanpy basic clustering tutorials (legacy and current), what are the exact cell-filter thresholds and comparison operators, what rationale is given for the upper limit on detected genes per cell, and what do Seurat, scanpy or 10x Genomics guidance say about whether that upper limit transfers to datasets of a different sequencing depth or should be set from each dataset's own distribution? ANSWER: Seurat pbmc3k: CreateSeuratObject(min.cells=3, min.features=200), then subset(pbmc, subset = nFeature_RNA > 200 & nFeature_RNA < 2500 & percent.mt < 5). The bounds are strict (exclusive), and the text says it filters cells with unique feature counts over 2,500 or less than 200 and with >5% mito. The stated reason for the upper limit is that cell doublets or multiplets may have an aberrantly high gene count. The tutorial says you filter 'based on any user-defined criteria' after looking at that dataset's violin and scatter plots. Scanpy legacy pbmc3k (clustering-2017): sc.pp.filter_cells(min_genes=200), meaning keep cells with at least 200 genes, and sc.pp.filter_genes(min_cells=3). The slicing step that follows (n_genes_by_counts < 2500, pct_counts_mt < 5, copied from Seurat) fell in the truncated part of the page and is not verified. Current scanpy clustering tutorial: no upper gene cap. It uses only filter_cells(min_genes=100) and filter_genes(min_cells=3), advises 'a very permissive filtering strategy' because poor-looking QC can be real biology, says QC should be done per sample because thresholds vary between batches, and handles doublets with scrublet. 10x Genomics: high feature counts may be multiplets, but thresholds in publications are either arbitrary or data-driven (2-5 SD/MAD from the median), and you should plot each sample's own distributions first. It warns that one threshold may not suit heterogeneous samples. None of these sources says 2500 carries over to data of a different depth. It is a value chosen for pbmc3k (shallow 10x v1 PBMCs), and all the guidance points to setting caps from each dataset's own distribution. HOW SURE: high for Seurat, current scanpy and 10x; medium for the legacy scanpy 2500/5% slicing (truncated page); high that no source says the 2500 cap transfers. SOURCES: https://satijalab.org/seurat/articles/pbmc3k_tutorial, https://scanpy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/tutorials/basics/clustering-2017.html, https://scanpy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/tutorials/basics/clustering.html, https://www.10xgenomics.com/analysis-guides/common-considerations-for-quality-control-filters-for-single-cell-rna-seq-data.

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: CellTypist annotate() defaults are majority_voting=False, min_prop=0 (so no subcluster becomes 'Heterogeneous'), mode='best match'; with majority voting and no over_clustering given, over_cluster() runs Leiden at resolution 5/10/15/20/25/30 for <5k/<20k/<40k/<100k/<200k/>=200k cells (100,000 cells -> 25, since 100k is not <100k) and each subcluster takes its dominant predicted label. If no graph exists it builds one with: (if X has negatives use .raw) sc.pp.filter_genes(min_cells=5); sc.pp.highly_variable_genes(n_top_genes=min(2500, n_vars)) on the log-normalised data; subset to HVGs; sc.pp.scale(max_value=10); sc.tl.pca(n_comps=50); sc.pp.neighbors(n_neighbors=10, n_pcs=50). The exact Leiden kwargs (CellTypist 1.7.0 says 'adjust leiden params to parallel scanpy', likely flavor/n_iterations) were not verified. QUESTION: CellTypist majority-voting graph construction, over-clustering and annotate() defaults. label: FINDING
text: FINDING: The error "'csr_array' object has no attribute 'getnnz'" in sc.pp.neighbors comes from pynndescent 0.7.0 (released 2026-10-27), not from scipy or anndata. PyNNDescentTransformer now returns a scipy csr_array, and scanpy's neighbors/_common.py _ind_dist_shortcut calls d.getnnz(axis=1). It was reported on scanpy 1.12.4 + pynndescent 0.7.0 + scipy 1.18.1. scanpy uses pynndescent by default for >=8192 cells with the euclidean metric, so CellTypist over-clustering on 100k cells hits it. Workaround: pin pynndescent<0.7 (0.6.0 works, graph identical to before), or use a scanpy build containing PR #4451 (merged 2026-10-29), which swaps getnnz for np.diff(d.indptr). That gives the same per-row counts, so the graph is unchanged. Equivalent monkeypatch: per-row counts = np.diff(d.indptr). Switching to transformer='sklearn' (exact kNN) avoids the error but can change the graph slightly. QUESTION: Which versions trigger the csr_array getnnz error in scanpy neighbors and what workaround leaves the graph unchanged. SOURCE: https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/issues/4444 ; https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/pull/4451 ; https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/issues/2773

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: TRDC and CD3E do not separate gamma-delta T from NK cells in scRNA-seq, because NK cells express both transcripts. The Human Protein Atlas classes TRDC blood RNA as 'Group enriched (gdT-cell, NK-cell)' and its single-cell cluster as NK & T cells. In mouse, germline (unrearranged) Tcrd is transcribed in all maturing NK cells. NK cells also carry CD3E mRNA. Use CD3D/CD3G (plus TRGC1/TRGC2, TRDV1/TRDV2, TRGV9) for T identity. Use their absence plus KLRF1, NCAM1, FCER1G, TYROBP, FCGR3A, NCR1 for NK, and judge at sub-cluster level. Vd2 gdT cells look like CD8 T and Vd1 gdT cells look like NK cells, and gdT cells only separated at high clustering resolution (1.2) in Pizzolato 2019. QUESTION: Are TRDC/CD3E detected in NK cells, and which transcripts separate gdT from NK? SOURCE: https://www.proteinatlas.org/ENSG00000211829-TRDC ; https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/eji.200737354 ; https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1818488116 ; https://apps.allenimmunology.org/aifi/resources/imm-health-atlas/cell-type-descriptions/cd8-t-cells-gdt-cells-and-mait-cells/

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: In healthy adult blood, gamma-delta T cells are about 5% of T cells and about 1% of PBMC. A flow-cytometry reference range from 238 Brazilian adults gives TCRgd at 1.0-15.9% of lymphocytes. The same study gives total NK cells at 3.7-28.5% of lymphocytes, CD3+ T at 51.3-83.5% and CD19+ B at 6.3-20.8%. Since PBMC also hold monocytes, NK cells are typically about 5-20% of PBMC. A transfer that calls gamma-delta T well above about 5% of all cells, or NK cells as a tiny fraction, deserves checking. QUESTION: Typical NK and gdT fractions in healthy adult PBMC. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7140678/ ; https://lbmms.paginas.ufsc.br/files/2017/09/1-s2.0-S0165247814002570-main.pdf ; https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1818488116

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: CellTypist scales the query with the reference's statistics, not its own. It stores a StandardScaler fitted on the training (reference) data. At prediction it computes (query - model.scaler.mean_)/model.scaler.scale_ per gene and clips values above 10. This requires the query to be log1p of counts normalised to 10,000 per cell. Seurat FindTransferAnchors (default reduction pcaproject) fits PCA on the reference and projects the query onto it, with a scale=TRUE option to scale the query. The pages read do not settle whether that query scaling uses query or reference statistics. No source read gives a published demonstration that z-scoring reference and query separately biases labels under composition differences. By reasoning, per-dataset z-scoring centres each dataset on its own composition-weighted mean, so it shifts the query when the cell-type mix differs; treat this as an unverified inference. QUESTION: How is the query scaled in linear-classifier label transfer, and does separate z-scoring bias labels? SOURCE: https://github.com/Teichlab/celltypist/issues/29 ; https://github.com/Teichlab/celltypist/issues/138 ; https://github.com/Teichlab/celltypist ; https://satijalab.org/seurat/reference/findtransferanchors

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In CellTypist, when majority voting is requested and the input AnnData has no precomputed neighbour graph, what exact steps and default parameters does the package use to build one (gene filtering, number of highly variable genes, scaling, number of principal components, number of neighbours), which clustering algorithm and which resolution rule by number of cells does over-clustering use, and what are the defaults of majority_voting and min_prop in annotate()? ANSWER: annotate() defaults: majority_voting=False, min_prop=0 (a subcluster is named 'Heterogeneous' only if its dominant label's share is below min_prop, so this never happens at 0), mode='best match', over_clustering=None, use_GPU=False. Majority voting is skipped when there are 50 cells or fewer. Over-clustering uses Leiden (scanpy sc.tl.leiden, leidenalg>=0.9) at resolution 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30 for datasets with fewer than 5k, 20k, 40k, 100k or 200k cells, or 200k and above. A dataset of exactly 100,000 cells therefore gets resolution 25. Each subcluster is then given its most frequent per-cell predicted label. If no neighbour graph exists, the graph is built as follows: if X has negative values, use adata.raw; sc.pp.filter_genes(min_cells=5); sc.pp.highly_variable_genes(n_top_genes=min(2500, n_vars)) on the log1p-CP10k data with scanpy's default flavor; subset to the HVGs; sc.pp.scale(max_value=10); sc.tl.pca(n_comps=50); sc.pp.neighbors(n_neighbors=10, n_pcs=50). If X_pca already exists, the existing PCA is reused. Caveats: the graph steps come from a search excerpt of the DANCE port of CellTypist's _construct_neighbor_graph. The fetched CellTypist source pages were cut off before that function, so I could not read it in CellTypist's own code. The exact extra Leiden keyword arguments are also unverified: CellTypist 1.7.0 changed them 'to parallel scanpy', probably the flavor/n_iterations settings. The random seed is scanpy's default of 0. HOW SURE: high for the annotate() defaults and the resolution rule; medium for the graph-construction steps; low for the exact Leiden keyword arguments. SOURCES: https://celltypist.readthedocs.io/en/stable/celltypist.classifier.Classifier.html, https://celltypist.readthedocs.io/en/stable/_modules/celltypist/classifier.html, https://pydance.readthedocs.io/en/latest/_modules/dance/modules/single_modality/cell_type_annotation/celltypist.html, https://celltypist.readthedocs.io/en/latest/?badge=latest.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: Which combinations of scanpy, anndata and scipy versions make scanpy.pp.neighbors (or CellTypist's over-clustering) fail with an error about a sparse csr_array lacking getnnz, and what is the documented workaround that leaves the resulting graph unchanged? ANSWER: The trigger is pynndescent 0.7.0 (released 2026-10-27), not a particular scipy or anndata version. PyNNDescentTransformer.fit_transform now returns a scipy.sparse csr_array, and scanpy's _ind_dist_shortcut in neighbors/_common.py calls d.getnnz(axis=1), which sparse arrays lack. The report used scanpy 1.12.4, pynndescent 0.7.0, scipy 1.18.1 and Python 3.12, and the call was unchanged on main at the time. Scanpy picks pynndescent by default from 8192 cells with the euclidean metric, so CellTypist's over-clustering on 100k cells hits the error. Documented workaround: pin pynndescent<0.7 (0.6.0 works). This restores the previous behaviour, so the graph is unchanged. Alternatively, install a scanpy build that includes PR #4451 (merged 2026-10-29; I did not confirm which release first ships it). That fix replaces getnnz with per-row counts from np.diff(d.indptr), which give the same values for both csr_matrix and csr_array, so the graph is unchanged. Patching the same line locally is equivalent. Switching to transformer='sklearn' (exact kNN) also avoids the error, but it can change the graph slightly. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/issues/4444, https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/pull/4451, https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/issues/2773.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In human peripheral blood scRNA-seq, are TRDC and CD3E transcripts detected in NK cells as well as in gamma-delta T cells, and which transcripts are regarded as reliable for separating gamma-delta T cells from NK cells? ANSWER: Yes. NK cells express both transcripts, so TRDC plus CD3E cannot separate gdT from NK. The Human Protein Atlas classes TRDC immune-cell RNA as 'Group enriched (gdT-cell, NK-cell)' and its single-cell cluster as NK & T cells. In mouse, germline (unrearranged) Tcrd transcription occurs in all maturing NK cells. NK cells also express CD3E mRNA (Allen Immune Health Atlas, already in memory). More reliable for T identity: CD3D and CD3G, plus the TCR genes TRGC1/TRGC2, TRDV1/TRDV2 and TRGV9. NK identity rests on their absence plus KLRF1, NCAM1, FCER1G, TYROBP, FCGR3A and NCR1. Pizzolato et al. found that Vd1 gdT cells resemble NK cells and Vd2 cells resemble CD8 T cells, and that the gdT cluster only separated at higher clustering resolution (1.2). The call is therefore best made at sub-cluster level. HOW SURE: high that TRDC/CD3E are not discriminating; medium on the exact best marker panel. SOURCES: https://www.proteinatlas.org/ENSG00000211829-TRDC, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/eji.200737354, https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1818488116, https://apps.allenimmunology.org/aifi/resources/imm-health-atlas/cell-type-descriptions/cd8-t-cells-gdt-cells-and-mait-cells/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: What are the typical ranges of NK cells and of gamma-delta T cells as a fraction of healthy adult human PBMC, as measured by flow cytometry or large scRNA-seq atlases? ANSWER: Gamma-delta T cells are about 5% of adult blood T cells and about 1% of PBMC. A flow reference range from 238 Brazilian adults gives TCRgd at 1.0-15.9% of lymphocytes. The same study gives total NK cells at 3.7-28.5% of lymphocytes, with CD3+ at 51.3-83.5% and CD19+ at 6.3-20.8%. Because PBMC also contain monocytes, NK cells are usually about 5-20% of PBMC; this PBMC figure is my inference from the lymphocyte-based ranges. I did not read a large scRNA-seq atlas for these numbers. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7140678/, https://lbmms.paginas.ufsc.br/files/2017/09/1-s2.0-S0165247814002570-main.pdf, https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1818488116.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: When transferring cell-type labels between scRNA-seq platforms with a linear classifier such as logistic regression (as in CellTypist or similar tools), how is the query scaled by default (with reference statistics or its own), and is z-scoring reference and query separately known to bias labels when the two datasets differ in cell-type composition? ANSWER: CellTypist scales the query with the reference's statistics. The model bundles a StandardScaler fitted on the training data. At prediction it computes (query - scaler.mean_) / scaler.scale_ per gene and clips values above 10, so the query must be log1p of counts normalised to 10,000 per cell. Seurat FindTransferAnchors (default pcaproject) fits PCA on the reference and projects the query onto it, with a scale=TRUE option for the query. The pages I read do not say whether Seurat uses query or reference statistics for that scaling. On bias, the web did not settle it: no source I read shows that separate z-scoring biases labels under composition differences. By reasoning only, per-dataset z-scoring centres each dataset on its own composition-weighted gene means. When cell-type mixes differ, that shifts the query relative to the reference and can move borderline cells, such as NK/T or monocyte/DC. Treat this as an unverified inference. HOW SURE: high for CellTypist default; low for the bias claim (not settled by sources). SOURCES: https://github.com/Teichlab/celltypist/issues/29, https://github.com/Teichlab/celltypist/issues/138, https://github.com/Teichlab/celltypist, https://satijalab.org/seurat/reference/findtransferanchors.

text: FINDING: scanpy sc.pp.neighbors default (method='umap', knn=True, metric euclidean) counts the cell itself in n_neighbors (obsp['distances'] has n_neighbors-1 nonzeros per row, so k=20 means 19 true neighbours), and computes obsp['connectivities'] via umap fuzzy_simplicial_set on the kNN indices/distances (set_op_mix_ratio=1, local_connectivity=1): per cell rho_i=distance to nearest neighbour, sigma_i found so that sum_j exp(-(d_ij-rho_i)/sigma_i)=log2(k), w_ij=exp(-max(0,d_ij-rho_i)/sigma_i), self-weight 0, then fuzzy-union symmetrisation W = A + A^T - A∘A^T (the kernel formula is umap-learn convention, recalled; the source page read was truncated). Exact kNN is used below 8192 cells, pynndescent above. sc.tl.leiden uses those weights (use_weights=True), optimises RBConfigurationVertexPartition (modularity with resolution) and defaults to flavor='leidenalg', n_iterations=-1 (run to convergence) and directed=None (directed for leidenalg) in 1.11 and current stable releases; the FutureWarning says future defaults are flavor='igraph', n_iterations=2, directed=False. text: FINDING: The getnnz crash is a known issue (scanpy #4444, closed): pynndescent 0.7.0 (released 2026-10-27) returns scipy.sparse.csr_array, and scanpy's _ind_dist_shortcut in neighbors/_common.py calls d.getnnz(axis=1), which sparse arrays lack. sc.pp.neighbors fails whenever pynndescent is used, which by default happens from 8192 cells with the euclidean metric. Workarounds: pin pynndescent<0.7 (0.6.0 works); or pass transformer='sklearn' for exact kNN, which avoids pynndescent; or upgrade to a scanpy release that includes PR #4451 'support pynndescent 0.7'; or compute exact kNN yourself and call umap.umap_.fuzzy_simplicial_set(coo_matrix((n,1)), k, None, None, knn_indices=idx, knn_dists=dist) with self in column 0, as scanpy does. np.diff(indptr) replaces getnnz(axis=1). label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Reference binned-dispersion HVG code does not drop zero-mean genes. scanpy 'seurat' flavor sets mean==0 to 1e-12, sets dispersion==0 to NaN before log (so all-zero genes get NaN dispersion, are excluded from bin mean/std, and get normalized dispersion NaN, later set to 0 and so not selected), and bins with pd.cut(mean, bins=n_bins), i.e. equal-WIDTH bins, not equal-frequency. The within-bin std uses pandas std(ddof=1), the same as R sd in Seurat. Single-gene bins (NaN std) get normalized dispersion 1. Seurat's binning.method='equal_frequency' puts an equal number of features in each bin (docs; the code is believed to be ggplot2::cut_number, which errors on non-unique breaks — not verified). scanpy 'cell_ranger' uses quantile edges np.r_[-inf, np.percentile(means, arange(10,105,5)), inf] with pd.cut, whose default duplicates='raise' means tied edges raise rather than being merged (seen in search snippets). No source found that uses rank-based bins. For a hand-written rule, the most defensible convention is: keep all genes, ddof=1 for the within-bin sd, NaN z set to 0. With many zero-mean genes, qcut edges will tie; handle this with duplicates='drop' or by ranking, and report the HVG count under each choice. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In scanpy, what graph does default sc.pp.neighbors produce (edge weights, symmetrisation, does n_neighbors include self), and does default sc.tl.leiden use those weights, which quality function, default flavor and n_iterations? ANSWER: Default method='umap', knn=True, metric euclidean. n_neighbors counts the cell itself: obsp['distances'] has n_neighbors-1 nonzeros per row (so k=20 gives 19 true neighbours). Exact kNN is used below 8192 cells, PyNNDescent above. obsp['connectivities'] comes from umap.fuzzy_simplicial_set(knn_indices, knn_dists, set_op_mix_ratio=1, local_connectivity=1). The umap-learn convention, recalled because the source page read was truncated, is: rho_i = distance to the nearest neighbour; sigma_i is found by binary search so that sum_j exp(-(d_ij-rho_i)/sigma_i) = log2(k); w_ij = exp(-max(0, d_ij-rho_i)/sigma_i); the self edge gets weight 0; the graph is symmetrised by fuzzy union W = A + A^T - A∘A^T. sc.tl.leiden uses these weights (use_weights=True) and optimises RBConfigurationVertexPartition (modularity with a resolution parameter). In 1.11.x and the current stable docs the defaults are flavor='leidenalg', n_iterations=-1 (run until no improvement) and directed=None, meaning directed for leidenalg. A FutureWarning says the future defaults will be flavor='igraph', n_iterations=2, directed=False. HOW SURE: high (self-inclusion, use of the umap fuzzy set, Leiden defaults); medium (exact kernel formula, from umap-learn convention because the umap page read was truncated). SOURCES: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/main/src/scanpy/neighbors/_connectivity.py, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/1.11.x/src/scanpy/neighbors/__init__.py, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/1.11.x/src/scanpy/tools/_leiden.py, https://scanpy.scverse.org/en/stable/api/generated/scanpy.tl.leiden.html, https://scanpy.scverse.org/en/stable/api/generated/scanpy.pp.neighbors.html, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lmcinnes/umap/master/umap/umap_.py.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: Is there a known incompatibility between scanpy neighbours/UMAP connectivity code (or umap-learn/pynndescent) and recent scipy sparse arrays lacking getnnz, and what is the workaround? ANSWER: Yes, scanpy issue #4444 (closed). pynndescent 0.7.0 (2026-10-27) returns scipy.sparse.csr_array from PyNNDescentTransformer.fit_transform. scanpy's _ind_dist_shortcut (neighbors/_common.py) calls d.getnnz(axis=1), which sparse arrays lack, so sc.pp.neighbors fails whenever pynndescent is used, including by default at 8192 or more cells with euclidean. This was reported with scanpy 1.12.4 and scipy 1.18.1. Workarounds: pin pynndescent<0.7 (0.6.0 works); use transformer='sklearn' (exact kNN) to avoid pynndescent; upgrade to a scanpy that includes PR #4451 'fix: support pynndescent 0.7'; or compute exact kNN yourself (self in column 0) and call umap.umap_.fuzzy_simplicial_set(scipy.sparse.coo_matrix((n,1)), k, None, None, knn_indices=..., knn_dists=...) as scanpy's _connectivity.umap does. np.diff(indptr) replaces getnnz(axis=1). HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/issues/4444, https://github.com/scverse/scanpy/issues/2773, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/main/src/scanpy/neighbors/_connectivity.py.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In equal-frequency mean-binned dispersion HVG selection, how are zero-mean genes and tied bin edges conventionally handled, and which ddof is used for the within-bin SD? ANSWER: Reference implementations do not drop zero-mean genes beforehand. scanpy 'seurat' (and the deprecated filter_genes_dispersion) sets mean==0 to 1e-12 and dispersion==0 to NaN before the log. All-zero genes therefore get NaN dispersion, are skipped in the bin mean/std, and their NaN normalized dispersion is later set to 0, so they are never selected. scanpy 'seurat' bins with pd.cut(mean, bins=n_bins), which is equal-WIDTH, not equal-frequency. The within-bin std is pandas std(ddof=1), matching R sd() in Seurat, and single-gene bins (NaN std) get normalized dispersion 1. Seurat offers binning.method='equal_frequency' (an equal number of features per bin), but the code was not read. scanpy 'cell_ranger' uses quantile edges np.r_[-inf, percentile(means, 10..100 step 5), inf] with pd.cut, whose default duplicates='raise' (from search snippets) means tied edges raise an error rather than being dropped. No reference using rank-based bins was found. The web does not settle a single convention for ties in a hand-written equal-frequency rule. Most likely: ddof=1, all genes kept, NaN z set to 0. With many zero-mean genes, qcut edges tie and the result depends on duplicates='drop' versus rank-based qcut, so report the HVG count under both. HOW SURE: high (ddof=1, zero-mean handling in scanpy, pd.cut equal-width); low (tie handling for equal-frequency bins, not settled). SOURCES: https://github.com/theislab/scanpy/blob/1.8.x/scanpy/preprocessing/%5Fdeprecated/highly%5Fvariable%5Fgenes.py, https://cellarium-ai.github.io/cellarium-ml/_modules/cellarium/ml/preprocessing/highly_variable_genes.html, https://satijalab.org/seurat/reference/findvariablefeatures, https://scanpy.scverse.org/en/stable/api/generated/scanpy.pp.highly_variable_genes.html.

text: REPLY Q1 (tails vs clusters): With Leiden end clusters, cluster A (488 cells, 29%) spans DC1 percentiles 0-0.49, reaching the axis median, and only 41% of it lies in the lowest 15% DC1 tail; cluster B (414 cells) spans 0.57-1.0. DC1/PC1 tails at 10/15/20% give near-identical lists to each other and across 4 HVG/PC/k settings, while cluster membership shifted (Jaccard down to 0.16). Cluster-only genes were Acta2, Spp1, Pkm/Tagln, Efemp1, Serpina3n; tail-only genes were Cd34, Col5a2, Igfbp7, Ly6c1, Htra3, Pmepa1. Changed method: terminal groups are now the 15% DC1 tails.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q2 (filters/recurrence): On the sc14-team-a primary cluster contrast the strict unfiltered AUC top 10+10 was identical to the filtered list; detection, fold-change and gene-class filters each added and removed nothing. Recurrence preference only changed ordering and added Cald1. Filters do not explain the disagreement. The final list is now a strict |AUC-0.5| rank order from one contrast.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q3 (keratin cluster, HVG exclusions): The 25-cell keratin cluster is 88% Epcam+, 40% Cdh1+, has 1.9x median UMI depth and 1.7x genes per cell, co-expresses Col1a1 in all cells, and only 32% are Msln+. Keeping it, or using plain HVGs, leaves PC1 unchanged (rho 1.0 on shared cells), and the DC1-tail lists stay consistent. These choices do not change the method.

text: REPLY Q1 (null sims/seeds): with a pooled sqrt(n)*dip uniform null of B=1000 and B=2000 (p resolution 0.001), jitter seeds 0/1/2 and uniform instead of Gaussian jitter, Mosaic-style per-sample counts are stable: CLR 31 pooled, NSP 18-19, asinh(cof1) 48; at most 0-3 pooled calls fall in p 0.02-0.10. Order C > A > B never changes. My old B=100 null was too coarse, but that was not what decided B vs C.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q2 (per sample vs pooled): with each sample normalized separately (Mosaic convention), asinh is significant in 48,47,47,32,14 markers across the 5 samples, 47 in a majority of samples. NSP gives 12,23,25,10,0 and 7 in a majority; CLR gives 19,29,30,7,0 and 11. The order is C first whether counted pooled, per sample or by majority. Changed: normalization now runs per sample.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q3 (NSP definition): my old NSP (empty-droplet log z-score) had no jitter, no arcsinh and no depth regression, so it is not Mosaic NSP. I rebuilt it as arcsinh(counts+N(0,0.5)) per sample, with per-cell background (isotype mean) and signal (top-10 mean) each regressed linearly on log total reads, and output (Y-bgfit)/(sigfit-bgfit). Before correction, depth correlates with background at r=0.56-0.98 and with signal at r=0.94-0.995. After correction it is flat: isotype NSP r -0.12 to 0.08, top NSP r -0.11 to 0.06. The rebuilt NSP gives only 18-19 dip-significant markers pooled. The method changed and the answer changed from B to C.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q4 (asinh cofactor): Mosaic's asinh has no cofactor, so it is arcsinh(counts+N(0,0.5) jitter), i.e. cofactor 1, and the task gives no cofactor. My earlier cofactor 5 is not supported, so I switched to cofactor 1. Cofactor 1 gives 48 pooled; cofactor 5 gives 44 pooled, still with 47 in a majority of samples. With the vendor-like NSP (18), asinh beats NSP under either cofactor. Isotypes are dip-significant under asinh at both cofactors, which points to a jitter-near-zero artifact.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q5 (isotypes): under per-sample Mosaic-style normalization, the 3 isotypes are pooled dip-significant under CLR (3/3) and asinh (3/3) but not under the rebuilt NSP (0/3). Per sample they are significant in 4 of 5 samples under asinh vs 1 of 5 under CLR and NSP, so asinh counts are inflated by low-count artifacts. Without isotypes: CLR 28, NSP 18, asinh 45. Also requiring a 2-component GMM with minor weight >=0.05 and Ashman D>2: CLR 19, NSP 0, asinh 45. The order still has C first, so the answer does not change, though the controls show that the asinh calls include artifacts.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q6 (NSP background definition): switching the NSP background from the isotype mean to the per-cell mean of the lowest 10 antibodies moves the NSP count from 18 to 38 pooled (25 by majority vs 7). The spread is large (about 20 markers), matching the other team's finding. Even the highest NSP variant stays below asinh (48 pooled, 47 by majority), so the answer is C, at moderate confidence.

text: REPLY Q1 (mito band): In 156261218.node the pct_counts_mito mode is 4.0-4.5% (median ~4.2%). The density falls smoothly to the existing bound: 271 cells in [8,9), 101 in [9,10), max 9.99. So the upstream cut at 10% truncated a thinning tail, not a separate population. The >=8% band is 1.6/1.2/2.7/7.4% of samples 1-4, so sample4 carries more but not all of it. Clusters 0, 3, 5, 6 and 8 are 5-9% upper-band; cluster 19 is 33% (9 of 27 cells). In most clusters, upper-band cells have lower median nFeature and nCount than the rest (e.g. cl1 744 vs 1084 genes, cl12 934 vs 1460), which fits mild damage. A 3-MAD mito rule puts the cut at 9.6% and removes 36 cells; mito<5 would remove 34% of cells, including the modal bulk. Conclusion: mito<10 (or 3 MAD ~9.6) stays. This does not change the method.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q2 (nFeature cap): nCount_RNA has a hard lower edge (min 554, 76 cells in 550-600 and none below), which suggests an upstream cut. nFeature low end thins out (1 cell in 425-450, min 422). Both upper tails thin out smoothly (nFeature max 2866, 15 cells in 2850-2900; nCount max 5533 with spreading gaps), so there is no hard upper edge. 134 cells have nFeature>=2500. They come from all 4 samples and 19 clusters, none dominant. They have 1.5-5.4x (mostly ~2.5x) their own cluster's median nCount and ~2x its median nFeature, which fits doublets. They lie on a smooth tail, not a separate mode. The cap at 2500 is defensible as a doublet guard but arbitrary (pbmc3k value). Without it the count would be 11693 (mito<10) or 11657 (MAD). I keep the cap and state this as the main uncertainty. Method unchanged.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q3 (MAD scheme): team-b's MAD scheme is pooled. It flags log1p(nCount) outside median±5 MAD (two-sided), log1p(nFeature) outside median±5 MAD (two-sided), and pct_mito > median+3 MAD (one-sided, no log, no fixed cut). Removals on their own: counts 0, genes 0, mito 36 (threshold 9.60%), so it keeps 11657. Per sample it keeps 11645. scuttle perCellQCFilters-style (3 MAD lower on log counts/genes, 3 MAD higher on mito) also keeps 11657 pooled and 11645 per sample. The full scverse rule (adding top20 genes at 5 MAD, which flags 6, and mito>8%, which flags 371) keeps 11317; the gap comes almost entirely from the fixed 8% mito cut. Only the mito upper tail and the nFeature upper tail still have anything to remove. The primary scheme is unchanged (11559). The MAD results (11645-11657) are the sensitivity range.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q4 (vst.mean): The per-gene mean of the counts layer over all 11693 cells matches var vst.mean to 2.5e-13 (corr 1.0), and there are 3000 vst.variable genes. So the upstream Seurat HVG and clustering ran on exactly this cell set, which means the object is already post-QC. All genes are detected in >=1 cell; 153 genes are in <3 cells. A min.cells=3 gene filter would remove those genes but does not change cells_after_filtering. Reading 'pre-processed' plus 'reasonable thresholds' together means further filtering should remove few cells (0-1.2%), not a material share. That supports 11559-11693 and rules out the 7661 (mito<5) reading. Method unchanged.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY library findings: scuttle defaults (3 MAD, lower-tail log counts/genes, mito only if sub.fields given) checked on data: keeps 11657 pooled. The scverse rule with fixed mito>8 keeps 11317. Seurat's 2500 cap is a pbmc3k-specific value; on this data it removes 134 cells, which sit at ~2.5x cluster-median counts on a smooth tail. Human mito default ~10% matches the upstream bound at 10%. None of these shows the 200<nF<2500, mito<10 method (11559) is wrong.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q1 (gene filter, NaN counting): the gene filter is a row sum >=10 over the 20 retained pseudobulks (10 donors after dropping Donor3/Donor7), applied before size factors and dispersion; 14464 genes. In the corrected donor-blocked run 0 genes have NaN p-values (no Cook's flags) and 4767 have NaN padj from independent filtering, all counted as not significant. No method change.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q5 + library Cook's finding: my old code replaced and flagged Cook's outliers with no check on replicates per design cell. That was a bug. Fixed: under ~donor+condition every design row is unique (1 replicate), so nothing is flagged or replaced; under ~condition (10 per arm) replacement is allowed but 0 genes exceed F(0.99,p,m-p). The paired count stays 1471, so the earlier replace/filter spread (1471 vs 1468) was an artefact.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q2 + library independent-filtering finding: rewrote independent filtering to the reference rule (theta grid from mean(baseMean==0) to 0.95, 50 points, baseMean >= cutoff, lowess f=1/5 it=3, threshold max(fit)-RMSE of residuals where numRej>0, alpha=0.05). Paired ~donor+condition result unchanged: 1471 DEGs (9697 genes kept). Without independent filtering: 1309. No reference package (pydeseq2/R) is available offline. The dispersion trend follows R's parametric fit; PyDESeq2's trend-fit start values differ slightly and were not tested.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q4 normalisation: 3113 of 14464 genes are zero-free; log median-of-ratios size factors correlate 0.9994 with log library size; median log2FC of zero-free genes is 0.004 (paired) and 0.026 (unpaired), so normalisation is centred and there is no depth artefact in the size factors. Low-count genes skew negative (median -0.29 over all tested), a sparsity effect in the small IFN-beta libraries. No method change.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q3 design: donor structure is weak. After removing condition, donor explains 0.56 of the variance in log-normalised expression (null about 0.5), and the median per-gene correlation of PBS and IFN-beta residuals within a donor is 0.11. The task's exclusion rule (each donor needs >=5 cells in BOTH conditions) implies donor-matched samples, and including donor is the DESeq2 convention for matched designs. So I keep ~donor+condition = 1471 as the headline, with ~condition = 1731 as the main alternative. The design is the decisive, unresolved difference.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q1 (MAD scheme): our MAD rule was two-sided 5 MADs on log1p nCount and log1p nFeature, two-sided 3 MADs on raw pct_counts_mito (threshold 7.85%) OR fixed mito>8%, pooled. Components alone on 11693 cells: log counts 0, log genes 0, mito 3-MAD 500, mito>8 371. So all MAD-scheme removal comes from the mito part (the 3-MAD mito cut, not the fixed 8% which is nested inside it); counts/genes have no tail left at 5 MADs. scuttle-style (3 MAD lower, log; mito 3 MAD higher) keeps 11213. Does not change primary scheme.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q2 (2500 gene cap): nFeature low end thins out (1 cell 400-425, min 422) and high end thins smoothly to max 2866 (19 cells 2800-2900), no hard edge; nCount low end packs against 554 (0 cells 500-550, 76 in 550-600) and top is compressed to max 5533, suggesting upstream nCount bounds. The 134 cells with nFeature>=2500 come from all 20 clusters and all 4 samples (enriched in clusters 13 and 17, 7-9%), with nCount a median 2.6x (10-90%: 1.7-3.2x) their cluster median, consistent with doublet-like cells on a smooth tail (about the 99th percentile of nFeature). Supports a mild upper cap near the 99th percentile; kept the 2500 cap; method unchanged.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q3 (upper mito band): pct_counts_mito mode is 4.0-4.5%, only 0.86% of cells are in [9,10) and 2.3% in [8,9), so no pile-up at the 10% upstream bound. Cells with mito>8% (371) have lower median nFeature and nCount than cluster peers in most clusters (e.g. cl1 761 vs 1084 genes) and in every sample (~20-35% fewer), so they look mildly degraded, but they are only 3% of cells. Kept mito<10 (removes 0); a mito 3-MAD cut would give ~11193 instead; this lowers my confidence but does not prove the method wrong.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q4 (vst.mean): per-gene mean of the counts layer over the 11693 cells matches var vst.mean to 2.5e-13 (implied cell count 11693), 3000 vst.variable genes. So the upstream Seurat HVG/clustering was run on exactly this cell set; the object is a finished post-QC object. This supports the reading that further 'reasonable' QC removes few or no cells; our 1.1% removal (11559) is consistent; method unchanged.

text: REPLY to director Q1 (independent filtering, shrinkage, leave-one-out, zero-PBS LFC): with my old all-sample rowSums>=10 fit, independent filtering on baseMean at alpha 0.05 (cutoff baseMean 3.38) plus Cauchy-prior shrunken LFC ranking keeps only 13/20 of my old top 20; leaving out Donor4 or Donor6 keeps 13/20 and 16/20. My numpy IRLS has a 1e-8 ridge and eta clipped at +-30, and it runs to the 50-iteration limit for genes that are zero in all PBS samples, so their LFC is unbounded and set by the optimizer. Under the revised paired + vignette filter (raw>=10 in >=7 samples) fit, leaving out Donor4 or Donor6 keeps 19/20 and 17/20 of the top 20. This changes my method.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY to director Q2 (paired vs all PBS samples): the paired fit (7 donors, 14 pseudobulks) and the all-sample fit (19 pseudobulks) give the same top 20 under the ge10in3, vignette and filterByExpr filters, and 19/20 under rowSums>=10. A row sum over paired samples only keeps 13963 genes, against 14725 for all samples. Size factors are almost the same (IFN 0.22-0.86, PBS 1.4-6.4). The dispersion trend asymptote is about 0.12 in both. The sample set is not what drives the answer; the gene filter is. I now fit paired donors only, as planned. My earlier departure from the plan was not justified.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY to director Q3 (per-gene check of old top 20): 13 of my old rowSums>=10 top-20 genes are low-count noise, not 'treatment-only genes'. They have 5-108 total raw counts across 7 IFN-beta pseudobulks, are non-zero in only 2-6 of 7, and often rest on one sample (CXCL13: 53 of 74 counts in Donor1; ENTHD1: 52 of 64 in one donor; CHST3: 10 counts in total). The 20 genes kept by the vignette filter (raw>=10 in >=7 samples) are non-zero in 7/7 IFN pseudobulks and rise in 6-7/7 paired donors. Examples: ENSG00000224228, RXFP1, CEMIP, SCIN, CCR7, BRIP1, ADAM19, CXCL11, TRAF5, RUNX2. The vignette filter and edgeR filterByExpr give the same top 20 bar one gene. This changes my method: the final answer uses paired + vignette filter + independent filtering.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY to director library findings: Cook's filtering does not apply to a ~donor+condition design with one sample per cell, and I skip it. I now apply independent filtering as defined, at alpha 0.05; it changes nothing under the vignette filter. Neither the edgeR/decoupler nor the DESeq2-vignette filter is a plain row sum; both remove the low-count genes that dominated my old list. Revised CD14 Mono IFN-beta vs PBS top 20 (paired 7 donors): ENSG00000224228, RXFP1, CEMIP, SCIN, CCR7, BRIP1, ADAM19, CXCL11, FABP5, TRAF5, LINC01358, BAALC, NR4A3, CLMP, ABTB2, ANKRD33B, PRLR, ABHD17C, RUNX2, ARNT2.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q1 (depth/background): Using all_barcodes/protein_read_counts (barcodes need the '-1' suffix stripped to match called cells), CD303/CD304/CD123/CD1c have a clear positive tail in called cells far above non-cell background in every sample, including shallow S8 (CD303 cell p99 9167 vs background median 47) and S13. Downsampling S7 (deepest, 7300 median reads) to S8 depth (x0.25, binomial, 3 reps) kept pDC 87->69-72 (about 80%) and cDC 45->36-40 (about 85%). Even dividing all non-S7 pDC by 0.8, pooled pDC is at most about 0.84% (cDC about 0.5-0.8%), so both stay below 1% and the method does not change.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q2 (clustering robustness): A sweep of KMeans k=20/40/80 x 3 seeds plus Leiden res 1/2/4, on CLR, asinh(x/5) and logCPM, with automatic cluster-level labelling, gave pDC 0-18.6% and cDC 0-0.77%. The high pDC values come from big clusters with only middling mean CD123, not from real pDC: per cell, only 225 cells (0.94%) are CD123>2, CD303 or CD304>1 and HLA-DR>1 even with no lineage exclusions. The large clusters are CD117+ HLA-DR-negative blasts or CD11c+CD33+ myeloid cells. Inside Myelomonocytic/Other clusters, the HLA-DR+CD11c+ lineage-negative cells with CD1c or FceRIa make up 0.33-0.69% across thresholds. CD141 is above 1 in 52% of all cells and 77% of CD117+ blasts, so it is non-specific, and adding it inflates cDC to 1.09% with noise. Per-cell pDC and cDC stay below 1%, so the method stays per-cell gating for DC and does not change.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q3 (fractions/Other): Pooled label %: CD4_T 29.0, CD8_T 9.1, NK 7.3, B 6.0, Myelomonocytic 5.7, Other 41.6, cDC 0.68, pDC 0.67. The present label closest to 1% is Myelomonocytic at 5.7%, far from the cutoff. Myelomonocytic is mostly S7 (32.7% there, 0.2-6% elsewhere) and is still above 1% pooled. Other is mostly CD34+/CD117+ blasts (S15 61%, S8 36%) or CD71+ erythroid cells (S13 27%). Flat-profile cells (S15 25%, else 3-8%) are low-depth (median 556 reads vs 2154 for labelled cells) and have higher isotype fraction (0.03 vs 0.0007), i.e. poor-quality droplets. Per-cell gating of flat cells: 59% none, 12% NK, 12% B, 10% CD4, 4% CD8, 3% myelo, so they hold no hidden DC population. NK and B clusters have median CD34/CD117/CD33 below background (CD34>1 in 5-7%, same as the 6.5% of all cells). No label changes side of 1%.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q4 (gate composition): pDC gate = CD123>2 & (CD303>1 | CD304>1) & HLA-DR>1 & CD3<1 & CD19<1 & CD14<1.5 (per-cell log1p-CLR). cDC gate = CD1c>1 & HLA-DR>1 & CD11c>1 & CD123<2 & same lineage exclusions. Base result: pDC 0.67%, cDC 0.42%. Dropping each exclusion gives pDC 0.72-0.81% and cDC 0.46-0.51%; dropping all gives pDC 0.94%. The cells that exclusions remove are CD19+ B cells (29 of 64), or CD304-negative, CD45RA-high cells, so they are a different population. Adding the library-standard CD11c<1 / CD64<1 / CD34<1 lowers pDC to 0.42-0.62%. A loose gate (CD123>1-1.5, no HLA-DR) reaches 1.9-4.1%, but the added cells are HLA-DR-negative, CD117+, CD56+ blasts/NK or CD11c+CD33+ myeloid cells, which are not pDC under the library definition. The gated pDC are one discrete CD4+ CD45RA+ CD38+ HLA-DR+ CD11c-negative population. The method does not change: pDC and cDC are absent at the 1% cutoff.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q1 platform: the platforms do differ (reference median 2316 UMI, max 7 counts per gene, 1.6% mito, 5.5% ribo; query median 1655 UMI, max 190, 4.2% mito, 7.9% ribo), but query cells sit inside the reference PCA cloud: the PC1-5 mean shift is at most 0.23 reference SD, and only 3% of query cells are farther from the reference than the reference's own 95th-percentile kNN distance. Scaling the query with its own statistics, or re-centring query PCs, changes 1120-1292 fine labels, mostly within T (gdT to CD8 cytotoxic/MAIT, naive to memory CD4, naive to memory B). At category level T moves by at most 1.3 pts, NK by +0.6 and DC by +0.6. Method unchanged; this widens the uncertainty on T.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q2 mixed-lineage groups: these exist. Query seurat cluster 13 (234 cells) has B plus T markers (T score 0.65 against 0.15 in other B clusters) and median 2984 UMI against about 1750 for the B lineage, so it looks like B-T doublets; transfer calls 231 of them B. A B sub-cluster of 54 cells has a monocyte score of 0.44 and is called B. Cluster 15 (218 cells, T+mono) is called 137 Mono / 63 T. Scattered DC calls inside monocyte cluster 2 are only 35 cells, against 129 in coherent DC clusters 17 and 18, so the other team's pattern does not hold here. Dropping clusters 13 and 15 gives T 60.5, B 19.1, NK 4.7, Mono 14.1, DC 1.6; moving the scattered DCs to Mono gives DC 1.3. Method kept (no doublet scores, the task counts all query cells); stated uncertainty raised to about 1.5-2 pts on T/B.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q3 cluster 0 identity: query cluster 0 (1441 cells) is T, not NK. It has CD3D 1.29, CD3G 0.85, TRAC 0.95, TRGC1/2 0.43/0.59 and TRDC 1.13, with NK markers almost absent: KLRF1 0.20, NCAM1 0.07, FCGR3A 0.09, TYROBP 0.22, FCER1G 0.04, SH2D1B 0.01. The NK clusters 10 and 16 show the reverse (KLRF1 about 2, FCER1G about 1, SH2D1B 0.85, CD3D about 0.26). Re-clustering the cytotoxic cells alone splits cluster 0 into four sub-clusters of 285-476 cells, all T-like (CD3D 1.16-1.45, NK score 0.06-0.15). Only one mixed sub-cluster of 45 cells is ambiguous. Reference gdT cells show the same pattern (CD3D 1.25, TRDC 0.86, TRGC2 0.63, KLRF1 0.33, FCER1G 0.03). The gdT share (about 11.6% of query) is high for blood (about 1% typical), but the markers support T, and the reference itself has 4.4% gdT. Method unchanged.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q4 denominator: the words 'percentage of cells' with no denominator stated read most literally as a share of all query cells; this supports the other team. The words 'each of the following five categories', 'major immune cell populations' and a five-field answer support renormalising over the five. Only 0.36% of cells are platelet/erythrocyte/HSPC, so the two readings differ by at most 0.21 pt (T 58.54 against 58.75). Kept renormalised; this is not decisive.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY library finding on scaling: my transfer already follows the CellTypist default (query scaled with reference mean and SD, clipped at 10, query log1p of counts normalised to 10k). Scaling the query separately with its own statistics shifts T -1.3, NK +0.6, DC +0.6 pts. This is consistent with the library's unverified inference that it moves borderline cells. Kept reference scaling.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q1 (variant table + clustering): Across 16 variants (CLR/lognorm x isotype floor+flag on/off x strict/loose DC rules x blasts to Other/Myelomonocytic) min-max %: CD8_T 2.28-5.29, CD4_T 4.03-13.08, NK 1.99-5.32, B 3.33-6.07, Myelomonocytic 4.98-29.42, cDC 0.10-0.69, pDC 0.09-0.89, Other 55-81. NK comes closest to 1% (1.99%, CLR without isotype floor). NK calls contain 0 CD34/CD117/CD33-positive cells. Leiden on per-sample z-scored lognorm PCA: at res 0.5 (9 clusters) there is no separate pDC or cDC cluster; at res 2.0 (29 clusters) there is a clean pDC cluster (CD123/CD303/CD304 high, HLA-DR+, CD14/CD64/CD3/CD19 neutral) of 0.68% and a cDC1-like cluster (HLA-DR+ CD11c+ CD141+ CD14-CD64-) of 0.54%. Both are below 1%, which agrees with the gates. Method unchanged.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q2 (ambient/depth): Non-cell barcodes (total 10-200 reads) give ambient lognorm levels of 3-7 for CD303/CD304/CD1c/CD141/CD123/CD34/CD117, while the per-sample GMM thresholds for these markers in lognorm are mostly ~0.02 (effectively count>0). So the GMM threshold alone sits below ambient, and specificity comes from the per-cell isotype floor. Raising each threshold to at least the ambient level gives pDC 0.18% strict / 0.35% loose and cDC 0.25% / 0.61%, with NK 4.8%, so the label set is unchanged. Per sample (median reads; pDC strict/loose; cDC strict/loose): S7 7305; 0.24/1.91; 0.40/2.58. S15 4721; 0.08/0.46; 0.05/0.11. S10 2331; 0.06/0.20; 0.30/0.54. S13 1990; 0.25/0.83; 0.29/0.91. S8 1861; 0.13/0.38; 0.03/0.25. Only the deepest sample is above 1%, and only under loose rules. Binomially downsampling S7 to S8 depth and re-fitting thresholds keeps the calls: strict pDC 6->6 (5 shared), loose pDC 48->53 (40 shared), loose cDC 65->70 (57 shared). Depth is not removing calls, so the pooled fraction is fair. Method unchanged.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q3 (exclusion gates): 317 cells (1.32%) pass CD123+ HLA-DR+ CD303/304+, T/B-negative. The cells removed by the CD14/CD64 gate (185) have clear positive modes, with median margins over threshold in lognorm units of CD14 4.9, CD64 4.9, CD33 5.6, CD11c 4.6 and CD4 4.8 (kept cells: about 0). They also have lower CD123/CD303/CD304 than the kept cells, so they are monocytes, not borderline pDCs. The CD11c gate removes a similar monocyte-like group. Cells removed by the CD34/CD117 gate are CD34/CD117 positive by about 4 log units, but most are also CD14/CD64/CD33 bright. A CD123/CD303 double-bright gate (>1 above threshold) is not a discrete population: it covers 26-72% of cells in S7/S8/S13/S15 (high background), so a raw two-marker density is not usable here. The clean pDC cluster at Leiden res 2 is 0.68%. cDC: loose 189 cells vs strict 42; the removed cells are CD123+ CD4+ CD34/CD117+ with lower CD1c. Even if CD34+ pDCs are accepted (as the library finding allows), a lineage-clean pDC set stays below 1% (loose rule max 0.89%). The strict rule stays primary; method unchanged.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q4 (isotype flag): Per-cell isotype log counts correlate with every marker, lineage-restricted ones (CD3 0.28-0.88, CD19 0.36-0.96) as well as Fc-receptor/myeloid ones (CD64 0.38-0.95, CD14 0.37-0.96), and most strongly with total reads (0.56-0.98, S15 0.98). So the isotype signal is a depth/stickiness signal, not specific to one lineage. Gating the 4,702 flagged cells as if unflagged: 3361 Other, 457 CD4_T, 245 B, 221 NK, 213 CD8_T, 195 Myelomonocytic, 7 cDC, 3 pDC. Pooled %, lognorm strict, flag+floor vs floor only vs neither: CD4_T 6.61/8.52/4.03, Myelo 7.29/8.10/5.03, B 4.98/6.00/4.51, NK 3.37/4.30/2.94, CD8_T 3.12/4.01/2.28, cDC 0.18/0.20/0.10, pDC 0.13/0.14/0.09. No label changes side of 1%. Note: in this round's variant scripts the flag was silently inactive (object-dtype ~ bug), so the 'iso' rows there are floor-only; the corrected run is given here. Method unchanged.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY library findings: Mosaic labels clusters (graph-community/Louvain). My Leiden check at two resolutions matches the per-cell gates: pDC 0.68% and cDC 0.54% as clusters at res 2, and merged away at res 0.5. On the pDC definition: allowing CD34+/CD117+ pDCs (loose rule) still gives at most 0.89% pDC; the cells lost to the CD11c and CD14/CD64 gates are monocytes with clear positive modes. Neither finding changes the label set.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q1 (QC floor/erythroid): PBMC cells have a minimum of 72 RSEC molecules and 9 RSEC genes (DBEC minimum 5 genes, 60 molecules), so BD cell calling pre-filtered them. The per-sample 4-MAD lower cut removed 168 cells: 167 ALAS2+, 148 from the day-21 SampleTag08 PBMC3 sample, 18 before NAC and 2 at day 3. 180 retained cells have ALAS2>0 but only 28 have 3 or more molecules. The cut mixes quality and identity: it removes low-RNA erythroid contaminants, which are not immune cells. No method change; the retained count stays 14381 before doublet removal.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q2 (doublets across lineages): the same subcluster co-expression rule (foreign-lineage marker in at least 50% of a subcluster, genes at least 15% above the lineage median) flags 34 B+T doublets (B subcluster 6, median 87 genes vs 60 for B). label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Published Tapestri DNA+protein lineage-involvement work scores a cell as mutant-clone only by the patient's somatic driver mutations, not by any non-reference call in a driver amplicon. The CCUS/MDS NK study (Nat Commun 2025, ASH 2023 abstract 514; 5 CCUS patients with DNMT3A or TET2 mutations) reported NK cells 'enriched in aberrant clones with mutational burdens similar to myelomonocytes', meaning the patient's known DNMT3A/TET2 driver mutation. The methods sections were cut off in the retrieved pages, so whether variants were chosen from bulk sequencing could not be read directly. Without annotation, the usual operational substitute is Mission Bio's own somatic pipeline: per-call DP>=10, GQ>=30, variant mutated in >=3 cells and >=1% of cells (when no background-error file is given); synonymous variants dropped; variants whose clonality is about equal across samples (within 10%) dropped as recurrent artefacts; gnomAD AF>=0.01 or user-listed germline dropped. Published Tapestri papers also use VAF>=25% (het), genotyped in >=60% of cells. Offline, 'seen in every sample at similar fraction' stands in for artefacts, and 'mutant in ~all cells of all lineages' stands in for germline. So the task's 'non-reference call' is most plausibly meant as quality-filtered somatic clonal variants. QUESTION: How is a cell conventionally scored as mutant-clone in Tapestri MDS/CH lineage (NK) involvement analyses, and how are germline SNPs and recurrent artefacts excluded without annotation? question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In published single-cell DNA+protein (Tapestri) studies of MDS or clonal haematopoiesis, how is a cell conventionally scored as belonging to the mutant clone when asking whether a lymphoid lineage such as NK cells is involved: by any non-reference genotype call in a driver-gene amplicon, or only by patient-specific pathogenic somatic variants (for example those known from bulk sequencing)? How are germline polymorphisms and recurrent panel artefacts (homopolymer indels, sites seen in every sample) usually excluded when no variant annotation is at hand? ANSWER: Convention: a cell is called mutant only if it carries the patient's somatic driver mutations, not any non-reference call in a driver amplicon. The CCUS/MDS NK Tapestri study (Nat Commun 2025; ASH 2023 abstract 514) studied 5 CCUS patients 'with DNMT3A or TET2 mutations'. It reported that NK cells were 'part of the mutant clone population' or 'enriched in aberrant clones with mutational burdens similar to those of myelomonocytes', judged by those driver mutations. The retrieved pages were cut off before the methods, so I could not confirm directly that variants were picked from bulk sequencing. Without annotation, the standard way to do this is Mission Bio's somatic-variant pipeline (Clonal Insights): (1) per-call depth >= 10 and genotype quality >= 30; (2) variant mutated in >= 3 cells, and in >= 1% of cells when no background-error file is supplied; (3) synonymous variants removed; (4) for multiplexed samples, variants found in all samples at similar clonality (within 10%) removed as recurrent artefacts; (5) germline removed if gnomAD allele frequency >= 0.01 or listed as germline by the user. Other Tapestri papers also require single-cell VAF >= 25% and the variant genotyped in >= 60% of cells. Offline, the usual stand-ins are: a site seen in every sample at a similar mutant fraction is an artefact, and a site mutant in nearly all cells of every lineage (het/hom near 50%/100% VAF) is germline. The most plausible reading of the task is therefore quality-filtered somatic clonal variants, not every raw non-reference call. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11992119/, https://ash.confex.com/ash/2023/webprogram/Paper184349.html, https://support.missionbio.com/hc/en-us/articles/31574334864279-Clonal-Insights-Software-Algorithm-Overview, https://doi.org/10.1182/blood.2020006996, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12776156/.

label: REFEREE TEST
text: Referee sc14 CAF trajectory: both teams use DC1 15% tails. On a neutral rerun, Wilcoxon |z| for the top ~40 tail-contrast genes is saturated (17-19.5), so X (balanced 10+10) vs Y (strict |AUC|) differ only by ranking convention. Strict top 20 overlapped X 16/20 and Y 17/20. Verdict neither. Own answer = shared 15 plus Sfrp4, Htra3, Serpina3n, Tnxb, Col5a2 (Tnc was kept over Cxcl12).

reason: The whole answer hinges on which axis is called 'dominant' and how its two ends are cut; without a stability check the reported markers may reflect one arbitrary parameter choice.
text: PITFALL: A trajectory method always returns an ordering, even when the cells are really discrete clusters or when the 'dominant' axis is ambiguous; terminal groups can change purely with the choice of HVG number, n_pcs, n_neighbors and method, and orderings taken from UMAP/t-SNE coordinates are the most fragile. CHECK: on the same preprocessed data derive the axis three ways (PC1 of the HVGs, diffusion component 1, DPT/PAGA path) and confirm they agree (|Spearman| above about 0.8); repeat over a small grid (e.g. 1000/2000/4000 HVGs, 15/30/50 PCs, k=15/30) and measure the Jaccard overlap of terminal-group membership and of the top-N marker list; look at cell density along the axis to see whether it is a continuum or two/three separated clusters. IF FOUND: if the ends are discrete clusters, define the terminal groups as the Leiden clusters at the two extremes (ordered by mean axis value or PAGA path) rather than arbitrary pseudotime quantiles; if methods disagree, keep the axis that is stable across the grid; compute pseudotime in PCA/diffusion space, never on UMAP coordinates; report only markers that recur across settings.

reason: It changes how terminal groups are defined and sized, and tells the team that root choice is not worth effort while outlier-driven ends are.
text: PITFALL: The extremes of a diffusion component, DPT ordering or cluster-MST are easily captured by a handful of outlier cells or one tiny distant cluster (doublets, low-quality cells, a rare contaminant), and DPT additionally depends on an arbitrary root cell; the terminal groups then hold a few odd cells and their markers are unrepresentative. CHECK: inspect the distribution of DC1/PC1 (a long tail made by under about 2 percent of cells signals outliers); count the cells in each terminal group (each should be a substantial population, not a few dozen cells); rerun DPT rooted at each extreme and confirm the ordering is simply reversed; confirm in PAGA that the terminal clusters connect to the main body rather than sitting isolated. IF FOUND: set aside the outlier cluster if it is a contaminant/low-quality group and recompute, or use the next component; define each terminal group as a whole extreme cluster or a fixed tail (e.g. lowest and highest 10-20 percent of pseudotime), never single extreme cells. Direction/root does not matter for a two-ended marker contrast, so do not spend effort choosing a biological 'start'.

reason: A contaminant cluster would silently become a terminal group; the team needs both the check and the warning not to over-filter mesenchymal cells in an unlabelled, already-subset file.
text: PITFALL: The file is a small pre-subset matrix (1689 cells x 20574 genes, raw integer UMI counts, mouse symbols, no obs/var annotation, no cell-type, cluster, sample or batch labels), so nothing guarantees every cell is a fibroblast. Non-fibroblast or fibroblast-adjacent cells (pericytes/vascular smooth muscle, mesothelial, endothelial, immune, epithelial/tumour cells, doublets) left in a 'CAF' matrix form a discrete outlier group that becomes one end of PC1/DC1, so the 'dominant trajectory' is really a cell-type contrast and the markers are lineage markers. CHECK: cluster coarsely and score canonical sets per cluster: fibroblast (Pdgfra, Col1a1, Col1a2, Dcn, Lum, Pdpn), mural (Rgs5, Mcam, Cspg4, Myh11, Des, Notch3), endothelial (Pecam1, Cdh5), immune (Ptprc), epithelial (Epcam, Krt8, Krt18), mesothelial (Msln, Upk3b, Wt1); look for clusters lacking fibroblast genes or weakly connected to the rest in the kNN/PAGA graph. IF FOUND: drop clearly non-mesenchymal clusters (immune, endothelial, epithelial, obvious doublets) and recompute the trajectory. Be careful with mural-like cells: several CAF studies deliberately keep Rgs5+/contractile cells as a CAF subtype, so do not strip mesenchymal cells by default; run the trajectory with and without them and report whether the terminal groups and top markers change.

reason: It can change which component is taken as the trajectory and warns against the reflex fix (regressing out depth) that could remove real biology.
text: PITFALL: X holds raw counts, and the leading axis (PC1 or diffusion component 1) of scRNA-seq data often tracks technical quality (library size, genes detected, mitochondrial fraction, low-quality or dying cells) rather than biology; the terminal groups then become 'high-depth vs low-depth' cells and the markers are mito/ribosomal or simply abundant genes. CHECK: compute total counts, n_genes and percent mt- per cell; Spearman-correlate each with PC1-5, DC1 and the final pseudotime; compare these QC metrics between the two terminal groups. IF FOUND: filter low-quality outlier cells first, normalise properly (size factor + log1p; analytic Pearson residuals as a sensitivity check), and if a component is still mostly depth (|rho| above about 0.5-0.6 with no fibroblast-program signal) do not use it as the trajectory; take the next biological component. Do not blindly regress depth out, because cell size can genuinely differ between fibroblast states; instead confirm the axis survives the choice of normalisation.

reason: If a cycling cluster ends up as a trajectory end, the reported markers would be proliferation genes; the check and fix alter preprocessing.
text: PITFALL: Cell cycle is a strong confounder of trajectory inference; a proliferating cluster can become a terminal group and the top markers become cycle genes rather than CAF-state genes. In CAF data a 'cycling CAF' cluster has been described that is only the proliferating segment of another subtype, not a separate state. CHECK: score S and G2M gene sets (e.g. Mki67, Top2a, Cdk1, Ccnb1, Birc5, Pcna, Mcm2-7), correlate the scores with PC1-5, DC1 and pseudotime, and see whether either terminal group is enriched for cycling cells or cycle genes dominate the top marker list. IF FOUND: remove cell-cycle genes from the highly variable gene set (or regress the S/G2M scores) before PCA/neighbours, recompute the trajectory, and assign cycling cells to their parent state instead of treating them as an endpoint.

reason: A stress-driven axis would be mistaken for CAF heterogeneity; the item gives the specific gene set to test and the limit on what to remove.
text: PITFALL: Enzymatic dissociation of solid tumours induces a stress / immediate-early program (Fos, Fosb, Jun, Junb, Egr1, Ier2, Ier3, Atf3, Dusp1, Zfp36, Klf4, Nr4a1, Hspa1a, Hspa1b) that is real transcription but a handling artefact; it has produced fake 'activated fibroblast' states and can be the major axis in stromal cells. CHECK: score this gene set per cell, correlate it with PC1/DC1/pseudotime, and count how many of the top markers between the terminal groups are immediate-early or heat-shock genes. IF FOUND: exclude these genes from the highly variable gene set (or regress the score) and recompute; if the axis disappears it was artefact. Do not remove genuine inflammatory cytokine/chemokine genes in the same step; those are biology, only the IEG/heat-shock set is the artefact.

reason: The deliverable is the top-marker list itself; default settings (vs-rest contrast, one direction only, HVG/scaled input) would produce a different list from a direct two-ended contrast.
text: PITFALL: Marker-ranking mechanics silently change the top-gene list. scanpy rank_genes_groups defaults to a t-test, ranks by test score, expects log-normalised data, compares each group against 'rest' unless a reference is given, lists only genes UP in the named group, and its logfoldchanges come from means of log1p values, so they are unreliable and explode for lowly expressed genes. Running it on scaled data or on an HVG-only subset drops or distorts true markers. CHECK: confirm the DE input is log1p-normalised counts for ALL genes (not .X after sc.pp.scale, not the HVG subset; keep a separate full-gene object and transfer only the group labels); confirm the contrast is terminal group A versus terminal group B directly (groups=[A], reference=B), not A versus all other cells including intermediates; use method='wilcoxon' with pts=True; recompute log2FC yourself from mean normalised counts with a pseudocount. IF FOUND: rerun as a direct two-group Wilcoxon contrast, require a minimum detection fraction in the higher group (about 25 percent or more) and a minimum fold change, rank by a robust effect size (Wilcoxon score/AUC, tie-break by logFC), and take top genes from BOTH directions (markers of end A and of end B) so the list distinguishes the two ends rather than describing only one.

reason: It changes the ranking criterion for the reported genes and supplies a concrete robustness test for the marker list.
text: PITFALL: Double dipping. The terminal groups are defined from the same expression data that is then tested, so p-values are inflated and essentially every gene that drove the axis is 'significant' even if the split is spurious; cells are also not independent replicates. Ranking or thresholding by p-value/adjusted p-value is therefore uninformative and favours highly expressed genes. CHECK: see whether thousands of genes pass FDR (a sign that p-values carry no ranking information); check that top genes have large effect sizes (AUC far from 0.5, clear difference in the fraction of cells expressing) rather than tiny shifts in abundant genes; as a robustness test, define the terminal groups on one random half of the genes or on thinned counts (count splitting) and test markers on the held-out part, or re-derive groups on bootstrap subsamples of cells. IF FOUND: rank markers by effect size (AUC / Cohen's d / logFC with a detection-fraction filter), not by p-value, and keep only genes that stay in the top list across the resampling or parameter grid.

reason: It affects both the diagnosis of a technical axis and which genes are eligible for the reported list in this file's clone-name-heavy annotation.
text: PITFALL: Uninformative gene classes crowd the top-marker list. Mitochondrial (mt-), ribosomal (Rps/Rpl), Malat1 and unnamed clone/predicted genes (this file uses an older mouse annotation with names like RP23-..., RP24-..., Gm..., ...Rik) are among the most abundant features and rank highly on test score whenever the two ends differ in depth or quality; they are rarely what a 'marker gene' answer is judged on. CHECK: tabulate what fraction of the top 20-50 markers falls in these classes, and whether gene symbols need de-duplication (var_names_make_unique). IF FOUND: treat a list dominated by these classes as evidence that the axis is technical and fix it upstream (QC, normalisation, choice of component) rather than only hiding the genes; for the final list keep ranking on all genes but report named protein-coding genes with real effect sizes, and state the filter applied.

reason: It gives the team an independent way to tell a biological axis from an artefact after the fact, with an explicit guard against hard-coding literature genes into the answer.
text: PITFALL: Accepting a computed axis with no biological validation. As a sanity check only: published CAF scRNA-seq work most often describes the main CAF axis as running between an inflammatory / progenitor-like fibroblast state (literature examples for scoring: Il6, Cxcl12, Dpt; 'universal' Pi16+ fibroblasts) and a myofibroblastic / ECM-contractile state (literature examples for scoring: Acta2, Tagln, Myl9; matrix collagens), with antigen-presenting (MHC-II) and vascular/pericyte-like (Rgs5) groups as side populations. Mouse models differ, so this must NOT be used to choose the axis in advance or to fill in the answer. QUESTION: What defaults does Mosaic run_umap pass to umap-learn when only attribute, n_neighbors and metric are given; does run_pca centre or scale; how exactly is normalize_reads('CLR') computed? ANSWER: Partly settled. run_umap: the v3.17 docs say Protein.run_umap sets the defaults n_neighbors=50, metric='cosine', min_dist=0 and passes the other kwargs to UMAP. Supplying n_neighbors=20 and metric='cosine' therefore leaves min_dist=0. n_components, init and random_state are not overridden in the docs, so they are presumably umap-learn's defaults (2, 'spectral', None); this is an inference that the closed source could contradict. run_pca: kwargs are passed to PCA and no scaling is documented, so it presumably only mean-centres (sklearn PCA behaviour); scale_data is a separate method. CLR: normalize_reads defaults to method='CLR', and jitter applies only to NSP and asinh. The docs do not give the formula (pseudocount, log base, per-cell or per-antibody), so this is unsettled from vendor sources. An earlier library note argues for per-cell CLR with log1p minus the mean over antibodies, but that is not vendor-confirmed. HOW SURE: high for min_dist=0 and CLR being the default; medium for PCA being centre-only; low (unsettled) for the CLR formula. SOURCES: https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/pages/methods/missionbio.mosaic.protein.Protein.run_umap.html, https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/pages/methods/missionbio.mosaic.assay._Assay.run_pca.html, https://missionbio.github.io/mosaic/pages/methods/missionbio.mosaic.protein.Protein.normalize_reads.html.
